specificity.statement: These steps are consistent with requiring our science system to be productive, to be efficient, to be sustainable, and to generate real value for New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues (productive, efficient, sustainable, real value) with no figures, mechanisms, or named steps.

specificity.statement: No, I’m encouraged by the last Stats NZ report that actually showed there was more scientists than we had previously and also new opportunities for science through the new emerging technologies: the Institute for Advanced Technology, through artificial intelligence, through quantum, through magnetic materials, through Robinson, and the $42 million by Biodiscovery Platform.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete initiatives and a $42m Biodiscovery Platform figure, though no detail on the job cuts at issue.

specificity.statement: I reject that member’s assertions, but, again, I return to the fact that the science system will need to be productive, efficient, financially sustainable, and generate real value for New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Vague platitudes with no figures, names, or commitments.

specificity.statement: No New Zealander wants to see children living in poverty. Again, that is why this Government is doing everything it can to grow the economy.
specificity.explanation: 'Doing everything it can to grow the economy' names no mechanism, target, or measure.

specificity.statement: Well, again, this Government’s actions to control spending and lower inflation is incredibly helpful for Kiwis that have been doing it tough: 3.1 percent inflation is better than 7.3 percent; nine interest rate falls are better than 12 interest rate rises; economic growth in the last quarter of 1.1 percent is better than a shrinking economy.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete figures: 3.1% vs 7.3% inflation, nine vs twelve interest moves, 1.1% quarterly growth.

specificity.statement: Currently, the savings provision in this bill only captures individuals who have lodged an appeal with the Social Security Appeal Authority or courts prior to the date of introduction. I am now proposing to also capture individuals who have made an application to MSD for a review of decision to the benefits review committee that has not been decided before the date of introduction.
specificity.explanation: Precise legislative mechanism: who the savings provision captures and exactly how the proposed amendment widens it.

specificity.statement: ACC deducts the full main benefit paid by MSD from the back-pay, sends that money to MSD, and the injured person gets what’s left. MSD then treats the lump sum as income and moves to recover all payments it has made, not just the main benefits.
specificity.explanation: Lays out the ACC/MSD recovery mechanism step by step.

specificity.statement: Our proposed solution going forward is that we can only continue to support this bill if it is changed so that MSD has clear discretion not to recover supplementary payments where that would be unfair and unequitable.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete change (MSD discretion in hardship/fairness cases) as a condition, though without drafting detail.

specificity.statement: This bill only came through because Community Law Centres Aotearoa, alongside others, challenged this unlawful practice in the High Court. The High Court agreed with people who fought the system. The High Court actually ruled in favour of them and said, and I quote, “The recipient of the supplementary assistance needed, and was eligible for, that assistance at the time.
specificity.explanation: Names the litigant, the forum, and quotes the ruling.

specificity.statement: Despite these hurdles, we had hundreds of written submissions, and less than 0.1 percent—only two submissions—were in favour of the bill.
specificity.explanation: Gives a percentage and an absolute count (two submissions).

specificity.statement: it was introduced during urgency and, as a concession, was given a one-week select committee process—two days for members of the public to make submissions, two days to ask survivors of sexual violence to put their thoughts on paper and to contribute to this bill
specificity.explanation: Concrete process detail: urgency, one week, two days for submissions.

specificity.statement: I also want to acknowledge that, yes, there are more than 37,000 people who will be affected by this change, but it’s important that we make this change right now, before more people come into this group. We don’t want more and more people being impacted because the policy is not delivering what it intends to deliver.
specificity.explanation: Names the affected population but is general about what 'making this change right now' concretely entails.

specificity.statement: And people should be receiving no more or no less; they should be receiving what they’re entitled to receive, and that is what this bill will do.
specificity.explanation: States a principle (entitlement parity) but no mechanism or figures for how the bill achieves it.

specificity.statement: I had the privilege, last week, to sit in these hearings and listen to the hearings of eight oral submissions, we received over 855 submissions in total.
specificity.explanation: Concrete counts of oral and total submissions.

specificity.statement: What this relates to is those 37,000-odd cases that this High Court judgment has made between 1998 and 2025 is captured.
specificity.explanation: Gives a case count and a date range.

specificity.statement: but we could actually look in the committee of the whole House stage of actually widening that out so those who were already engaged in the review process—that would actually gain those people into that.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the savings-provision issue to widen, though without precise drafting.

specificity.statement: I think the majority of the paybacks were something like under $2,000—what is a sum of money for anyone to pay back—but the rate of that payback will definitely depend on the individual person’s circumstances.
specificity.explanation: Offers a dollar threshold for the typical payback.

specificity.statement: We’d seen the event in Levin where seven people, including two police officers, were injured.
specificity.explanation: Names the place and exact injury counts.

specificity.statement: It will produce and introduce a presumptive sentence in favour of forfeiture or forfeiture and destruction of vehicles involved in street racing, fleeing police, burnouts, and failing to provide details to help identify offenders.
specificity.explanation: Precise legal mechanism (presumptive sentence of forfeiture/destruction) and the offences it covers.

specificity.statement: And it will increase the fine for excessive noise from vehicles through speakers and sirens from an infringement fee of $50—rima tekau tāra—to $300. The maximum court fine will increase from $1,000 to $3,000—more than the price of a Crusaders and Chiefs game.
specificity.explanation: Exact before/after figures for both the infringement fee and the maximum court fine.

specificity.statement: I want to be clear that this bill does not target legitimate car enthusiasts and legal car meets, like that big—
specificity.explanation: Draws the scope line (illegal antisocial events only) but the example is cut off.

specificity.statement: if someone fails to provide that information without good reason, then the outcome could be that that vehicle is impounded for a 28-day period.
specificity.explanation: States the precise consequence and duration (28-day impoundment) of the new disclosure duty.

forthrightness.statement: No, I’m encouraged by the last Stats NZ report that actually showed there was more scientists than we had previously and also new opportunities for science through the new emerging technologies: the Institute for Advanced Technology, through artificial intelligence, through quantum, through magnetic materials, through Robinson, and the $42 million by Biodiscovery Platform.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he takes responsibility for job cuts caused by underfunding; he answers 'No' but then pivots to positive news rather than engaging the underfunding charge.

forthrightness.statement: I reject that member’s assertions, but, again, I return to the fact that the science system will need to be productive, efficient, financially sustainable, and generate real value for New Zealanders.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked where the next round of job losses will come from; gives no answer and retreats to repeated talking points.

forthrightness.statement: Considering we’re still progressing through the science reforms, that’s a decision and an analysis to be had at the end of the reforms, but I have high expectations and I’m encouraged by the reforms to date.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the Parliamentary Commissioner's warning was proven right; defers the judgement to a later point rather than addressing it now.

forthrightness.statement: No New Zealander wants to see children living in poverty. Again, that is why this Government is doing everything it can to grow the economy.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he thinks New Zealanders are comfortable with 12–14% child poverty; sidesteps the comfort question and pivots to the economy.

forthrightness.statement: It has no doubt been a very difficult and tough time for many New Zealanders, and that is why, if you care about low and middle income working New Zealanders, you run the economy; you don’t create high inflation and put an economy into recession.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to describe the choices hardship whānau face; does not describe them and pivots to a critique of the previous government.

forthrightness.statement: Well, that’s why this Government’s working incredibly hard to control spending so we lower inflation, lower interest rates, get the economy growing, and get people into work.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the Children's Commissioner that children cannot wait for the economy to improve; does not engage the urgency point and returns to economic talking points.

forthrightness.statement: Well, again, this Government’s actions to control spending and lower inflation is incredibly helpful for Kiwis that have been doing it tough: 3.1 percent inflation is better than 7.3 percent; nine interest rate falls are better than 12 interest rate rises; economic growth in the last quarter of 1.1 percent is better than a shrinking economy.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether any of his Government's policies contributed to rising child material hardship; never addresses that and deflects to favourable macro figures.

veracity.statement: No, I’m encouraged by the last Stats NZ report that actually showed there was more scientists than we had previously and also new opportunities for science through the new emerging technologies: the Institute for Advanced Technology, through artificial intelligence, through quantum, through magnetic materials, through Robinson, and the $42 million by Biodiscovery Platform.
veracity.explanation: Claims a Stats NZ report shows more scientists than before; plausible but not verifiable from the text and used selectively against a job-cuts question.

veracity.statement: When he cut Callaghan Innovation, ransacked the Marsden Fund, and is now cutting 134 jobs from the new science institute, where can New Zealanders expect the next round of job losses to come from?
veracity.explanation: The factual scaffolding (cuts to Callaghan, Marsden changes, 134 jobs) is broadly grounded, but 'ransacked' is hyperbolic and overstated.

veracity.statement: Well, again, this Government’s actions to control spending and lower inflation is incredibly helpful for Kiwis that have been doing it tough: 3.1 percent inflation is better than 7.3 percent; nine interest rate falls are better than 12 interest rate rises; economic growth in the last quarter of 1.1 percent is better than a shrinking economy.
veracity.explanation: The headline figures are directionally consistent with NZ data of the period, though presented as a favourable comparison that dodges the hardship question.

veracity.statement: Does he think New Zealanders are comfortable with the 12 to 14 percent of our children—roughly the population of Tauranga—living in poverty?
veracity.explanation: The 12–14% child-poverty range and the Tauranga-population comparison are broadly accurate framings.

veracity.statement: ACC deducts the full main benefit paid by MSD from the back-pay, sends that money to MSD, and the injured person gets what’s left. MSD then treats the lump sum as income and moves to recover all payments it has made, not just the main benefits.
veracity.explanation: A detailed description of the inter-agency arrangement; plausible and committee-sourced but a contested characterisation.

veracity.statement: This bill only came through because Community Law Centres Aotearoa, alongside others, challenged this unlawful practice in the High Court. The High Court agreed with people who fought the system. The High Court actually ruled in favour of them and said, and I quote, “The recipient of the supplementary assistance needed, and was eligible for, that assistance at the time.
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific High Court ruling and quotes from it to support the claim the practice was unlawful.

veracity.statement: Despite these hurdles, we had hundreds of written submissions, and less than 0.1 percent—only two submissions—were in favour of the bill.
veracity.explanation: A specific, falsifiable claim about submission counts consistent with the rushed-process account; not independently confirmed here.

veracity.statement: it was introduced during urgency and, as a concession, was given a one-week select committee process—two days for members of the public to make submissions, two days to ask survivors of sexual violence to put their thoughts on paper and to contribute to this bill
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable claims about urgency and the truncated one-week committee timetable.

veracity.statement: I see that there were more than 800 submissions. So we can’t say that, because of the select committee, it didn’t receive submissions—for submissions, that number looks quite reasonable to me, and I would say that that is reflective of what people would have otherwise said.
veracity.explanation: The 800+ submissions figure is consistent with other members' counts.

veracity.statement: I also want to acknowledge that, yes, there are more than 37,000 people who will be affected by this change, but it’s important that we make this change right now, before more people come into this group. We don’t want more and more people being impacted because the policy is not delivering what it intends to deliver.
veracity.explanation: The 37,000-affected figure aligns with other speakers' numbers.

veracity.statement: I had the privilege, last week, to sit in these hearings and listen to the hearings of eight oral submissions, we received over 855 submissions in total.
veracity.explanation: Specific first-hand figures (eight oral submissions, 855 total) consistent with other members' accounts.

veracity.statement: What this relates to is those 37,000-odd cases that this High Court judgment has made between 1998 and 2025 is captured.
veracity.explanation: Cites the ~37,000 cases and a 1998–2025 window; broadly consistent with the debate's figures.

veracity.statement: I think the majority of the paybacks were something like under $2,000—what is a sum of money for anyone to pay back—but the rate of that payback will definitely depend on the individual person’s circumstances.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a 'majority under $2,000' figure to MSD evidence; specific but hedged ('something like') and unverified here.

veracity.statement: We’d seen the event in Levin where seven people, including two police officers, were injured.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable incident claim (Levin; seven injured, two officers).

veracity.statement: I also thank the committee chair and the rest of the Justice Committee for their swiftness, their pace, as they reported back two months earlier than scheduled.
veracity.explanation: Specific claim that the committee reported back two months early; plausible and falsifiable, not confirmed here.

veracity.statement: but Judith Collins indicated that when that law was brought in, there would be more than 10 vehicles a year that would actually be crushed. Now, when we look at the reality around how many were actually crushed, you only need one hand, excluding the thumb, and you’d have one spare finger, to come up with the number of vehicles that actually went through this process.
veracity.explanation: The claim that very few vehicles were ever crushed under the earlier crusher law is broadly consistent with the historical record.

civility.statement: When he cut Callaghan Innovation, ransacked the Marsden Fund, and is now cutting 134 jobs from the new science institute, where can New Zealanders expect the next round of job losses to come from?
civility.explanation: Loaded question; 'ransacked' is sensationalising rather than engaging the substance, though aimed at policy not character.

civility.statement: It has no doubt been a very difficult and tough time for many New Zealanders, and that is why, if you care about low and middle income working New Zealanders, you run the economy; you don’t create high inflation and put an economy into recession.
civility.explanation: An implied jab at opponents' economic management, but framed around policy (inflation, recession) rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: Does he think New Zealanders are comfortable with the 12 to 14 percent of our children—roughly the population of Tauranga—living in poverty?
civility.explanation: Pointed but policy-focused; challenges on substance (child poverty) without personal attack.

civility.statement: I respect and thank the members of the select committee, who worked diligently to ensure that we were able to improve the bill.
civility.explanation: Respectful, cross-party acknowledgement of the committee's work.

civility.statement: We don’t want MSD sending—and this is how bad it could get—in debt collectors to hound that woman and to hound that whānau who are just in struggle street—just in struggle street. So we need to be supportive of that whānau. We need to show some humanity here.
civility.explanation: Impassioned and hyperbolic but directed at the policy's human impact, not at opponents personally.

civility.statement: I will say there’s been some goodwill from the Minister and also goodwill in terms of the committee that worked, I think, well on this over the last week, even though we all have different philosophical positions.
civility.explanation: Generous, respectful framing of opponents despite disagreement.

civility.statement: This is such a perfect example of the Government not wanting the public to know that they have been trampling over tens of thousands of people who are living, often, in deep poverty, waiting for their ACC claims to come through, and who have been unlawfully put in debt for decades.
civility.explanation: Imputes a bad-faith motive ('not wanting the public to know') and uses charged language ('trampling over').

civility.statement: it was introduced during urgency and, as a concession, was given a one-week select committee process—two days for members of the public to make submissions, two days to ask survivors of sexual violence to put their thoughts on paper and to contribute to this bill
civility.explanation: Sharp process critique that is largely factual rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: For the Minister to claim that this is some great concession is a joke, when she knows—and legal experts and survivors have told her—that this bill leaves tens of thousands of people with debts that diminish their ability to make ends meet
civility.explanation: 'Is a joke' belittles the Minister and asserts she knowingly acts against the evidence.

civility.statement: History tells me that this is not a Minister that has previously engaged constructively in these debates.
civility.explanation: A personalised criticism of the Minister's conduct rather than engagement with her arguments.

civility.statement: I want to start by conveying my gratitude to the Social Services and Community Committee because, I must say, they have worked really hard with the time constraint that they had. I also want to acknowledge the clerk of the committee, because I know they do a lot of work in the background.
civility.explanation: Respectful, gracious acknowledgement of the committee and staff.

civility.statement: I also thank the committee chair and the rest of the Justice Committee for their swiftness, their pace, as they reported back two months earlier than scheduled.
civility.explanation: Cross-party thanks to the committee, focused on their work.

strength.statement: Currently, the savings provision in this bill only captures individuals who have lodged an appeal with the Social Security Appeal Authority or courts prior to the date of introduction. I am now proposing to also capture individuals who have made an application to MSD for a review of decision to the benefits review committee that has not been decided before the date of introduction.
strength.explanation: A concrete amendment actually proposed through the select committee process, but follow-through (passage) is still in progress.

strength.statement: Our proposed solution going forward is that we can only continue to support this bill if it is changed so that MSD has clear discretion not to recover supplementary payments where that would be unfair and unequitable.
strength.explanation: A conditional commitment tabled in committee; delivery depends on whether the amendment is adopted.

strength.statement: It will produce and introduce a presumptive sentence in favour of forfeiture or forfeiture and destruction of vehicles involved in street racing, fleeing police, burnouts, and failing to provide details to help identify offenders.
strength.explanation: A concrete measure being legislated, but at second reading it is enacted-in-progress rather than delivered.

charisma.statement: I respect and thank the members of the select committee, who worked diligently to ensure that we were able to improve the bill.
charisma.explanation: Gracious tone that credits others, mildly bridge-building.

charisma.statement: So Labour’s prepared to work with National on this, but it has to be with the wellbeing of people at the centre.
charisma.explanation: Explicit cross-party offer to cooperate while stating a condition; consensus-seeking.

charisma.statement: I will say there’s been some goodwill from the Minister and also goodwill in terms of the committee that worked, I think, well on this over the last week, even though we all have different philosophical positions.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges goodwill from opponents and shared work across philosophical divides; consensus-building.

charisma.statement: I urge my Labour colleagues to stop supporting this bill, and to stand on the right side of history and vote it down at this second reading.
charisma.explanation: A rallying appeal to allies framed in moralising 'right side of history' terms; persuasive to one's own side rather than bridge-building.

charisma.statement: I want to start by conveying my gratitude to the Social Services and Community Committee because, I must say, they have worked really hard with the time constraint that they had. I also want to acknowledge the clerk of the committee, because I know they do a lot of work in the background.
charisma.explanation: Warm, inclusive opening that credits others' work.

charisma.statement: but we could actually look in the committee of the whole House stage of actually widening that out so those who were already engaged in the review process—that would actually gain those people into that.
charisma.explanation: Signals openness to amend the bill to address submitters' concerns at the next stage; constructive.

charisma.statement: I want to be clear that this bill does not target legitimate car enthusiasts and legal car meets, like that big—
charisma.explanation: Reassures a group worried about the bill, addressing civil-liberties concerns rather than dismissing them.

rigor.statement: We don’t want MSD sending—and this is how bad it could get—in debt collectors to hound that woman and to hound that whānau who are just in struggle street—just in struggle street. So we need to be supportive of that whānau. We need to show some humanity here.
rigor.explanation: Persuades chiefly through an emotive worst-case anecdote ('hound that woman') rather than data.

rigor.statement: ACC deducts the full main benefit paid by MSD from the back-pay, sends that money to MSD, and the injured person gets what’s left. MSD then treats the lump sum as income and moves to recover all payments it has made, not just the main benefits.
rigor.explanation: Builds a clear causal chain to its conclusion that injured people pay for their own rehab.

rigor.statement: This is such a perfect example of the Government not wanting the public to know that they have been trampling over tens of thousands of people who are living, often, in deep poverty, waiting for their ACC claims to come through, and who have been unlawfully put in debt for decades.
rigor.explanation: Asserts hidden intent rather than evidencing it, though the underlying 'unlawful debt' claim is grounded later.

rigor.statement: This bill only came through because Community Law Centres Aotearoa, alongside others, challenged this unlawful practice in the High Court. The High Court agreed with people who fought the system. The High Court actually ruled in favour of them and said, and I quote, “The recipient of the supplementary assistance needed, and was eligible for, that assistance at the time.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in a court finding rather than assertion; evidence-based.

rigor.statement: Despite these hurdles, we had hundreds of written submissions, and less than 0.1 percent—only two submissions—were in favour of the bill.
rigor.explanation: Uses submission data to argue the bill lacks support, though near-unanimous submitter opposition is not the same as the bill being wrong on the merits.

rigor.statement: I see that there were more than 800 submissions. So we can’t say that, because of the select committee, it didn’t receive submissions—for submissions, that number looks quite reasonable to me, and I would say that that is reflective of what people would have otherwise said.
rigor.explanation: Counters the rushed-process objection, but 'reflective of what people would have otherwise said' is an unsupported assumption that more time would not have changed input.

rigor.statement: I also want to acknowledge that, yes, there are more than 37,000 people who will be affected by this change, but it’s important that we make this change right now, before more people come into this group. We don’t want more and more people being impacted because the policy is not delivering what it intends to deliver.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable urgency argument, but asserts the policy 'is not delivering its intent' without supporting detail.

rigor.statement: And people should be receiving no more or no less; they should be receiving what they’re entitled to receive, and that is what this bill will do.
rigor.explanation: A fairness-to-entitlement framing that assumes, rather than demonstrates, the bill produces that outcome.

rigor.statement: but Judith Collins indicated that when that law was brought in, there would be more than 10 vehicles a year that would actually be crushed. Now, when we look at the reality around how many were actually crushed, you only need one hand, excluding the thumb, and you’d have one spare finger, to come up with the number of vehicles that actually went through this process.
rigor.explanation: Tests a prior prediction against the actual outcome (10+/year predicted vs roughly four delivered) to argue this bill may be similarly unworkable.

divination.statement: the real risk is that the community will think that there is going to be this mass level of crushing going on and the forfeiture of vehicles, but it’s going to be very easy for people to plead hardship and get out of it.
divination.explanation: Predicts hardship exemptions will blunt the forfeiture regime in practice; plausible given the cited record of the earlier crusher law, but the bill's outcome is unverified.

divination.statement: there would be more than 10 vehicles a year that would actually be crushed
divination.explanation: A past prediction (quoted by Utikere) about the earlier crusher law that, per the account, was not borne out — far fewer vehicles were crushed.

veracity.statement: It has been more than two decades since Iran's nuclear programme was exposed and New Zealand began demanding that Tehran comply with its nuclear non-proliferation obligations—it still has not.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate: Iran's nuclear programme was exposed in 2002-03 and non-compliance with NPT obligations is well documented.

veracity.statement: It was in 2022 that the New Zealand Government again reset our engagement with Iran, after Mahsa Amini died at the hands of the regime's police. She was fatally beaten for failing to wear her hijab in accordance with Government regulations.
veracity.explanation: Mahsa Amini's 2022 death in custody and the resulting protests are well documented; cause-of-death details are contested but the account is broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: Just last week, the Minister of Foreign Affairs announced further measures against 40 members of the Iranian regime implicated in the recent brutal killing of tens of thousands of protesters.
veracity.explanation: Specific sanctions claim is plausible, but 'tens of thousands of protesters' killed appears to be a large, unverified figure.

veracity.statement: The US and Israel bombing of Iran is a clear breach of international law. There is no UN mandate for it. There is no evidence that these attacks were a necessary act of self-defence.
veracity.explanation: The legal characterisation is contested but aligns with the UN Secretary-General's stated view; absence of a UN mandate is accurate.

veracity.statement: New Zealand opposed the US invasion of Iraq and history proved that was the correct decision.
veracity.explanation: NZ did decline to join the 2003 Iraq invasion; the judgment that history vindicated it is widely held though evaluative.

veracity.statement: In the last day, we've heard the Pentagon telling Congress there was no sign that Iran was going to attack the US first, and no evidence to support the claim that the US attacked Iran in defence. We've heard the Senate Intelligence Committee vice chair say he had seen no intelligence that Iran was on the verge of launching any kind of pre-emptive strike against the United States of America.
veracity.explanation: Reports attributed testimony; accuracy depends on those sources, which cannot be confirmed here.

veracity.statement: The price of crude oil has risen this week, but to nothing like the levels seen when Russia invaded Ukraine. When US markets closed at 10 a.m. today, it was up 7 percent on last Friday's close, at just under US$78 a barrel. That compares with the price of US$128 a barrel on 8 March 2022.
veracity.explanation: Figures are internally consistent and plausible; the US$128 March 2022 peak matches the historical record.

veracity.statement: Total exports to the region last year were $3.3 billion, representing 3 percent of New Zealand's total exports.
veracity.explanation: Plausible order of magnitude for NZ Middle East exports; cannot be independently confirmed here.

veracity.statement: I note that in July 2024, the Government did provide promised cost of living relief through tax changes that benefited around 1.9 million New Zealand households by an average of $60 extra a fortnight in their hand—$60 a fortnight I take the member would want to take back.
veracity.explanation: Tax changes are real; the '$60 average' figure is plausible but averages can obscure distribution.

veracity.statement: The video which Mr Hipkins has referred to previously, in which he said that I made the statement that "National would make groceries cheaper"—that statement is not included in that video at any stage. I have provided the full transcript to Mr Hipkins; he has chosen not to correct his statement.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable factual rebuttal about the video's contents; later partly conceded by Hipkins's correction.

veracity.statement: since 2002, successive Governments have had a target for the Reserve Bank of annual Consumers Price Index (CPI) inflation of between 1 and 3 percent on average over the medium term... During that period, I note that annual inflation reached the heights of 7.3 percent and stayed out of target for 33 consecutive months.
veracity.explanation: The 1-3% target band and a ~7.3% peak match the public record; the 33-month figure is specific and plausible.

veracity.statement: annual CPI inflation is almost never negative, which is to say that, overall, prices don't reduce across the economy on average... Inflation did turn mildly negative in 1999 when the Asian financial crisis reduced the price of imports. Before that, you have to go back to 1946 to find another example of negative inflation.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with NZ inflation history; deflation is indeed rare, with a late-1990s episode.

veracity.statement: I absolutely stand on the side of anyone who wants to work hard and get ahead, and, as I said in my answer to the primary question, that's why we as a Government have worked so hard on restoring the economic conditions needed for job creation. I hope the member joins me in welcoming the fact that the latest statistics show that, in the December quarter, 15,000 more New Zealanders were employed.
veracity.explanation: The 15,000 December-quarter employment figure is specific and plausible, not verifiable here.

veracity.statement: I was actually quoting from a transcript of the Hon Nicola Willis' press conference on 27 August 2025, where she said, "The purpose of this briefing is to update you on the Government's next steps to increase grocery competition and reduce food prices for Kiwis."
veracity.explanation: Presents a dated, verbatim quote to correct the record; accuracy depends on the transcript but is precise and checkable.

veracity.statement: We've seen a significant drop in the number of victims of violent crime since this Government was elected, with the latest New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey showing there were 49,000 fewer victims of violent crime in the year to October 2025 than two years previously.
veracity.explanation: Cites a named official source; the figure is plausible but unverifiable here.

veracity.statement: When we came into Government in October 2023, there were 185,000 victims of violent crime, and the Government set a target of reducing that figure to 165,000, a reduction of 20,000 victims, by 2029.
veracity.explanation: Specific, internally consistent figures attributed to the target-setting; not independently confirmable here.

veracity.statement: the latest figure is that there are 136,000 victims of crime, a reduction of 49,000. That's 49,000 families that don't have to go through the pain and suffering of dealing with the victims of violent crime and being the victims and being the families of those victims. That is great progress.
veracity.explanation: Figures plausible but the loose 'victims of crime' phrasing risks slight overstatement.

veracity.statement: MSD also found that nearly 99 percent of clients are fulfilling their obligations, and the number of sanctions has dropped by 10.6 percent between September 2024 and September 2025 quarters. The changes we have made have increased client activity and engagement with MSD.
veracity.explanation: Attributed to MSD data; plausible but unverifiable here.

veracity.statement: this Government isn't intending to import LNG to replace natural gas, or for it to be imported regularly enough to see it set the gas price overall. LNG is simply a backup option to be imported during dry years. The alternative is we have no fuel to make electricity, and that was the policy that we inherited and which drove power prices in 2024 to over $800 per megawatt hour and put New Zealand businesses and New Zealanders out of business.
veracity.explanation: Wholesale prices did spike in 2024; the >$800/MWh figure is plausible but not confirmable here.

veracity.statement: This is the third consecutive drop from the previous quarters, and shows a consistent downward trend in serious and persistent youth offending by children and young people. The downward trend remains positive and continues to exceed expectations. It is also consistent across the majority of the country, with drops of 20 percent or more in eight of the 12 police districts.
veracity.explanation: Specific, internally consistent claims attributed to data; not confirmable here.

specificity.statement: It has been more than two decades since Iran's nuclear programme was exposed and New Zealand began demanding that Tehran comply with its nuclear non-proliferation obligations—it still has not.
specificity.explanation: Gives a timeframe and a named obligation, but no figures or specifics on the programme.

specificity.statement: It was in 2022 that the New Zealand Government again reset our engagement with Iran, after Mahsa Amini died at the hands of the regime's police. She was fatally beaten for failing to wear her hijab in accordance with Government regulations.
specificity.explanation: Names the year, person, and circumstances precisely.

specificity.statement: Just last week, the Minister of Foreign Affairs announced further measures against 40 members of the Iranian regime implicated in the recent brutal killing of tens of thousands of protesters.
specificity.explanation: Names the actor, count (40), and timing, though 'tens of thousands' is imprecise.

specificity.statement: Well, as I've said yesterday, we have long supported action that stops Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon that sponsors State terrorism around the world and also brutally represses its people. But these are independent actions by the US and Israel. We are not party to them, we have not had advance warning, and we have not had a subsequent briefing.
specificity.explanation: Clear on NZ's non-involvement but vague on the actual question of support.

specificity.statement: Well, as I've said to the member before, I'm very proud that we've made house purchasing more affordable. Rents have come down, I think 6,000 or 7,000 people have come off the social housing wait-list, and, when I last looked, 2,100 children have been moved out of emergency housing into proper, dry homes, and there's big investment going in and support happening in homeless situations as well.
specificity.explanation: Cites several figures, though hedged ('I think', 'when I last looked').

specificity.statement: Well, as I've said to the member before, our record on housing is much better than that member's, where homelessness went up 37 percent and a billion dollars was spent... we've seen 6,000 people come off the social housing wait-list; 2,124 kids come out of squalid motels and into proper homes; ... Auckland Council, as I understand, is doing daily counts of rough sleepers—there's about 30 in the CBD; and the good news is that of the 300 Housing First places that we've made available, 203 have been tenanted, and 13 have signed leases.
specificity.explanation: Dense with concrete figures and named programmes.

specificity.statement: New Zealand is a small country, but we can be a country that leads the world on international matters, not because we are the biggest, not because we are the loudest, not because we have the largest military or the biggest economy, but because as a country we know who we are, we know what our values are, and we have the courage to stick up for the things that we think are important around the world.
specificity.explanation: Stirring but offers no concrete mechanism or policy.

specificity.statement: Speaking in the House recently, I alluded to a Facebook post of Nicola Willis where she was unpacking some groceries. I said in that Facebook post that she had committed to lowering grocery prices—I was mistaken. I should have referred to her press statements of 14 June 2023, 13 July 2023, 12 October 2023, her press conference on 27 August 2025, her Facebook video in September 2025—all of which committed her to lowering grocery prices.
specificity.explanation: Lists precise dates of the statements he relies on.

specificity.statement: We support the addition to the motion made by Chris Hipkins and we absolutely—absolutely—call for peace on this particular issue. We want to ensure that our people understand the impacts that it will have on our people living here in Aotearoa.
specificity.explanation: General call for peace with no concrete proposal or detail.

specificity.statement: In the last day, we've heard the Pentagon telling Congress there was no sign that Iran was going to attack the US first, and no evidence to support the claim that the US attacked Iran in defence. We've heard the Senate Intelligence Committee vice chair say he had seen no intelligence that Iran was on the verge of launching any kind of pre-emptive strike against the United States of America.
specificity.explanation: Names specific bodies and timeframe ('in the last day').

specificity.statement: The price of crude oil has risen this week, but to nothing like the levels seen when Russia invaded Ukraine. When US markets closed at 10 a.m. today, it was up 7 percent on last Friday's close, at just under US$78 a barrel. That compares with the price of US$128 a barrel on 8 March 2022.
specificity.explanation: Precise prices, percentages, dates and times.

specificity.statement: Total exports to the region last year were $3.3 billion, representing 3 percent of New Zealand's total exports.
specificity.explanation: Exact value and share given.

specificity.statement: Recently introduced regulations require fuel importers to maintain at least 28 days of petrol and 21 days of diesel reserves, with the Government having acted to increase that requirement.
specificity.explanation: Names exact reserve-day requirements for each fuel.

specificity.statement: I note that in July 2024, the Government did provide promised cost of living relief through tax changes that benefited around 1.9 million New Zealand households by an average of $60 extra a fortnight in their hand—$60 a fortnight I take the member would want to take back.
specificity.explanation: Cites date, household count, and dollar figure.

specificity.statement: the FamilyBoost tax credit, we made changes to that last year, which I note the member's party supported—having earlier opposed—which mean that many families have now got more than $150 a fortnight in relief from that policy
specificity.explanation: Names the policy and a dollar figure.

specificity.statement: It is the case that when inflation is higher, grocery prices increase more rapidly, and that with inflation under control, they have not risen as fast as could have been the case with a more profligate and higher-spending Government... our Government has taken action to do what we can to support more competition in the grocery sector. Those actions include changes to the fast-track legislation and changes to building consent rules to enable new entrants to compete... I join with those New Zealanders who wish to see grocery prices cheaper. I am realistic about the role of Government in that.
specificity.explanation: Names specific legislative levers (fast-track, building consent).

specificity.statement: since 2002, successive Governments have had a target for the Reserve Bank of annual Consumers Price Index (CPI) inflation of between 1 and 3 percent on average over the medium term... During that period, I note that annual inflation reached the heights of 7.3 percent and stayed out of target for 33 consecutive months.
specificity.explanation: Exact band, peak figure, and duration.

specificity.statement: annual CPI inflation is almost never negative, which is to say that, overall, prices don't reduce across the economy on average... Inflation did turn mildly negative in 1999 when the Asian financial crisis reduced the price of imports. Before that, you have to go back to 1946 to find another example of negative inflation.
specificity.explanation: Cites specific years (1999, 1946).

specificity.statement: Yes. This Government is on the side of New Zealanders who want to work and get ahead. That is why we have been focused on restoring the economic conditions needed for job creation. That is also why we have supported the fast-tracking of job-rich projects, why we have supported the Investment Boost tax relief, and why we have taken action to reduce red tape and restore confidence across a range of industries from farming through to the film sector through to tourism.
specificity.explanation: Names policies and sectors but few figures or timeframes.

specificity.statement: I absolutely stand on the side of anyone who wants to work hard and get ahead, and, as I said in my answer to the primary question, that's why we as a Government have worked so hard on restoring the economic conditions needed for job creation. I hope the member joins me in welcoming the fact that the latest statistics show that, in the December quarter, 15,000 more New Zealanders were employed.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete employment figure and period.

specificity.statement: I was actually quoting from a transcript of the Hon Nicola Willis' press conference on 27 August 2025, where she said, "The purpose of this briefing is to update you on the Government's next steps to increase grocery competition and reduce food prices for Kiwis."
specificity.explanation: Exact date and verbatim quotation.

specificity.statement: We've seen a significant drop in the number of victims of violent crime since this Government was elected, with the latest New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey showing there were 49,000 fewer victims of violent crime in the year to October 2025 than two years previously.
specificity.explanation: Names the survey, the figure (49,000), and the period.

specificity.statement: When we came into Government in October 2023, there were 185,000 victims of violent crime, and the Government set a target of reducing that figure to 165,000, a reduction of 20,000 victims, by 2029.
specificity.explanation: Baseline, target, reduction amount, and deadline all stated precisely.

specificity.statement: the latest figure is that there are 136,000 victims of crime, a reduction of 49,000. That's 49,000 families that don't have to go through the pain and suffering of dealing with the victims of violent crime and being the victims and being the families of those victims. That is great progress.
specificity.explanation: Gives current figure and reduction, though slips from 'victims of violent crime' to 'victims of crime'.

specificity.statement: Very shortly, we'll be introducing legislation to strengthen trespass laws in New Zealand, followed by legislation to provide police with the power to deal with antisocial disorderly behaviour in our CBDs, and our Crime Amendment Bill is making its way through the House.
specificity.explanation: Names specific bills and areas, though 'very shortly' is vague on timing.

specificity.statement: MSD also found that nearly 99 percent of clients are fulfilling their obligations, and the number of sanctions has dropped by 10.6 percent between September 2024 and September 2025 quarters. The changes we have made have increased client activity and engagement with MSD.
specificity.explanation: Precise percentages and the quarters compared.

specificity.statement: We've also introduced phone-based case management, supporting 10,000 more people in case management at any time. We've also improved the way MSD works with businesses to provide opportunities for job seekers to gain employment.
specificity.explanation: Gives one concrete figure (10,000) but the business-engagement claim is general.

specificity.statement: Yes, I have received advice on the impacts of high levels of rooftop solar and household batteries on wholesale markets and distribution costs. It identified potential benefits to household bills, while also requiring significant investment in the grid. That is why the Government is making a number of regulatory changes to make it easier to install rooftop solar and batteries—this includes removing building consent requirements for installing rooftop solar and batteries, mandating retailers to pay a fair price for electricity sold back into the grid from 1 July, along with a number of other regulatory changes.
specificity.explanation: Names specific regulatory changes and a date (1 July).

specificity.statement: this Government isn't intending to import LNG to replace natural gas, or for it to be imported regularly enough to see it set the gas price overall. LNG is simply a backup option to be imported during dry years. The alternative is we have no fuel to make electricity, and that was the policy that we inherited and which drove power prices in 2024 to over $800 per megawatt hour and put New Zealand businesses and New Zealanders out of business.
specificity.explanation: Cites the >$800/MWh 2024 figure and the backup-only role.

specificity.statement: This is the third consecutive drop from the previous quarters, and shows a consistent downward trend in serious and persistent youth offending by children and young people. The downward trend remains positive and continues to exceed expectations. It is also consistent across the majority of the country, with drops of 20 percent or more in eight of the 12 police districts.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the trend (third drop, 20%+ in 8 of 12 districts).

specificity.statement: There are a number of initiatives that have contributed to this success, such as intensive case management teams and the Fast Track youth offending programme, which I acknowledge was started by the previous Government. This Government took what was working with the Fast Track programme and increased its funding by $30.6 million in Budget 2024 to continue and expand the programme to 14- to 17-year-olds in Hamilton, Auckland, Rotorua, and Christchurch.
specificity.explanation: Names the funding ($30.6m), the budget year, age range, and cities.

specificity.statement: I have recently confirmed the Government's move to make RNZAF Base Ōhakea available 24/7 as an alternative runway for wide-body aircraft, resolving a longstanding constraint for airlines... To fix this, we have approved funding for Airways New Zealand to provide round-the-clock air traffic control services. Opening up Ōhakea 24/7 was one of the key actions within the aviation action plan. I am proud to see it delivered.
specificity.explanation: Names the base, the 24/7 change, the funded provider, and the underlying constraint.

specificity.statement: In addition to our Ōhakea investment, we are also investing $1.1 million from the regional connectivity package to the first concessionary loan to Golden Bay Air. This loan will ensure that the regional airline can refinance existing aircraft debt and fund essential ongoing major maintenance checks.
specificity.explanation: States the amount, recipient, source package, and purpose.

specificity.statement: last year we announced a $3.35 million investment for Whanganui Airport to complete construction of the new sealed parallel taxiway. This will address longstanding safety issues by reducing the need for aircraft to backtrack on the active runway before take-off and after landing.
specificity.explanation: Names the figure, location, project, and safety rationale.

strength.statement: Just last week, the Minister of Foreign Affairs announced further measures against 40 members of the Iranian regime implicated in the recent brutal killing of tens of thousands of protesters.
strength.explanation: Describes a concrete delivered government action (targeted measures), though enforcement impact unclear.

strength.statement: Well, as I've said to the member before, I'm very proud that we've made house purchasing more affordable. Rents have come down, I think 6,000 or 7,000 people have come off the social housing wait-list, and, when I last looked, 2,100 children have been moved out of emergency housing into proper, dry homes, and there's big investment going in and support happening in homeless situations as well.
strength.explanation: Claims concrete delivered outcomes on housing, but figures are approximate and unverified here.

strength.explanation: Points to a concrete delivered regulatory change increasing reserves.

strength.statement: I note that in July 2024, the Government did provide promised cost of living relief through tax changes that benefited around 1.9 million New Zealand households by an average of $60 extra a fortnight in their hand—$60 a fortnight I take the member would want to take back.
strength.explanation: Points to a delivered tax change as a fulfilled commitment, though the 'average' framing softens it.

strength.explanation: Claims measurable progress toward a stated target attributed to government action.

That's 49,000 families that don't have to go through the pain and suffering of dealing with the victims of violent crime and being the victims and being the families of those victims. That is great progress.
strength.explanation: Claims the target was beaten ahead of schedule, a concrete delivered outcome.

strength.explanation: Mix of announced-but-not-yet-introduced legislation and one bill in progress — intent more than delivery.

strength.explanation: Claims its changes produced measurable engagement effects.

strength.statement: We've also introduced phone-based case management, supporting 10,000 more people in case management at any time. We've also improved the way MSD works with businesses to provide opportunities for job seekers to gain employment.
strength.explanation: Describes a concrete delivered programme expansion.

It identified potential benefits to household bills, while also requiring significant investment in the grid. That is why the Government is making a number of regulatory changes to make it easier to install rooftop solar and batteries—this includes removing building consent requirements for installing rooftop solar and batteries, mandating retailers to pay a fair price for electricity sold back into the grid from 1 July, along with a number of other regulatory changes.
strength.explanation: Describes regulatory changes underway rather than fully implemented outcomes.

The downward trend remains positive and continues to exceed expectations. It is also consistent across the majority of the country, with drops of 20 percent or more in eight of the 12 police districts.
strength.explanation: Points to measured progress against a target.

strength.statement: There are a number of initiatives that have contributed to this success, such as intensive case management teams and the Fast Track youth offending programme, which I acknowledge was started by the previous Government. strength.explanation: Describes a concretely funded and expanded programme.

To fix this, we have approved funding for Airways New Zealand to provide round-the-clock air traffic control services. Opening up Ōhakea 24/7 was one of the key actions within the aviation action plan. I am proud to see it delivered.
strength.explanation: Describes a concrete, funded, delivered action against a stated plan item.

strength.statement: In addition to our Ōhakea investment, we are also investing $1.1 million from the regional connectivity package to the first concessionary loan to Golden Bay Air. This loan will ensure that the regional airline can refinance existing aircraft debt and fund essential ongoing major maintenance checks.
strength.explanation: A concrete funded measure, though described as ensuring future outcomes.

strength.statement: last year we announced a $3.35 million investment for Whanganui Airport to complete construction of the new sealed parallel taxiway. This will address longstanding safety issues by reducing the need for aircraft to backtrack on the active runway before take-off and after landing.
strength.explanation: An announced/funded investment; delivery framed as future completion.

charisma.statement: I want to acknowledge that there are different views on the legitimacy of the actions taken by the US and Israel. I respect those views and the vigour with which they have been offered.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges opposing views respectfully, an attempt to bring others along.

charisma.statement: New Zealand is a small country, but we can be a country that leads the world on international matters, not because we are the biggest, not because we are the loudest, not because we have the largest military or the biggest economy, but because as a country we know who we are, we know what our values are, and we have the courage to stick up for the things that we think are important around the world.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, aspirational national framing intended to unite rather than divide.

charisma.statement: The Iranian Government is a brutal, oppressive, and barbaric regime. It is possible to condemn their repression, to condemn the repression of their regime, and still to be clear that unilateral military escalation is not the answer.
charisma.explanation: Nuanced framing that seeks to bridge those who detest the regime and those who oppose the strikes.

charisma.statement: International law applies to everyone, including our friends and allies. No country should place itself above international law.
charisma.explanation: Principled, universal framing, though appeals mainly to those already sympathetic.

charisma.statement: We support the addition to the motion made by Chris Hipkins and we absolutely—absolutely—call for peace on this particular issue. We want to ensure that our people understand the impacts that it will have on our people living here in Aotearoa.
charisma.explanation: Conciliatory, peace-focused and supportive of a cross-party amendment.

charisma.statement: We respect international law because the alternative is worse. The alternative is a world where only force dictates outcomes.
charisma.explanation: Values-based appeal for upholding law over force.

charisma.statement: Absolutely not. Just because we have achieved the target well ahead of expectations doesn't mean we stop now. Every young person deserves the opportunity to be the best version of themselves.
charisma.explanation: Aspirational, inclusive note about young people.

charisma.statement: There are a number of initiatives that have contributed to this success, such as intensive case management teams and the Fast Track youth offending programme, which I acknowledge was started by the previous Government. This Government took what was working with the Fast Track programme and increased its funding by $30.6 million in Budget 2024 to continue and expand the programme to 14- to 17-year-olds in Hamilton, Auckland, Rotorua, and Christchurch.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party acknowledgement builds goodwill rather than partisan point-scoring.

civility.statement: I want to acknowledge that there are different views on the legitimacy of the actions taken by the US and Israel. I respect those views and the vigour with which they have been offered.
civility.explanation: Respectful recognition of disagreement, no personal attack.

civility.statement: New Zealand is far from the Middle East, and I do not overestimate our influence over events there. We are not central to this region or this conflict.
civility.explanation: Sober, non-inflammatory framing.

civility.statement: Well, as I've said to the member before, our record on housing is much better than that member's, where homelessness went up 37 percent and a billion dollars was spent... we've seen 6,000 people come off the social housing wait-list; 2,124 kids come out of squalid motels and into proper homes; ... Auckland Council, as I understand, is doing daily counts of rough sleepers—there's about 30 in the CBD; and the good news is that of the 300 Housing First places that we've made available, 203 have been tenanted, and 13 have signed leases.
civility.explanation: Comparative jab at the opponent's record, but framed around figures rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: Speaking in the House recently, I alluded to a Facebook post of Nicola Willis where she was unpacking some groceries. I said in that Facebook post that she had committed to lowering grocery prices—I was mistaken. I should have referred to her press statements of 14 June 2023, 13 July 2023, 12 October 2023, her press conference on 27 August 2025, her Facebook video in September 2025—all of which committed her to lowering grocery prices.
civility.explanation: Concedes his slip but immediately reasserts the substantive charge with dated references.

civility.statement: We have two obligations in respect of the rules-based order. The first is to follow the rules. The second is to hold others accountable to them. New Zealand has, throughout our history, upheld both these obligations, but this week we have seen a Government shrugging its shoulders at the second of those obligations.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism ('shrugging its shoulders') aimed at the Government's conduct, not personal abuse.

civility.statement: Well, it is absolutely the case that the price of crude oil by the barrel has an impact on the fuel prices that New Zealanders pay at the pump, and that's why I will continue to monitor those movements closely. It also of course has an impact on the cost of freight, food, and other factors in the economy; I acknowledge that. The member overestimates my importance and influence. My ability to end the conflict in the Middle East is limited.
civility.explanation: Candid and self-deprecating rather than combative.

civility.statement: the FamilyBoost tax credit, we made changes to that last year, which I note the member's party supported—having earlier opposed—which mean that many families have now got more than $150 a fortnight in relief from that policy
civility.explanation: Substantive jab at the opponent's flip-flop, no personal abuse.

civility.statement: The video which Mr Hipkins has referred to previously, in which he said that I made the statement that "National would make groceries cheaper"—that statement is not included in that video at any stage. I have provided the full transcript to Mr Hipkins; he has chosen not to correct his statement.
civility.explanation: Accuses the opponent of failing to correct the record, but grounded in a factual dispute.

civility.statement: I understand some people are actively considering bringing back a dual mandate. It shows they are not serious about getting inflation under control.
civility.explanation: Attacks the opponents' seriousness, but tied to a policy position.

civility.statement: The loudest false promise I have heard in recent times has been from those who out of one side of their mouth say that they care deeply about the cost of living and out the other side of their mouth say that they would change the inflation targeting regime, would introduce new taxes on tenants, and at the same time would remove the Investment Boost tax policy that is the very thing that Treasury says will drive future wage growth. I care deeply about the cost of living, but it is not enough to care; that member needs to come up with serious policies on the cost of living if she wants to be taken seriously.
civility.explanation: Sharp 'out of both sides of their mouth' framing edges toward sneering, though policy-anchored.

civility.statement: There are a number of initiatives that have contributed to this success, such as intensive case management teams and the Fast Track youth offending programme, which I acknowledge was started by the previous Government. This Government took what was working with the Fast Track programme and increased its funding by $30.6 million in Budget 2024 to continue and expand the programme to 14- to 17-year-olds in Hamilton, Auckland, Rotorua, and Christchurch.
civility.explanation: Generously credits the previous Government for starting a programme that is working.

rigor.statement: New Zealand is far from the Middle East, and I do not overestimate our influence over events there. We are not central to this region or this conflict.
rigor.explanation: Measured, realistic appraisal of NZ's limited influence rather than overclaiming.

rigor.statement: Well, again, I've noted the member's comments and his remarks today in the House and I'd just say that I'm unsure as to how he would possibly make the assessment that they are illegal or legal, and that is because the member—or any of the members—does not have access to the information. New Zealand cannot jump to conclusions either way, because, actually, at the end of the day, we have not been party to the information or intelligence around these strikes.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable evidentiary caution, but used to avoid engaging the legal question at all.

rigor.statement: The US and Israel bombing of Iran is a clear breach of international law. There is no UN mandate for it. There is no evidence that these attacks were a necessary act of self-defence.
rigor.explanation: Structured argument citing absence of UN mandate and of a self-defence basis.

rigor.statement: The Iranian Government is a brutal, oppressive, and barbaric regime. It is possible to condemn their repression, to condemn the repression of their regime, and still to be clear that unilateral military escalation is not the answer.
rigor.explanation: Holds two positions coherently (condemn regime; oppose unilateral strikes) without contradiction.

rigor.statement: It didn't work in Iraq, it didn't work in Afghanistan, and it won't work in Iran.
rigor.explanation: Leans on historical analogy rather than evidence specific to Iran.

rigor.statement: When Russia invaded Ukraine, we called that out as a breach of the international rules-based order, and we were right to do that. When Vladimir Putin invades his next country of choice, what moral authority will we have as a country to call on him to obey the international rules-based order if we are not willing to ask the same standard of countries that we have a closer relationship with?
rigor.explanation: Consistency argument: applies the same standard regardless of the actor, a logically coherent point.

rigor.statement: International law applies to everyone, including our friends and allies. No country should place itself above international law.
rigor.explanation: Coherent principle of even-handed application, stated without supporting detail.

rigor.statement: In the last day, we've heard the Pentagon telling Congress there was no sign that Iran was going to attack the US first, and no evidence to support the claim that the US attacked Iran in defence. We've heard the Senate Intelligence Committee vice chair say he had seen no intelligence that Iran was on the verge of launching any kind of pre-emptive strike against the United States of America.
rigor.explanation: Marshals specific evidentiary sources to rebut the self-defence justification.

rigor.statement: We have two obligations in respect of the rules-based order. The first is to follow the rules. The second is to hold others accountable to them. New Zealand has, throughout our history, upheld both these obligations, but this week we have seen a Government shrugging its shoulders at the second of those obligations.
rigor.explanation: Clear premise-to-conclusion structure identifying which obligation she says is being neglected.

rigor.statement: We respect international law because the alternative is worse. The alternative is a world where only force dictates outcomes.
rigor.explanation: Coherent but rests on a somewhat binary framing of the alternatives.

rigor.statement: It is the case that when inflation is higher, grocery prices increase more rapidly, and that with inflation under control, they have not risen as fast as could have been the case with a more profligate and higher-spending Government... our Government has taken action to do what we can to support more competition in the grocery sector. Those actions include changes to the fast-track legislation and changes to building consent rules to enable new entrants to compete... I join with those New Zealanders who wish to see grocery prices cheaper. I am realistic about the role of Government in that.
rigor.explanation: Links inflation to grocery prices and names specific competition measures, with a candid caveat on government's limits.

rigor.statement: I understand some people are actively considering bringing back a dual mandate. It shows they are not serious about getting inflation under control.
rigor.explanation: Treats favouring a dual mandate as proof of unseriousness — an inference asserted rather than argued.

rigor.statement: The loudest false promise I have heard in recent times has been from those who out of one side of their mouth say that they care deeply about the cost of living and out the other side of their mouth say that they would change the inflation targeting regime, would introduce new taxes on tenants, and at the same time would remove the Investment Boost tax policy that is the very thing that Treasury says will drive future wage growth. I care deeply about the cost of living, but it is not enough to care; that member needs to come up with serious policies on the cost of living if she wants to be taken seriously.
rigor.explanation: Cites Treasury on Investment Boost but largely an attack listing opponent positions.

rigor.statement: annual CPI inflation is almost never negative, which is to say that, overall, prices don't reduce across the economy on average... Inflation did turn mildly negative in 1999 when the Asian financial crisis reduced the price of imports. Before that, you have to go back to 1946 to find another example of negative inflation.
rigor.explanation: Explains why governments target positive inflation, with conclusion following from the premise.

rigor.statement: this Government isn't intending to import LNG to replace natural gas, or for it to be imported regularly enough to see it set the gas price overall. LNG is simply a backup option to be imported during dry years. The alternative is we have no fuel to make electricity, and that was the policy that we inherited and which drove power prices in 2024 to over $800 per megawatt hour and put New Zealand businesses and New Zealanders out of business.
rigor.explanation: Clear rationale for LNG as dry-year backup, though leans on a stark 'no fuel' alternative.
