specificity.explanation: Names the residents' group and the concrete concern (development outpacing confirmed infrastructure).

specificity.statement: This is why we decided to make a change in this bill to reduce the minimum housing capacity in plan change 120 from 2 million homes to 1.4 million. This is a more realistic approach, focusing growth in the city centre, around town centres, and along major transport routes.
specificity.explanation: Gives the figures and where growth is to be focused (city centre, town centres, transport routes).

divination.statement: The amendments proposed in this bill threaten that. They threaten kaitiakitanga, they threaten the value of consulting with kaitiaki and, therefore, the sustainability of our kāpata kai and, potentially, the sustainability of our commercial interests.
divination.explanation: Predicts harm to sustainability of food sources and commercial interests if the bill proceeds — plausible but magnitude and timeframe uncertain.

divination.statement: the bill will pass its first reading, but be assured that our position is crystal clear; we will take out the sections of the bill that remove the minimum size limits.
divination.explanation: Predicts the bill will pass first reading — confirmed by the party vote (National 49, ACT 11, NZ First 8) recorded immediately after.

divination.statement: I've been working closely with the Balmoral Residents Association, and the residents are particularly concerned that enabling large-scale development, often without confirming the infrastructure capacity, could lead to isolated and out-of-scale development.
divination.explanation: Predicts that development without confirmed infrastructure 'could lead to' isolated, out-of-scale outcomes — plausible, conditional, uncertain.

strength.statement: the bill will pass its first reading, but be assured that our position is crystal clear; we will take out the sections of the bill that remove the minimum size limits.
strength.explanation: Clear commitment to remove specific clauses, but delivery depends on the select committee process and is not yet enacted.

strength.statement: National is committed to constructive change. We believe that if the bill, however, does not undergo real, meaningful improvements during the select committee stage, we will not be able to support it beyond that point.
strength.explanation: A conditional commitment with follow-through dependent on the select committee outcome — intent stated, delivery unproven.

strength.statement: we campaigned and won an agreement to remove that three by three storey house rule, and it will be gone.
strength.explanation: A campaign commitment now being delivered through the bill before the House — concrete follow-through, though final passage is pending.

authenticity.statement: the capacity that will be unlocked as a result of this will be, roughly, around 1.6 million homes. That is a substantial advance on the status quo, which is in the Auckland Unitary Plan—which hasn't been updated for years—which is around 1.2 million homes.
authenticity.explanation: Framing the bill as 'unlocking' more housing is in tension with the bill's own text reducing the required capacity from ~2m to 1.4m, which opponents quote against him.

authenticity.statement: we campaigned and won an agreement to remove that three by three storey house rule, and it will be gone.
authenticity.explanation: Action matches ACT's campaign position; words and deeds are consistent here.

specificity.statement: I have a personal view that I think New Zealand is far overregulated for the size of our country.
specificity.explanation: A broad value judgement with no figures, named regulations, or mechanism — 'overregulated' is left undefined.

specificity.statement: It is not legislative; it is cultural, and I would love a debate about how we improve the cultural attitude towards alcohol in this country.
specificity.explanation: Identifies culture as the lever but offers no concrete proposal for how to change it.

specificity.statement: I want to reassure members of the public that the National Party values families. Indeed, one of our 10 values is strong families and caring communities, and notwithstanding this bill perhaps going through today, our party values strong families and caring communities.
specificity.explanation: Cites a named party value ('strong families and caring communities') but offers no policy detail or measure.

specificity.statement: The change is that, at the moment, if people want to drink in the on-licence on these days, they have to have a meal, and that is what this change is about. It’s about the meal, not about whether you can drink on these days or not.
specificity.explanation: Precisely identifies the actual legal mechanism the bill changes (the substantial-meal requirement).

specificity.statement: one survey found that one in eight ED admissions on Christmas Day was due to excess drinking.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete figure (one in eight) tied to a specific day and source (a survey).

specificity.statement: But it’s the consequences of that happening on these days, and we will unleash far-reaching harms on our society.
specificity.explanation: No quantification of the predicted harm.

specificity.statement: Those shops, those restaurants, and those bars could be open to 3 a.m. on Christmas Day. They could be open to 3 a.m. on your Fridays or your Sundays. There is no restriction.
specificity.explanation: Concrete in naming times (3 a.m.) and days, even though the underlying claim is challenged.

specificity.statement: this is a minor change which affects those on-licences that can already sell alcohol on these days. It just changes quite a minor thing, which is that, unlike every other day of the year, they don’t have to sell a substantial meal with the alcohol; on these days, they do.
specificity.explanation: Names the precise mechanism being altered (the substantial-meal requirement on existing on-licences).

specificity.statement: One of the safest places you could probably have a few beverages in is a licensed premise like one of our pubs, one of our restaurants.
specificity.explanation: Names the comparison (licensed premises vs elsewhere) but no figures.

specificity.statement: I can indicate, straight up, ACT will be supporting this through the first reading because we actually do believe in free speech.
specificity.explanation: States position and reason but at the level of principle rather than detail.

specificity.statement: This Green Party bill is a narrow, carefully considered change to the Copyright Act 1994. It provides certainty for our creative sector, aligns us with international best practices, and strengthens the foundational principles of democracy and freedom of expression.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute (Copyright Act 1994) and the intended effects, though the claimed benefits stay fairly general.

specificity.statement: It is also important that we uphold protection for Māori intellectual and cultural property. This bill offers an opportunity to reinforce protections and include the Wai 262 recommendations through the select committee process, ensuring that tikanga Māori remains central to how we approach copyright and artistic expression in Aotearoa.
specificity.explanation: Points to a concrete vehicle (Wai 262 recommendations via select committee) but without detailing what provisions would be added.

specificity.statement: being able to have that as part of our culture is absolutely essential to a thriving political discourse. It’s not all about the cost of living—although most of it’s about cost of living, isn’t it? Housing, health, jobs, got it? But also it’s about seeing politicians as people; seeing people who are part of our communities who we can laugh with and at.
specificity.explanation: Gestures at cost-of-living themes (housing, health, jobs) but as a list of topics rather than detail.

specificity.statement: The question I have to ask, though, is: what is the problem that we’re trying to solve here? There have been no specific guiding court cases in New Zealand that have established a clear precedent or defence for copyright infringement based on parody or satire. Legal experts, actually, have noted there is a distinct lack of litigation in this area.
specificity.explanation: Concrete claim about lack of precedent/litigation, citing legal experts, though no case names.

specificity.statement: The only other thing I’d like to quickly mention is that this bill does not address moral rights. It’s silent on moral rights. How will moral rights be assessed?
specificity.explanation: Pinpoints a defined legal concept (moral rights: attribution, integrity, against false attribution) the bill omits.

specificity.statement: This does bring us in line with other countries, such as Australia, the US, Belgium, France, the Netherlands, Spain, and Germany—I could go on. Currently, our Copyright Act, from back in 1994, is a bit of an outlier.
specificity.explanation: Names specific comparator countries and the statute, grounding the comparative claim.

specificity.statement: Back in 2008, a then Labour-led Government considered a fair dealing exemption for parody and satire, yet it never saw the light of day. In 2011, a former Green MP drafted a member’s bill to do exactly this... Then, in 2018, Simeon Brown introduced his own bill to seek a very similar thing.
specificity.explanation: Names specific years, actors, and prior bills — a detailed legislative history.

specificity.statement: This is a bill that will provide an update to reflect what is, I think, a modern approach to the way in which we all go about our lives; in particular, being able to debate and participate within a democracy and as part of a democratic process.
specificity.explanation: Endorses the bill in general 'modernising democracy' terms without identifying any concrete provision or effect.

rigor.statement: I have a personal view that I think New Zealand is far overregulated for the size of our country.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a sweeping claim; the supporting basis offered later is personal experience ('I've lived all over the world') — an anecdotal appeal rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: If you look at why we are low income, low productivity relative to the rest of the world—and I’ve lived all over the world and seen that actually we are well overregulated.
rigor.explanation: Causally links NZ's low productivity to over-regulation but supports it with personal travel anecdote rather than data — appeal to personal experience.

rigor.statement: It is so important for the functioning of a free and liberal democratic society that we enable these satirists to contribute to the public discourse in a way that connects with the public.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable principle but asserted rather than evidenced; leans on the value of free speech.

rigor.statement: I’m talking about the parents in South Auckland that don’t have a lot of self-control because of their unfortunate addiction to alcohol.
rigor.explanation: Argument from personal observation at Papakura Marae; an emotionally framed anecdotal appeal rather than data on harm.

rigor.statement: this bill is about on-licence that are already able to operate on these days, so it’s not that these days—which, I acknowledge, are very important days—are being opened up.
rigor.explanation: Carefully distinguishes what the bill does from what it does not, with clear logical structure.

rigor.statement: The change is that, at the moment, if people want to drink in the on-licence on these days, they have to have a meal, and that is what this change is about. It’s about the meal, not about whether you can drink on these days or not.
rigor.explanation: Tight reasoning isolating the single variable that changes, distinguishing it from consumption generally.

rigor.statement: My third point is I noticed that New Zealand First is opposing this legislation because it is the—and this is to quote the Hon Mark Patterson—“the scourge of consumerism—consumeralism”... So there’s going to be too much people consuming too many things. I do wonder what their policy position then leads to.
rigor.explanation: Tests the consistency of NZ First's anti-consumerism rationale against the bill's actual effect on consumption.

rigor.statement: But it’s the consequences of that happening on these days, and we will unleash far-reaching harms on our society.
rigor.explanation: Hyperbolic ('unleash far-reaching harms') and overstates the effect of a narrow measure — closer to an appeal to fear than evidenced inference.

rigor.statement: we’ve almost got to the point that this bill has to be passed because of a rugby game.
rigor.explanation: Attributes the legislation to a single ulterior cause without evidence; other members explicitly dispute this framing.

rigor.statement: this is a minor change which affects those on-licences that can already sell alcohol on these days. It just changes quite a minor thing, which is that, unlike every other day of the year, they don’t have to sell a substantial meal with the alcohol; on these days, they do.
rigor.explanation: Clear premise-to-conclusion reasoning that the change does not alter consumption, hours, or which premises open.

rigor.statement: I know that Jamie Arbuckle mentioned that this is going to go into shop trading hours. These bars will be able to stay open all kinds of hours. It doesn’t actually affect their normal trading hours, and we are not changing the Shop Trading Hours Act. I get where that concern may land, but this piece of legislation doesn’t actually do that.
rigor.explanation: Counters the opposing argument by pointing to what the bill does and does not amend.

rigor.statement: One of the safest places you could probably have a few beverages in is a licensed premise like one of our pubs, one of our restaurants.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned argument that supervised licensed premises with intoxication rules are safer than home drinking; plausible but asserted without data.

rigor.statement: I know a few members have said that these amendments have just been passed in a hurry to open up a stadium for the sake of a football match. That is actually not true... but I do think that this would happen anyway. Whether it happens right now—it was going to happen anyway, and it’s just standard process.
rigor.explanation: Distinguishes media attention from legislative cause to rebut the stadium-motive argument.

rigor.statement: The question I have to ask, though, is: what is the problem that we’re trying to solve here? There have been no specific guiding court cases in New Zealand that have established a clear precedent or defence for copyright infringement based on parody or satire. Legal experts, actually, have noted there is a distinct lack of litigation in this area.
rigor.explanation: Frames a clear analytical question and supports it with the observed absence of NZ litigation and expert commentary.

rigor.statement: The only other thing I’d like to quickly mention is that this bill does not address moral rights. It’s silent on moral rights. How will moral rights be assessed?
rigor.explanation: Identifies a concrete legislative gap (moral rights) and poses how it would be handled — substantive, well-targeted critique.

rigor.statement: This does bring us in line with other countries, such as Australia, the US, Belgium, France, the Netherlands, Spain, and Germany—I could go on. Currently, our Copyright Act, from back in 1994, is a bit of an outlier.
rigor.explanation: Uses comparative practice to support reform, though leaning partly on an appeal to international norms.

rigor.statement: Back in 2008, a then Labour-led Government considered a fair dealing exemption for parody and satire, yet it never saw the light of day. In 2011, a former Green MP drafted a member’s bill to do exactly this... Then, in 2018, Simeon Brown introduced his own bill to seek a very similar thing.
rigor.explanation: Marshals a chronology to argue the reform is overdue and cross-partisan in origin.

veracity.statement: If you look at why we are low income, low productivity relative to the rest of the world—and I’ve lived all over the world and seen that actually we are well overregulated.
veracity.explanation: NZ does have comparatively low labour productivity and income vs other OECD nations (broadly true), but the regulation-as-cause framing is contestable.

veracity.statement: this bill is about on-licence that are already able to operate on these days, so it’s not that these days—which, I acknowledge, are very important days—are being opened up.
veracity.explanation: Accurate clarification that the bill concerns premises already permitted to trade on these days, correcting a common misframing.

veracity.statement: The change is that, at the moment, if people want to drink in the on-licence on these days, they have to have a meal, and that is what this change is about. It’s about the meal, not about whether you can drink on these days or not.
veracity.explanation: Accurate description of the existing on-licence meal requirement and the narrow scope of the amendment.

veracity.statement: one survey found that one in eight ED admissions on Christmas Day was due to excess drinking.
veracity.explanation: A plausible, sourced statistic consistent with known holiday ED data, but the unnamed survey can't be verified from the text.

veracity.statement: Those shops, those restaurants, and those bars could be open to 3 a.m. on Christmas Day. They could be open to 3 a.m. on your Fridays or your Sundays. There is no restriction.
veracity.explanation: Claim of 'no restriction' is contested and rebutted by Mooney and McClure, who say the bill does not amend the Shop Trading Hours Act or normal trading hours — likely misleading.

veracity.statement: this is a minor change which affects those on-licences that can already sell alcohol on these days. It just changes quite a minor thing, which is that, unlike every other day of the year, they don’t have to sell a substantial meal with the alcohol; on these days, they do.
veracity.explanation: Accurately characterises the existing meal requirement and the narrow scope, consistent with Brooking's account.

veracity.statement: I know that Jamie Arbuckle mentioned that this is going to go into shop trading hours. These bars will be able to stay open all kinds of hours. It doesn’t actually affect their normal trading hours, and we are not changing the Shop Trading Hours Act. I get where that concern may land, but this piece of legislation doesn’t actually do that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the bill does not change the Shop Trading Hours Act, contradicting Arbuckle; corroborated by Mooney.

veracity.statement: I know a few members have said that these amendments have just been passed in a hurry to open up a stadium for the sake of a football match. That is actually not true... but I do think that this would happen anyway. Whether it happens right now—it was going to happen anyway, and it’s just standard process.
veracity.explanation: Directly disputes the 'rushed for a stadium' claim, asserting standard process; reasonable but offered without documentary backing.

veracity.statement: The question I have to ask, though, is: what is the problem that we’re trying to solve here? There have been no specific guiding court cases in New Zealand that have established a clear precedent or defence for copyright infringement based on parody or satire. Legal experts, actually, have noted there is a distinct lack of litigation in this area.
veracity.explanation: Plausible and broadly accurate that NZ has little parody/satire copyright case law, supporting the 'no demonstrated problem' point.

veracity.statement: This does bring us in line with other countries, such as Australia, the US, Belgium, France, the Netherlands, Spain, and Germany—I could go on. Currently, our Copyright Act, from back in 1994, is a bit of an outlier.
veracity.explanation: Accurate that many of those jurisdictions have parody/satire copyright exceptions and NZ's 1994 Act lacks one — NZ is comparatively an outlier.

veracity.statement: Back in 2008, a then Labour-led Government considered a fair dealing exemption for parody and satire, yet it never saw the light of day. In 2011, a former Green MP drafted a member’s bill to do exactly this... Then, in 2018, Simeon Brown introduced his own bill to seek a very similar thing.
veracity.explanation: Recounts a plausible, specific sequence of prior attempts; consistent with the bill being a long-standing recurring proposal.

charisma.statement: It is not legislative; it is cultural, and I would love a debate about how we improve the cultural attitude towards alcohol in this country.
charisma.explanation: Reframes a contentious vote toward a shared, cross-cutting goal and invites broad debate rather than attacking opponents.

charisma.statement: It is so important for the functioning of a free and liberal democratic society that we enable these satirists to contribute to the public discourse in a way that connects with the public.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to a widely shared democratic value to build cross-bench support for the copyright bill.

charisma.statement: I do oppose this bill and I continue to oppose this bill, notwithstanding the fact that I respect the views—particularly from my colleagues in the National Party and Government and also across the House—on this.
charisma.explanation: Gracious, bridge-respecting tone, though ultimately argues one side.

charisma.statement: this bill is about on-licence that are already able to operate on these days, so it’s not that these days—which, I acknowledge, are very important days—are being opened up.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the importance of the days to others while making her case — concedes a point to the other side.

charisma.statement: I do note—you know, reasonable minds can disagree on this and certainly we hear that in this House.
charisma.explanation: Magnanimous, consensus-acknowledging framing of a conscience vote.

charisma.statement: I really do want to acknowledge all of the members and all of their views, because I do know that there are quite a lot of different views on this.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive recognition of the full range of views in a conscience debate — bridge-building.

charisma.statement: So, look, I’m very happy to unite with other people across the House in favour of this. It really is increasing people’s freedom in New Zealand, and that’s the reason I’ll be supporting it and also other ACT MPs will be supporting it.
charisma.explanation: Frames the vote as cross-House unity around a shared value of freedom.

charisma.statement: This Green Party bill is a narrow, carefully considered change to the Copyright Act 1994. It provides certainty for our creative sector, aligns us with international best practices, and strengthens the foundational principles of democracy and freedom of expression.
charisma.explanation: Frames a narrow bill in broadly appealing democratic terms to invite cross-party support.

charisma.statement: It is also important that we uphold protection for Māori intellectual and cultural property. This bill offers an opportunity to reinforce protections and include the Wai 262 recommendations through the select committee process, ensuring that tikanga Māori remains central to how we approach copyright and artistic expression in Aotearoa.
charisma.explanation: Invites submissions and broadens the bill's appeal to Māori cultural-property concerns.

charisma.statement: being able to have that as part of our culture is absolutely essential to a thriving political discourse. It’s not all about the cost of living—although most of it’s about cost of living, isn’t it? Housing, health, jobs, got it? But also it’s about seeing politicians as people; seeing people who are part of our communities who we can laugh with and at.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, humanising framing inviting people to see politicians as part of the community; warm and consensus-oriented.

charisma.statement: This is a bill that will provide an update to reflect what is, I think, a modern approach to the way in which we all go about our lives; in particular, being able to debate and participate within a democracy and as part of a democratic process.
charisma.explanation: Warm, inclusive support framed around shared democratic participation, but appeals broadly rather than persuading the unconvinced.

civility.statement: To play politics with things like this is utterly unacceptable, and I do hope that members on the opposite side reflect that with future debates.
civility.explanation: Criticises opponents' conduct (accusing them of playing politics over an earlier bill) rather than their persons; pointed but aimed at behaviour, with 'utterly unacceptable' adding heat.

civility.statement: I do oppose this bill and I continue to oppose this bill, notwithstanding the fact that I respect the views—particularly from my colleagues in the National Party and Government and also across the House—on this.
civility.explanation: Explicitly respects opposing colleagues while stating her own disagreement — disagreement framed without disparagement.

civility.statement: I’m talking about the parents in South Auckland that don’t have a lot of self-control because of their unfortunate addiction to alcohol.
civility.explanation: Raises a genuine social concern about vulnerable families without personal attack, though generalising about a community.

civility.statement: My third point is I noticed that New Zealand First is opposing this legislation because it is the—and this is to quote the Hon Mark Patterson—“the scourge of consumerism—consumeralism”... So there’s going to be too much people consuming too many things. I do wonder what their policy position then leads to.
civility.explanation: Engages an opponent's stated reasoning (quoting it) and questions where it leads, with a light mocking edge but no personal attack.

civility.statement: we’ve almost got to the point that this bill has to be passed because of a rugby game.
civility.explanation: Imputes a trivial, cynical motive to the bill's supporters; criticises their motives rather than engaging the merits.

civility.statement: I do note—you know, reasonable minds can disagree on this and certainly we hear that in this House.
civility.explanation: Explicitly legitimises opposing views as reasonable — respectful of disagreement.

civility.statement: I know that Jamie Arbuckle mentioned that this is going to go into shop trading hours. These bars will be able to stay open all kinds of hours. It doesn’t actually affect their normal trading hours, and we are not changing the Shop Trading Hours Act. I get where that concern may land, but this piece of legislation doesn’t actually do that.
civility.explanation: Directly rebuts a colleague's claim while acknowledging where the concern comes from — engages the substance without personal attack.

civility.statement: I really do want to acknowledge all of the members and all of their views, because I do know that there are quite a lot of different views on this.
civility.explanation: Respectful framing that validates differing positions.

civility.statement: it was even recently with us last year with a billboard that appeared in Wellington saying “Defund da Police”. And, actually, the Green Party complained to the billboard company asserting copyright breaches—hmm, curious.
civility.explanation: A pointed jab implying Green hypocrisy ('hmm, curious') aimed at the bill's party; targets the opponent's conduct rather than a person, but the insinuation is a mild cheap shot.

civility.statement: I actually thought it was already the law—if you see some of the Green Party’s social media—however, it turns out that’s not parody or satire; they’re actually being serious.
civility.explanation: A joke at the Green Party's expense implying their genuine posts read as parody; humorous but a dig at opponents rather than substance.

civility.statement: There are bills of consequence in this Parliament, bills where you think, “This is why I came to this House.” Sadly, this is not one of those bills, but I do wish to acknowledge that it is an anon-nomoly.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the bill's importance but does so good-naturedly and still acknowledges the member who brought it — no personal attack.

authenticity.statement: To play politics with things like this is utterly unacceptable, and I do hope that members on the opposite side reflect that with future debates.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with his stated support for the earlier Luxton bill — he is reproaching others for a reversal he himself did not make.

authenticity.statement: I do oppose this bill and I continue to oppose this bill, notwithstanding the fact that I respect the views—particularly from my colleagues in the National Party and Government and also across the House—on this.
authenticity.explanation: Reaffirms a position she held at the committee stage and continues to hold — a consistent, principled stance even against her own party's majority.

authenticity.statement: I want to reassure members of the public that the National Party values families. Indeed, one of our 10 values is strong families and caring communities, and notwithstanding this bill perhaps going through today, our party values strong families and caring communities.
authenticity.explanation: Her opposing vote aligns with the family-protection value she invokes, so words and action are consistent here.

authenticity.statement: So, look, I’m very happy to unite with other people across the House in favour of this. It really is increasing people’s freedom in New Zealand, and that’s the reason I’ll be supporting it and also other ACT MPs will be supporting it.
authenticity.explanation: Voting to liberalise alcohol law on freedom grounds is consistent with ACT's stated deregulatory, liberty-focused positioning.

authenticity.statement: I can indicate, straight up, ACT will be supporting this through the first reading because we actually do believe in free speech.
authenticity.explanation: Support for a free-speech-oriented parody/satire bill is consistent with ACT's long-standing free-speech advocacy.

divination.statement: But it’s the consequences of that happening on these days, and we will unleash far-reaching harms on our society.
divination.explanation: Predicts the bill will cause 'far-reaching harms', but the narrow change (meal requirement on existing on-licences) makes large new harm unlikely; timeframe and magnitude vague.

divination.statement: Those shops, those restaurants, and those bars could be open to 3 a.m. on Christmas Day. They could be open to 3 a.m. on your Fridays or your Sundays. There is no restriction.
divination.explanation: Predicts venues opening to 3 a.m. as a consequence; the prediction rests on the disputed claim that restrictions are removed.

forthrightness.statement: Well, again, what we did last Friday was we outlined the four phases of our national fuel response plan. We are very much in a place where we have sufficient stocks and sufficient supplies, and so there is no significant supply disruptions. All we are doing is preparing for the eventuality that that may possibly happen in future months.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically to release all internal modelling on fuel supply risk; never addresses the request to publish modelling, pivots to the four-phase plan.

forthrightness.statement: We are meeting with officials every morning, and many times through the course of the day. But, at this point, our major focus, as you know, is to secure fuel supply; without it, that is the thing that can do the most damage to incomes and jobs. That is why we are doing everything we can to secure fuel.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the plan has been operationally tested and what role iwi have; answers neither part, restates general focus on supply.

forthrightness.statement: There is no windfall gain or benefit from higher fuel prices for the Government. Petrol excise tax, as everyone will understand, is fixed. While there may be a slight increase in GST theoretically increasing, there is an offset as people spend less money on other categories other than fuel.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to commit the extra $11.8m GST to mileage subsidies; doesn't say yes/no but directly rebuts the question's premise of a windfall.

forthrightness.statement: We're freely admitting that we will not be able to alleviate the pressure for everybody, but we have also learnt the mistakes from COVID, which is to make sure that we are also being economically responsible and not creating more of an impact on rising inflation and also growth. That is very much our frame. We're very pleased to say that we've been able to extend support to 143,000 working families, as we announced last week—an extra $50 per week. That comes to about $375 million of total cost for the Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what support beyond the package for Papakura whānau; offers no new measure but candidly admits limits and restates the existing package.

forthrightness.statement: Because, as we've been reiterating many times in regular media engagements, New Zealand does not have a fuel supply problem at this time. The market is operating effectively. There is plenty of supply and stock in country. That's why we're working so hard to make sure we work on phases 1 and 2, so that we never have to get to phases 3 and 4.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why there has been no public communication on what levels 3 and 4 mean; explains the no-problem rationale but never addresses the communication gap.

forthrightness.statement: This Government is supporting, with $550 million a year, agencies and organisations on housing—$5 billion a year. We've opened up 300 extra Housing First places. We've put $10 million into rough sleeping. Auckland Council now are doing a daily count of homelessness in the Auckland CBD, and typically the numbers are running at 24 to 30 people.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked for real solutions for homeless whānau; lists existing spending rather than new solutions, partially responsive.

forthrightness.statement: Well, as we've previously discussed in this House, obviously, our new Government framework on director fees is designed so that we can attract good talent to make very important decisions on governance. There is about $60 billion worth of Government spending, and as that member knows, having lost half of the $66 billion of COVID spending, it's important that it's well-governed.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why directors got an ~80% rise while firefighters got none; defends director fees generally but pivots to attacking Hipkins rather than addressing the firefighter contrast.

forthrightness.statement: Well, again, it is. That is why we've gone through the in-work tax credit where 143, 000 families are earning $50 a week. We have been up front: we are not going to repeat the mistakes of COVID that that member created when he was the Prime Minister.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why support isn't targeted to lowest-income families with children; asserts it is but doesn't engage the part-time exclusion.

forthrightness.statement: We are doing everything we can to support Kiwis, but we are also not going to repeat the mistakes of COVID that led to a 32-year high in inflation and $180 billion worth of debt, and so the frame is very simple. We need to be economically responsible so we don't drive, and have a further impact on, inflation and debt, which ends up causing huge pain and suffering to New Zealanders.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why low-income childless workers get no support; never addresses that group, restates the fiscal frame.

forthrightness.statement: But with respect to pay equity, there is still a pay equity regime in this country. No. What has happened is that it was unworkable and it was unaffordable, and I look forward to the member saying whether or not he will reinstate another $10 billion to be able to go back to what he previously put in place.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he regrets cancelling the pay equity claim; doesn't answer on regret, asserts a regime still exists and challenges the questioner instead.

forthrightness.statement: I'm well aware that our Government passed a law to make sure an unworkable system and an unaffordable system is now workable and affordable.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether he is aware the law prohibits care workers raising a new claim; reframes the law's purpose rather than confirming the prohibition.

forthrightness.statement: That's why the Minister's taking advice on it. We'll have more to say about it shortly.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what the impact is on patients when care workers can't afford fuel; deflects to 'taking advice' with no substantive answer.

forthrightness.statement: As I've said, we are a Government that is freely admitting we will not be able to alleviate the pressure on everybody across the country. We know it's an incredibly difficult time for households and businesses, but our frame is very clear. We need to be economically responsible so we don't hurt working New Zealanders with higher levels of inflation and more debt, but, equally, we need to make sure we're doing everything we can to give them timely, targeted, and temporary support.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked if he's comfortable with workers refusing remote visits; doesn't address comfort directly but candidly admits the government won't help everyone.

forthrightness.statement: The most immediate and noticeable impact of the Middle East conflict has been on the price of oil and, therefore, on the price of refined fuels in New Zealand. Prices have risen markedly since the start of the conflict. Petrol has gone up 34 percent and diesel has gone up 86 percent. Petrol and other fuels make up just under 4 percent of the basket of goods and services in the Consumers Price Index, so these price rises will have a direct impact on overall inflation.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and fully answers how the conflict is affecting the economy.

forthrightness.statement: Current advice is that fuel supply remains sufficient. New Zealand has 58.7 days of petrol, 52.2 days of diesel, and 46.2 days of jet fuel in country, within our exclusive economic zone, and on the water heading here. That data is updated twice-weekly using maritime tracking and cross-checked against shipping information, giving us a high level of confidence in its accuracy.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers whether there is enough supply with precise data.

forthrightness.statement: I will absolutely present the forecasts in May, and I expect that they will be significantly worse than the forecasts previously presented. I'm not going to give a running commentary on all the discussions Treasury has with me as they develop their understanding of how the conflict will impact the economy.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why she can't share the latest scenarios now; declines to release them but explains why and commits to a date.

forthrightness.statement: It's not my responsibility to agree or disagree with a particular forecast. As I just noted in my earlier answer, there are a range of forecasts from bank economists and others that predict a higher rate of inflation this year than would have been the case without the Middle East conflict. It is my view that I concur that inflation will go higher this year as a result of the Middle East conflict.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically whether she agrees with ASB's 4.2% forecast; won't endorse the number but states her own directional view.

forthrightness.statement: Absolutely, I do. It's not enough to just say, "overseas factors meant I had to throw out the rule book and take bad decisions". The grave responsibility we now have as a Government is to take these world events and control our response to blunt the impacts, and that is exactly what we are doing.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked if she agrees with her own past statement; answers 'Absolutely, I do' and applies it to herself.

forthrightness.statement: It is not within my power to end the conflict in the Middle East. However, I know that to blunt the impact on New Zealand firms, it is essential that we do everything we can to ensure they continue to have the fuel supplies needed to support jobs, incomes, and economic activity. It is also the case that the Government must take a measured and careful fiscal response, which should include temporary, timely, and targeted measures.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how she'll blunt impacts on care workers and on 93% of businesses; gives a general supply-and-fiscal answer without addressing either group concretely.

forthrightness.statement: Yesterday, we announced that recovery work on the Napier to Wairoa corridor following Cyclone Gabrielle has been completed. The final asphalting is now done, meaning the 4-kilometre road rebuild at State Highway 2—known as "Devil's Elbow"—is once again open to traffic. It's a major milestone in recovery works in Hawke's Bay and will mean a more efficient connection between Wairoa and Napier.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers what he announced regarding the corridor.

forthrightness.statement: In the face of increasing fuel prices, the Government is committed to students being able to access and attend school. It is this Government's priority to ensure that students are learning in school as learning was significantly disrupted by COVID, and our Government will be prioritising making sure children are learning in classrooms. The situation in the Middle East is dynamic, and, as you would expect, the Ministry of Education is planning for a range of different scenarios.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to commit to maintaining at least current school transport delivery; states a priority but makes no commitment, citing scenario planning.

forthrightness.statement: As I've already stated, the Ministry of Education is gathering that information at the moment. All options are on the table, as of course you would expect in that dynamically shifting environment. We are planning for a range of different scenarios.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to commit to raising the 27c/km allowance given AT's 80c/km figure; gives no commitment and falls back on 'all options on the table'.

forthrightness.statement: Firstly, can I say that I need to congratulate and thank parents for prioritising getting their children to school, because what we have seen is that school attendance has held at broadly the same rate as it was at this time last year.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether attendance will decline without extra transport funding; doesn't commit but rebuts the premise with a current attendance comparison.

forthrightness.statement: As I've said in every answer to every single question today, everything is on the table, depending on what happens in a dynamically shifting environment. We're gathering together a range of options. We're responding to this, and at the right time, we will be able to announce those.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to relax transport eligibility temporarily; gives the same non-committal 'everything on the table' answer, explicitly acknowledging she's repeating it.

forthrightness.statement: It is time for us to strip the fiction away. At no point had Megan Woods either sought a budgetary allocation, nor did she have the necessary permits.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he saw advice that the levy surplus could fund a 70m-litre reserve; ignores the advice question and attacks the former minister's record.

forthrightness.statement: Ah, yes. I have sought advice on this issue and I have been advised that the 960 million litres worth of fuel we may have access to by dint of international options was paid for by money in a levy account. That money has been well spent, and, of course, it could not have been spent on an imaginary, non-existent dream.
forthrightness.explanation: Concedes 'yes' he sought advice but reframes the answer around international options rather than the specific surplus-funded reserve asked about.

forthrightness.statement: Yes. I'm very happy to report that the funding, having gone into the levy account referred to, has enabled us to secure 960 million litres of fuel. Had that money been squandered to meet the threshold of some scribbling left behind by the member as she fled from her office, we wouldn't have access to the 960 million litres.
forthrightness.explanation: Says 'yes' to seeing the advice but pivots away from confirming the actual surplus balances asked about.

forthrightness.statement: Far be it for to add to such tawdry discussions. This is a serious issue where Kiwis are deeply concerned about the cost of living, the security of fuel, and options going forward. It really doesn't uphold the status of the House—that tawdry contribution.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he's deflecting to cover his own failure; doesn't engage the substance, dismisses the question as 'tawdry'.

forthrightness.statement: Because the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) is leading work to coordinate with Government agencies as well as non-Government entities to consider coordination in the future hypothetical event of fuel shortages. Of course, at the moment, it's business as usual for them to be planning for emergencies of various types, including the possibility of concurrent emergencies of a natural disaster type, but also in the event that an emergency of one category coincides with any future fuel shortages.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the 'if so, why' part by explaining NEMA's coordination role and concurrent-emergency planning.

forthrightness.statement: The Government's consulting on what some of the detail of further phases might look like, in particular phases 3 and 4, and so it's the Government's advice to submit to its process of understanding critical activities across the economy and society, including but not limited to emergency response. Of course, if, in the circumstance where fuel shortages were to occur, then there would be rationalisation or coordination or prioritisation decisions that would need to be made then in response to those unique and particular circumstances.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked the specific either/or (all-of-emergency-services vs per-service response); describes a consultation process instead, prompting a point of order that he didn't answer.

forthrightness.statement: On behalf of the Minister, it's not clear to me that it would necessarily be within my ministerial remit to make such decisions.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked the trigger point for activating priority fuel access; deflects on grounds of remit without giving any threshold.

forthrightness.statement: The availability of hygienic, food-grade packaging underpins New Zealand's world-class food safety system and relies on the supply of both oil and fuel. Businesses report that sufficient packaging is available. We are working closely with domestic and export-focused food businesses to ensure their on-hand stocks of packaging are sufficient. We are monitoring medium- to long-term availability as part of the work of the Government's ministerial oversight group.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers what advice he has received on fuel disruption's impact on food safety.

forthrightness.statement: Our regulatory system is well placed to support companies to meet any availability challenges because it is not prescriptive about packaging. The legislation is focused on outcomes and is flexible enough for food producers to pivot to alternative supplies without a whole lot of red tape.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers how the regulatory system can respond if needed.

forthrightness.statement: I've had a number of farmers contact me with concerns about the availability of both fuel and fertiliser. While I understand there have been some local challenges with getting diesel delivered, overall fuel supply remains sufficient, with good levels of fuel in the country and more on the way. I understand from the fertiliser industry that there is enough product both in New Zealand and ordered to meet demand until spring. I just want to say to farmers that at this stage, we just have to keep calm, plan ahead, work closely with suppliers, and make sensible business decisions about the use of inputs.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers what he's heard, candidly acknowledging local diesel-delivery challenges alongside overall sufficiency.

veracity.statement: Well, again, what we did last Friday was we outlined the four phases of our national fuel response plan. We are very much in a place where we have sufficient stocks and sufficient supplies, and so there is no significant supply disruptions. All we are doing is preparing for the eventuality that that may possibly happen in future months.
veracity.explanation: Claim of sufficient stocks and no significant disruption is consistent with the day-count data Willis cites later in the same session; broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: There is no windfall gain or benefit from higher fuel prices for the Government. Petrol excise tax, as everyone will understand, is fixed. While there may be a slight increase in GST theoretically increasing, there is an offset as people spend less money on other categories other than fuel.
veracity.explanation: Excise being a fixed per-litre charge is correct; the substitution/offset argument is economically reasonable, though it understates the net GST effect.

veracity.statement: Because, as we've been reiterating many times in regular media engagements, New Zealand does not have a fuel supply problem at this time. The market is operating effectively. There is plenty of supply and stock in country. That's why we're working so hard to make sure we work on phases 1 and 2, so that we never have to get to phases 3 and 4.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the supply-day data presented later; the 'plenty of supply' claim is broadly supported.

veracity.statement: Well, as we've previously discussed in this House, obviously, our new Government framework on director fees is designed so that we can attract good talent to make very important decisions on governance. There is about $60 billion worth of Government spending, and as that member knows, having lost half of the $66 billion of COVID spending, it's important that it's well-governed.
veracity.explanation: The 'lost half of $66 billion' characterisation is a contested rhetorical framing of COVID spending, not a clean factual claim.

veracity.statement: We are doing everything we can to support Kiwis, but we are also not going to repeat the mistakes of COVID that led to a 32-year high in inflation and $180 billion worth of debt, and so the frame is very simple. We need to be economically responsible so we don't drive, and have a further impact on, inflation and debt, which ends up causing huge pain and suffering to New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: '32-year high in inflation' is roughly defensible, but attributing it and '$180 billion of debt' wholly to COVID policy is a contestable, partial framing.

veracity.statement: But with respect to pay equity, there is still a pay equity regime in this country. No. What has happened is that it was unworkable and it was unaffordable, and I look forward to the member saying whether or not he will reinstate another $10 billion to be able to go back to what he previously put in place.
veracity.explanation: 'there is still a pay equity regime' is technically true but misleading given the same law barred these workers' new claims, which he later concedes existed.

veracity.statement: I'm well aware that our Government passed a law to make sure an unworkable system and an unaffordable system is now workable and affordable.
veracity.explanation: Characterising a law that blocks new claims as merely making the system 'workable and affordable' omits its prohibitive effect, which is misleading.

veracity.statement: The most immediate and noticeable impact of the Middle East conflict has been on the price of oil and, therefore, on the price of refined fuels in New Zealand. Prices have risen markedly since the start of the conflict. Petrol has gone up 34 percent and diesel has gone up 86 percent. Petrol and other fuels make up just under 4 percent of the basket of goods and services in the Consumers Price Index, so these price rises will have a direct impact on overall inflation.
veracity.explanation: Magnitudes are specific and plausible for a fuel-price shock; the CPI weight is accurate.

veracity.statement: Current advice is that fuel supply remains sufficient. New Zealand has 58.7 days of petrol, 52.2 days of diesel, and 46.2 days of jet fuel in country, within our exclusive economic zone, and on the water heading here. That data is updated twice-weekly using maritime tracking and cross-checked against shipping information, giving us a high level of confidence in its accuracy.
veracity.explanation: Highly specific, sourced figures; presented with stated methodology, plausible and checkable.

veracity.statement: Why has the Government prioritised an almost 80 percent pay rise for the directors of Fire and Emergency New Zealand, while front-line firefighters are getting no pay rise and have to continue to work in unsafe conditions with equipment that keeps breaking down?
veracity.explanation: Contains specific factual claims (~80% director rise, no firefighter rise, failing equipment) that are plausible but not verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: 960,000 Kiwis receiving superannuation and veterans pension will get more money in their pockets. Superannuation for a married couple who both qualify will lift more than $50, to $1,708 a fortnight. This is an increase of over $180 since the 2023 general election, which, of course, has helped to ease the cost of living pressures.
veracity.explanation: Figures are specific and consistent with indexation; the causal credit-claim ('helped ease pressures') is more contestable.

veracity.statement: How can she claim that this is a new cost of living measure when this happens automatically every single year?
veracity.explanation: Benefit and superannuation rates are indeed adjusted automatically each year, so the factual premise is accurate.

veracity.statement: Firstly, can I say that I need to congratulate and thank parents for prioritising getting their children to school, because what we have seen is that school attendance has held at broadly the same rate as it was at this time last year.
veracity.explanation: Specific empirical claim that attendance has held at last year's rate; plausible but unverified and early in the price spike.

veracity.statement: Yes, especially when the Minister gave her consent for the decommissioning of the refinery.
veracity.explanation: Specific claim about Woods consenting to decommissioning; plausible but contested and unsupported in the text.

veracity.statement: The availability of hygienic, food-grade packaging underpins New Zealand's world-class food safety system and relies on the supply of both oil and fuel. Businesses report that sufficient packaging is available. We are working closely with domestic and export-focused food businesses to ensure their on-hand stocks of packaging are sufficient. We are monitoring medium- to long-term availability as part of the work of the Government's ministerial oversight group.
veracity.explanation: Reports current business advice that packaging is sufficient; specific and plausible.

veracity.statement: I've had a number of farmers contact me with concerns about the availability of both fuel and fertiliser. While I understand there have been some local challenges with getting diesel delivered, overall fuel supply remains sufficient, with good levels of fuel in the country and more on the way. I understand from the fertiliser industry that there is enough product both in New Zealand and ordered to meet demand until spring. I just want to say to farmers that at this stage, we just have to keep calm, plan ahead, work closely with suppliers, and make sensible business decisions about the use of inputs.
veracity.explanation: Balanced claim that concedes local problems while asserting adequate national supply and fertiliser to spring.

specificity.statement: Well, again, what we did last Friday was we outlined the four phases of our national fuel response plan. We are very much in a place where we have sufficient stocks and sufficient supplies, and so there is no significant supply disruptions. All we are doing is preparing for the eventuality that that may possibly happen in future months.
specificity.explanation: References a named plan with four phases but gives no figures, thresholds, or detail.

specificity.statement: Obviously, making reductions to excise tax is not particularly targeted. It often benefits higher-income people and, importantly, can also drive more consumption. For us, it's not meeting the criteria of what we need, which is timely, targeted, and temporary.
specificity.explanation: Names a clear decision framework (timely, targeted, temporary) but no quantified thresholds.

specificity.statement: We're freely admitting that we will not be able to alleviate the pressure for everybody, but we have also learnt the mistakes from COVID, which is to make sure that we are also being economically responsible and not creating more of an impact on rising inflation and also growth. That is very much our frame. We're very pleased to say that we've been able to extend support to 143,000 working families, as we announced last week—an extra $50 per week. That comes to about $375 million of total cost for the Government.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures: 143,000 families, $50/week, $375m total cost.

specificity.statement: This Government is supporting, with $550 million a year, agencies and organisations on housing—$5 billion a year. We've opened up 300 extra Housing First places. We've put $10 million into rough sleeping. Auckland Council now are doing a daily count of homelessness in the Auckland CBD, and typically the numbers are running at 24 to 30 people.
specificity.explanation: Multiple concrete figures: $550m, $5bn, 300 Housing First places, $10m, 24–30 people.

specificity.statement: The most immediate and noticeable impact of the Middle East conflict has been on the price of oil and, therefore, on the price of refined fuels in New Zealand. Prices have risen markedly since the start of the conflict. Petrol has gone up 34 percent and diesel has gone up 86 percent. Petrol and other fuels make up just under 4 percent of the basket of goods and services in the Consumers Price Index, so these price rises will have a direct impact on overall inflation.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures: petrol +34%, diesel +86%, fuel ~4% of CPI basket.

specificity.statement: We can anticipate that inflation forecasts will be higher than previously expected, at least in the short term. The Reserve Bank will release its next set of forecasts on 27 May, and the Treasury will follow suit the day after, in the Budget update.
specificity.explanation: Names exact forecast release dates (27 May, the day after).

specificity.statement: Current advice is that fuel supply remains sufficient. New Zealand has 58.7 days of petrol, 52.2 days of diesel, and 46.2 days of jet fuel in country, within our exclusive economic zone, and on the water heading here. That data is updated twice-weekly using maritime tracking and cross-checked against shipping information, giving us a high level of confidence in its accuracy.
specificity.explanation: Exact day-counts (58.7 petrol, 52.2 diesel, 46.2 jet) and the data methodology.

specificity.statement: The conflict will have a negative impact on the economy, through prices, but also, potentially, through other channels like shipping disruptions, freight costs, reduced demand for New Zealand exports, financial markets disruption, and greater uncertainty. The Government can take the sharpest edges off for vulnerable New Zealanders, and you've seen that with the $50 a week increase in the in-work tax credit, but there is a real cost from this conflict: New Zealand is poorer because of these global events.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete channels and the $50 in-work tax credit, but no magnitudes on the GDP impact.

specificity.statement: Putting us in a position where we are highly indebted and fragile, subject to global interest rate fluctuations, and unable to finance public services is not a position I am prepared to take. It is also the case that we need to be careful that our choices don't inadvertently add to the inflation fire.
specificity.explanation: States a fiscal posture and risks but no figures or concrete policy detail.

specificity.statement: It is not within my power to end the conflict in the Middle East. However, I know that to blunt the impact on New Zealand firms, it is essential that we do everything we can to ensure they continue to have the fuel supplies needed to support jobs, incomes, and economic activity. It is also the case that the Government must take a measured and careful fiscal response, which should include temporary, timely, and targeted measures.
specificity.explanation: Restates the timely/targeted/temporary frame plus engagement with industry, but no specific measures or numbers.

specificity.statement: Why has the Government prioritised an almost 80 percent pay rise for the directors of Fire and Emergency New Zealand, while front-line firefighters are getting no pay rise and have to continue to work in unsafe conditions with equipment that keeps breaking down?
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the director rise and names concrete frontline concerns.

specificity.statement: From today, students will receive a boost in support for living costs. Around 52,000 students receiving student allowance and loans will get an increase in financial support—for example, a single person over the age of 24 receiving the student allowance will gain an additional $22 a fortnight.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures: 52,000 students, $22 a fortnight for a specified cohort.

specificity.statement: 960,000 Kiwis receiving superannuation and veterans pension will get more money in their pockets. Superannuation for a married couple who both qualify will lift more than $50, to $1,708 a fortnight. This is an increase of over $180 since the 2023 general election, which, of course, has helped to ease the cost of living pressures.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures: 960,000 recipients, +$50 to $1,708/fortnight, +$180 since 2023.

specificity.statement: 435,000 working-age beneficiaries will get increased support for the cost of living, and approximately 67,000 non-beneficiaries will get an increase in their supplementary assistance. A couple with children, receiving jobseeker support, will receive an increase of more than $40 a fortnight. A sole parent receiving sole parent support will receive an increase of more than $30 a fortnight.
specificity.explanation: Multiple concrete figures across recipient groups and dollar increases.

specificity.statement: Does she agree with Nicola Willis, Opposition Finance Spokesperson in May 2022, who said, "it can't simply blame these issues on overseas factors"?
specificity.explanation: Cites a dated, verbatim prior quote (May 2022).

specificity.statement: Yesterday, we announced that recovery work on the Napier to Wairoa corridor following Cyclone Gabrielle has been completed. The final asphalting is now done, meaning the 4-kilometre road rebuild at State Highway 2—known as "Devil's Elbow"—is once again open to traffic. It's a major milestone in recovery works in Hawke's Bay and will mean a more efficient connection between Wairoa and Napier.
specificity.explanation: Names the corridor, the 4km rebuild, SH2, and 'Devil's Elbow'.

specificity.statement: There were crews from local contractors working alongside Transport Rebuild East Coast (TREC) since 2023 to repair that extensive damage. Since Cyclone Gabrielle, there have been 11 recovery projects along this corridor. Major underslip repairs include a 12-metre-high retaining wall where a 40-metre long and 10-metre high underslip took out the southbound lane. They've also completed a full culvert replacement and repair programme.
specificity.explanation: Highly detailed: 11 projects, 12m retaining wall, 40m × 10m underslip, culvert programme.

specificity.statement: Quite to the contrary of mutterings from the other side that these projects are a "waste of money"—the local residents of Napier and Wairoa and the Napier electorate will be interested to discover that members opposite consider these projects a waste of money—we are, in fact, making good progress. The final repairs are under way on Rail Bridge 217, the rail line between Hastings and Napier, expected to be completed by the middle of the year.
specificity.explanation: Names Rail Bridge 217, the Hastings–Napier line, SH38, and completion timing.

specificity.statement: In the face of increasing fuel prices, the Government is committed to students being able to access and attend school. It is this Government's priority to ensure that students are learning in school as learning was significantly disrupted by COVID, and our Government will be prioritising making sure children are learning in classrooms. The situation in the Middle East is dynamic, and, as you would expect, the Ministry of Education is planning for a range of different scenarios.
specificity.explanation: General commitment with no measures, funding, or service-level detail.

specificity.statement: Ah, yes. I have sought advice on this issue and I have been advised that the 960 million litres worth of fuel we may have access to by dint of international options was paid for by money in a levy account. That money has been well spent, and, of course, it could not have been spent on an imaginary, non-existent dream.
specificity.explanation: Cites 960 million litres and the levy-account funding source.

specificity.statement: South Auckland and North Waikato are some of the fastest-growing regions in the country, whilst also having some of the highest health needs in New Zealand. These communities experience higher rates of infectious disease and long-term conditions, while existing hospitals like Middlemore and Auckland City are already faced with increased demand. The next step recognises both the scale of growth and the need to ensure access to timely healthcare in this part of Auckland.
specificity.explanation: Names regions and hospitals and the drivers, but no figures or timelines here.

specificity.statement: A new hospital in South Auckland will mean better access to care closer to home. Drury was identified as a strong location due to its proximity to key transport corridors, including our roads of regional significance and planned public transport connections, making it easier for patients, staff, and visitors to access care. Over time, this will reduce pressure on existing hospitals, improve wait times, and ensure that Aucklanders can have confidence that high-quality healthcare will be there when they need it.
specificity.explanation: Names Drury and the locational rationale, but the benefits are stated without quantification or timing.

specificity.statement: Health New Zealand has issued a request for a proposal to landowners identified following an earlier request for information, released to market in October 2025. The site of the land being sought would enable a wide range of future health developments, including a major general hospital.
specificity.explanation: Concrete process detail and a date (October 2025), though the project remains at land-acquisition stage.

specificity.statement: Because the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) is leading work to coordinate with Government agencies as well as non-Government entities to consider coordination in the future hypothetical event of fuel shortages. Of course, at the moment, it's business as usual for them to be planning for emergencies of various types, including the possibility of concurrent emergencies of a natural disaster type, but also in the event that an emergency of one category coincides with any future fuel shortages.
specificity.explanation: Names NEMA and the concurrent-emergency scenario but no concrete plans or thresholds.

specificity.statement: The availability of hygienic, food-grade packaging underpins New Zealand's world-class food safety system and relies on the supply of both oil and fuel. Businesses report that sufficient packaging is available. We are working closely with domestic and export-focused food businesses to ensure their on-hand stocks of packaging are sufficient. We are monitoring medium- to long-term availability as part of the work of the Government's ministerial oversight group.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the packaging dependency and the oversight group, but no figures.

While there may be a slight increase in GST theoretically increasing, there is an offset as people spend less money on other categories other than fuel.
rigor.explanation: Coherent economic argument: fixed excise plus a substitution offset, logically connecting premises to the no-windfall conclusion.

rigor.statement: Well, I think the learning from COVID, as talked about in the royal commission of inquiry, was that it's all very easy to fire a cash bazooka around. That creates lots of short-term gain, but it creates endless long-term pain. We only have to look at the last two years to see the pain and suffering that low and middle income working New Zealanders have endured because of reckless economic management through the COVID period.
rigor.explanation: Cites a royal commission for authority but the 'cash bazooka → long-term pain' causal chain is asserted rhetorically rather than evidenced.

rigor.explanation: Sound causal chain from oil price to fuel price to CPI weight to inflation, with quantified premises.

rigor.statement: We can anticipate that inflation forecasts will be higher than previously expected, at least in the short term. The Reserve Bank will release its next set of forecasts on 27 May, and the Treasury will follow suit the day after, in the Budget update.
rigor.explanation: Links fuel input costs through producers and imports to broader prices, a defensible mechanism.

rigor.statement: The conflict will have a negative impact on the economy, through prices, but also, potentially, through other channels like shipping disruptions, freight costs, reduced demand for New Zealand exports, financial markets disruption, and greater uncertainty. The Government can take the sharpest edges off for vulnerable New Zealanders, and you've seen that with the $50 a week increase in the in-work tax credit, but there is a real cost from this conflict: New Zealand is poorer because of these global events.
rigor.explanation: Enumerates plausible transmission channels and acknowledges dependence on how the conflict evolves.

rigor.statement: Putting us in a position where we are highly indebted and fragile, subject to global interest rate fluctuations, and unable to finance public services is not a position I am prepared to take. It is also the case that we need to be careful that our choices don't inadvertently add to the inflation fire.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned argument linking high debt to fragility and inflation risk; coherent but light on specific evidence.

rigor.statement: Does the Government have a finite amount of money to spend, or does he subscribe to the economic philosophy of Fred Dagg that we can always borrow a few billion more?
rigor.explanation: False-dichotomy framing (finite budget vs limitless borrowing) plus a ridiculing analogy rather than an argument.

rigor.statement: South Auckland and North Waikato are some of the fastest-growing regions in the country, whilst also having some of the highest health needs in New Zealand. These communities experience higher rates of infectious disease and long-term conditions, while existing hospitals like Middlemore and Auckland City are already faced with increased demand. The next step recognises both the scale of growth and the need to ensure access to timely healthcare in this part of Auckland.
rigor.explanation: Premises (growth, high health need, existing hospital pressure) logically support the case for new capacity.

rigor.statement: Our regulatory system is well placed to support companies to meet any availability challenges because it is not prescriptive about packaging. The legislation is focused on outcomes and is flexible enough for food producers to pivot to alternative supplies without a whole lot of red tape.
rigor.explanation: Reasoning that outcome-based (non-prescriptive) rules permit substitution is coherent and follows from the premise.

civility.statement: We're freely admitting that we will not be able to alleviate the pressure for everybody, but we have also learnt the mistakes from COVID, which is to make sure that we are also being economically responsible and not creating more of an impact on rising inflation and also growth. That is very much our frame. We're very pleased to say that we've been able to extend support to 143,000 working families, as we announced last week—an extra $50 per week. That comes to about $375 million of total cost for the Government.
civility.explanation: The recurring 'mistakes from COVID' line is a mild partisan jab but framed as policy lesson, not personal attack.

civility.statement: Well, as we've previously discussed in this House, obviously, our new Government framework on director fees is designed so that we can attract good talent to make very important decisions on governance. There is about $60 billion worth of Government spending, and as that member knows, having lost half of the $66 billion of COVID spending, it's important that it's well-governed.
civility.explanation: 'having lost half of the $66 billion of COVID spending' is a personalised dig at the questioner.

civility.statement: Well, again, it is. That is why we've gone through the in-work tax credit where 143, 000 families are earning $50 a week. We have been up front: we are not going to repeat the mistakes of COVID that that member created when he was the Prime Minister.
civility.explanation: 'mistakes of COVID that that member created' personalises blame onto the questioner.

civility.statement: We are doing everything we can to support Kiwis, but we are also not going to repeat the mistakes of COVID that led to a 32-year high in inflation and $180 billion worth of debt, and so the frame is very simple. We need to be economically responsible so we don't drive, and have a further impact on, inflation and debt, which ends up causing huge pain and suffering to New Zealanders.
civility.explanation: Repeated COVID blame is partisan but aimed at past policy rather than personal character.

civility.statement: Well, I think the learning from COVID, as talked about in the royal commission of inquiry, was that it's all very easy to fire a cash bazooka around. That creates lots of short-term gain, but it creates endless long-term pain. We only have to look at the last two years to see the pain and suffering that low and middle income working New Zealanders have endured because of reckless economic management through the COVID period.
civility.explanation: 'reckless economic management' is harsh criticism of the prior government's policy, bordering on character framing.

civility.statement: As I've said, we are a Government that is freely admitting we will not be able to alleviate the pressure on everybody across the country. We know it's an incredibly difficult time for households and businesses, but our frame is very clear. We need to be economically responsible so we don't hurt working New Zealanders with higher levels of inflation and more debt, but, equally, we need to make sure we're doing everything we can to give them timely, targeted, and temporary support.
civility.explanation: Calm, non-attacking restatement of the policy frame engaging the substance of the pressure on households.

civility.statement: Absolutely, I do. It's not enough to just say, "overseas factors meant I had to throw out the rule book and take bad decisions". The grave responsibility we now have as a Government is to take these world events and control our response to blunt the impacts, and that is exactly what we are doing.
civility.explanation: Includes a pointed paraphrase of the prior government's stance but engages the substance of fiscal responsibility.

civility.statement: Why has the Government prioritised an almost 80 percent pay rise for the directors of Fire and Emergency New Zealand, while front-line firefighters are getting no pay rise and have to continue to work in unsafe conditions with equipment that keeps breaking down?
civility.explanation: Sharp contrast framing but aimed at a policy/spending decision rather than personal character.

civility.statement: Does the Government believe that low-income New Zealanders with children and who are working part-time are less deserving of additional support than low-income New Zealanders with children and who are getting the support?
civility.explanation: Pointed but substantive question about eligibility design; the 'less deserving' framing is mildly loaded but engages the policy.

civility.statement: Does the Government have a finite amount of money to spend, or does he subscribe to the economic philosophy of Fred Dagg that we can always borrow a few billion more?
civility.explanation: Mocking 'Fred Dagg' jibe at the opposition's stance, but indirect and not a personal insult.

civility.statement: How can she claim that this is a new cost of living measure when this happens automatically every single year?
civility.explanation: Direct challenge to the framing of the announcement, focused on substance not character.

civility.statement: Does she agree with Nicola Willis, Opposition Finance Spokesperson in May 2022, who said, "it can't simply blame these issues on overseas factors"?
civility.explanation: Uses the minister's own prior words to test consistency — sharp but legitimate, no personal attack.

civility.statement: Quite to the contrary of mutterings from the other side that these projects are a "waste of money"—the local residents of Napier and Wairoa and the Napier electorate will be interested to discover that members opposite consider these projects a waste of money—we are, in fact, making good progress. The final repairs are under way on Rail Bridge 217, the rail line between Hastings and Napier, expected to be completed by the middle of the year.
civility.explanation: Repeats a 'waste of money' characterisation of opponents and amplifies it for electorate effect — verges on strawmanning their position.

civility.statement: Yes, especially when the Minister gave her consent for the decommissioning of the refinery.
civility.explanation: Turns a routine 'do you stand by' question into a jab pinning the refinery's decommissioning on the questioner.
