civility.statement: It is time for us to strip the fiction away. At no point had Megan Woods either sought a budgetary allocation, nor did she have the necessary permits.
civility.explanation: 'strip the fiction away' frames the opponent as deceptive rather than engaging the question.

civility.statement: Ah, yes. I have sought advice on this issue and I have been advised that the 960 million litres worth of fuel we may have access to by dint of international options was paid for by money in a levy account. That money has been well spent, and, of course, it could not have been spent on an imaginary, non-existent dream.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the opposition's reserve plan as an 'imaginary, non-existent dream'.

civility.statement: Yes. I'm very happy to report that the funding, having gone into the levy account referred to, has enabled us to secure 960 million litres of fuel. Had that money been squandered to meet the threshold of some scribbling left behind by the member as she fled from her office, we wouldn't have access to the 960 million litres.
civility.explanation: 'some scribbling left behind by the member as she fled from her office' is a personal, derisive attack.

civility.statement: Far be it for to add to such tawdry discussions. This is a serious issue where Kiwis are deeply concerned about the cost of living, the security of fuel, and options going forward. It really doesn't uphold the status of the House—that tawdry contribution.
civility.explanation: Labels the opponent's question 'tawdry' twice; dismissive of the contribution but not a personal slur.

strength.statement: This Government is supporting, with $550 million a year, agencies and organisations on housing—$5 billion a year. We've opened up 300 extra Housing First places. We've put $10 million into rough sleeping. Auckland Council now are doing a daily count of homelessness in the Auckland CBD, and typically the numbers are running at 24 to 30 people.
strength.explanation: Claims delivered actions (opened 300 places, funded rough sleeping) but mixes delivery with ongoing baseline spend.

strength.statement: From today, students will receive a boost in support for living costs. Around 52,000 students receiving student allowance and loans will get an increase in financial support—for example, a single person over the age of 24 receiving the student allowance will gain an additional $22 a fortnight.
strength.explanation: Describes a change taking effect 'from today', though it is largely the automatic annual adjustment rather than a new initiative.

strength.statement: Yesterday, we announced that recovery work on the Napier to Wairoa corridor following Cyclone Gabrielle has been completed. The final asphalting is now done, meaning the 4-kilometre road rebuild at State Highway 2—known as "Devil's Elbow"—is once again open to traffic. It's a major milestone in recovery works in Hawke's Bay and will mean a more efficient connection between Wairoa and Napier.
strength.explanation: Describes a concrete project actually completed and reopened, not merely announced.

strength.statement: There were crews from local contractors working alongside Transport Rebuild East Coast (TREC) since 2023 to repair that extensive damage. Since Cyclone Gabrielle, there have been 11 recovery projects along this corridor. Major underslip repairs include a 12-metre-high retaining wall where a 40-metre long and 10-metre high underslip took out the southbound lane. They've also completed a full culvert replacement and repair programme.
strength.explanation: Documents completed engineering works delivered since 2023.

strength.statement: A new hospital in South Auckland will mean better access to care closer to home. Drury was identified as a strong location due to its proximity to key transport corridors, including our roads of regional significance and planned public transport connections, making it easier for patients, staff, and visitors to access care. Over time, this will reduce pressure on existing hospitals, improve wait times, and ensure that Aucklanders can have confidence that high-quality healthcare will be there when they need it.
strength.explanation: Describes a project at request-for-proposal stage rather than a delivered facility.

strength.statement: Health New Zealand has issued a request for a proposal to landowners identified following an earlier request for information, released to market in October 2025. The site of the land being sought would enable a wide range of future health developments, including a major general hospital.
strength.explanation: Early procurement step, not yet delivered infrastructure.

divination.statement: We can anticipate that inflation forecasts will be higher than previously expected, at least in the short term. The Reserve Bank will release its next set of forecasts on 27 May, and the Treasury will follow suit the day after, in the Budget update.
divination.explanation: Predicts higher near-term inflation forecasts; well-supported given a clear fuel-price shock, though magnitude unstated.

divination.statement: The conflict will have a negative impact on the economy, through prices, but also, potentially, through other channels like shipping disruptions, freight costs, reduced demand for New Zealand exports, financial markets disruption, and greater uncertainty. The Government can take the sharpest edges off for vulnerable New Zealanders, and you've seen that with the $50 a week increase in the in-work tax credit, but there is a real cost from this conflict: New Zealand is poorer because of these global events.
divination.explanation: Predicts net negative economic impact via several channels; directionally well-supported but magnitude explicitly uncertain.

divination.statement: I will absolutely present the forecasts in May, and I expect that they will be significantly worse than the forecasts previously presented. I'm not going to give a running commentary on all the discussions Treasury has with me as they develop their understanding of how the conflict will impact the economy.
divination.explanation: Predicts the May forecasts will be 'significantly worse'; plausible given the fuel shock, but unquantified.

divination.statement: It's not my responsibility to agree or disagree with a particular forecast. As I just noted in my earlier answer, there are a range of forecasts from bank economists and others that predict a higher rate of inflation this year than would have been the case without the Middle East conflict. It is my view that I concur that inflation will go higher this year as a result of the Middle East conflict.
divination.explanation: Predicts higher inflation this year due to the conflict; well-grounded directional call, magnitude left open.

divination.statement: Quite to the contrary of mutterings from the other side that these projects are a "waste of money"—the local residents of Napier and Wairoa and the Napier electorate will be interested to discover that members opposite consider these projects a waste of money—we are, in fact, making good progress. The final repairs are under way on Rail Bridge 217, the rail line between Hastings and Napier, expected to be completed by the middle of the year.
divination.explanation: Predicts Rail Bridge 217 and TREC works complete by mid-year; plausible for works already under way.

divination.statement: A new hospital in South Auckland will mean better access to care closer to home. Drury was identified as a strong location due to its proximity to key transport corridors, including our roads of regional significance and planned public transport connections, making it easier for patients, staff, and visitors to access care. Over time, this will reduce pressure on existing hospitals, improve wait times, and ensure that Aucklanders can have confidence that high-quality healthcare will be there when they need it.
divination.explanation: Predicts reduced pressure and improved wait times 'over time'; plausible but contingent on a hospital still only at RFP stage.

authenticity.statement: Absolutely, I do. It's not enough to just say, "overseas factors meant I had to throw out the rule book and take bad decisions". The grave responsibility we now have as a Government is to take these world events and control our response to blunt the impacts, and that is exactly what we are doing.
authenticity.explanation: Endorses her own 2022 opposition principle ('can't simply blame overseas factors') and accepts it now binds her own government — consistency between past and present position.

charisma.statement: I've had a number of farmers contact me with concerns about the availability of both fuel and fertiliser. While I understand there have been some local challenges with getting diesel delivered, overall fuel supply remains sufficient, with good levels of fuel in the country and more on the way. I understand from the fertiliser industry that there is enough product both in New Zealand and ordered to meet demand until spring. I just want to say to farmers that at this stage, we just have to keep calm, plan ahead, work closely with suppliers, and make sensible business decisions about the use of inputs.
charisma.explanation: Reassuring, inclusive 'keep calm, plan ahead' message addressed to all farmers without partisan framing.

specificity.statement: From 1 January 2027, Tai Poutini Polytechnic will operate within The Open Polytechnic of New Zealand. This will ensure that in-person, campus-based vocational education remains available on the West Coast.
specificity.explanation: Names a date, the named entities and the delivery model, though the financial/operational mechanism stays general.

specificity.statement: From 1 January, NorthTec will be reestablished as a stand-alone regional polytechnic. Among other financial supports to ensure its continued viability, I am delighted to announce the in-principle investment of $34.7 million for the development of a new Whangārei tertiary hub—subject to business case
specificity.explanation: Names the institution, a dollar figure ($34.7m) and a named project, though 'subject to business case' leaves the timeline conditional.

specificity.statement: the Eastern Institute of Technology—EIT—will be receiving $10 million to support the rebuild and improvement of its Hawke's Bay campus in Taradale, following Cyclone Gabrielle.
specificity.explanation: Named institution, named campus/location, exact figure and the triggering event.

specificity.statement: the unique residential agricultural training facility Telford will be receiving $2.4 million to address deferred maintenance to ensure a fit for purpose, fully functioning agricultural campus.
specificity.explanation: Exact dollar figure, named facility and purpose (deferred maintenance).

specificity.statement: We are fixing the basics and building the future of the West Coast.
specificity.explanation: A repeated slogan with no figures, mechanism or measurable commitment.

specificity.statement: this industry was not built in Wellington by MPs in this House or by fancy suits in the Beehive. This industry was built by hard-working New Zealanders—Kiwis with rough hands
specificity.explanation: Evocative imagery but no concrete claim, figure or mechanism.

specificity.statement: My proposal was simple: that revenue from overseas betting should be ring-fenced, used only for animal welfare purposes, greyhound rehoming, or compensation for those affected.
specificity.explanation: A concrete, named mechanism (ring-fencing overseas betting revenue for defined purposes).

specificity.statement: I just want to commend the good work by the Primary Production Committee to do their very best to reach better outcomes in some very challenging circumstances. There's been a lot of passion and emotion involved in this bill. I want to just leave our thoughts with all of those people who are involved and all of those animals who will find new homes, hopefully.
specificity.explanation: Expresses sentiment with no concrete content or commitment.

specificity.statement: First, the bill will increase the maximum period that someone can be trespassed for from two years to three years. It will also give all occupiers the discretion to set a trespass period of any time, up to the three-year maximum.
specificity.explanation: Exact before/after figures and a clear mechanism (occupier discretion up to the maximum).

specificity.statement: The bill will increase penalties from $1,000 to $2,000. The penalty will also apply to the new offence for trespassing on specified retail premises. The bill will also increase the penalty for a person who fails to give their name or address to a constable or to a private occupier to $1,000.
specificity.explanation: Multiple precise dollar figures attached to named offences.

specificity.statement: Under this bill, a customer will be allowed one serving of alcohol, limited to once per day. It reduces compliance cost, while maintaining all existing safeguards against serving minors or intoxicated persons.
specificity.explanation: Concrete limit (one serving, once per day) and a stated effect, though the magnitude of cost reduction is unquantified.

specificity.statement: It also extends cellar-door provisions beyond wineries, to breweries and distilleries. Currently, wineries are the only alcohol producers who can charge for samples without holding an on-licence.
specificity.explanation: Names the producers affected and the change, but no figures or timing.

specificity.statement: those members could have a drink at their own club and wouldn't have to get any special licences, but when they go to register at the Kapiti Boating Club on Friday they need to pay $330 for an extra one and then the same the next night when they have the after-match at Waikanae. This bill is all about simplifying those
specificity.explanation: Uses a concrete local example with a dollar figure ($330) to illustrate the licensing problem the bill addresses.

specificity.statement: because the largest item that they sold by turnover was Snapper—that is the Wellington public transport card—and it was slightly, slightly bigger—fractionally bigger—than the amount of food that they sold, we couldn't give them a liquor licence. They had a choice between either giving up the ability to sell public transport cards or not getting a liquor licence.
specificity.explanation: A concrete, detailed real example illustrating an arbitrary licensing rule, though drawn from personal recollection.

specificity.statement: parts of this bill are tightening up the alcohol availability, including clarifying responsibilities for rapid delivery services, which will reduce the risk of delivery to intoxicated and under-age people. It is making common-sense changes to our law; therefore I commend it to the House.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a specific provision (rapid delivery responsibilities) but stays general on how the risk reduction is achieved.

strength.statement: From 1 January 2027, Tai Poutini Polytechnic will operate within The Open Polytechnic of New Zealand. This will ensure that in-person, campus-based vocational education remains available on the West Coast.
strength.explanation: As the Minister driving the vocational-education restructure she is describing a concrete structural change with a set start date, but it is an announcement of a future arrangement rather than completed delivery.

strength.statement: From 1 January, NorthTec will be reestablished as a stand-alone regional polytechnic. Among other financial supports to ensure its continued viability, I am delighted to announce the in-principle investment of $34.7 million for the development of a new Whangārei tertiary hub—subject to business case
strength.explanation: An 'in-principle' investment 'subject to business case' is an announced intention, not yet delivered spending or built facilities.

strength.statement: the unique residential agricultural training facility Telford will be receiving $2.4 million to address deferred maintenance to ensure a fit for purpose, fully functioning agricultural campus.
strength.explanation: A concrete committed allocation to an existing facility, slightly above mid because it is targeted maintenance funding rather than yet-delivered work.

strength.statement: My proposal was simple: that revenue from overseas betting should be ring-fenced, used only for animal welfare purposes, greyhound rehoming, or compensation for those affected.
strength.explanation: Describes a tabled amendment he actually advanced, but it was not adopted, so it is action without delivered result.

forthrightness.statement: From 1 January, NorthTec will be reestablished as a stand-alone regional polytechnic. Among other financial supports to ensure its continued viability, I am delighted to announce the in-principle investment of $34.7 million for the development of a new Whangārei tertiary hub—subject to business case
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers McCallum's question 'What does this announcement mean for Northland?' with concrete figures.

forthrightness.statement: the Eastern Institute of Technology—EIT—will be receiving $10 million to support the rebuild and improvement of its Hawke's Bay campus in Taradale, following Cyclone Gabrielle.
forthrightness.explanation: Direct answer to Kirkpatrick's question about the East Coast, with a specific allocation.

forthrightness.statement: the unique residential agricultural training facility Telford will be receiving $2.4 million to address deferred maintenance to ensure a fit for purpose, fully functioning agricultural campus.
forthrightness.explanation: Direct answer to Patterson's supplementary question about Telford.

forthrightness.statement: She loves running. It's great.
forthrightness.explanation: Answering 'Do you want your dog to race?' he deflects to the dog enjoying running without addressing whether he wants it to race.

veracity.statement: the Eastern Institute of Technology—EIT—will be receiving $10 million to support the rebuild and improvement of its Hawke's Bay campus in Taradale, following Cyclone Gabrielle.
veracity.explanation: A concrete funding figure presented as fact; plausible and consistent with a Government announcement, accepted as accurate absent contrary evidence.

veracity.statement: In 1833, when it became clear it was no longer acceptable for there to be slavery in the world, the British Parliament passed legislation against that slavery, but they made the terrible error of compensating the slave owners for the loss of their industry.
veracity.explanation: Historically accurate: the Slavery Abolition Act 1833 did compensate slave owners; the framing is broadly correct.

veracity.statement: ACT was the only party that stood against the zero carbon Act while every other party in the House voted for it.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate — ACT (David Seymour) cast the sole vote against the Zero Carbon Act in 2019 while other parties supported it.

veracity.statement: Lawful firearm owners were treated as criminals. This House passed legislation, unfairly taking their firearms, and, back then, ACT was the only party that stood up for them.
veracity.explanation: ACT did oppose the 2019 firearm reforms, making 'only party' broadly defensible, but 'treated as criminals' and 'unfairly taking' are loaded characterisations.

veracity.statement: We are shutting down a domestic industry on animal welfare grounds while continuing to allow betting on overseas greyhound racing through the TAB.
veracity.explanation: Accurate — the closure stops domestic racing while overseas greyhound betting via the TAB continues.

veracity.statement: About 230,000 people work in our retail sector, and the cost of retail crime in this country is in the billions.
veracity.explanation: The ~230,000 retail workforce figure is broadly accurate; 'in the billions' for retail crime cost is plausible but loosely stated and unsourced.

veracity.statement: This law has remained virtually unchanged since the 1980s, when its focus was the removal of people from places like farms and private dwellings where the general public had no reason to be.
veracity.explanation: Accurate — the Trespass Act dates from 1980 and has had limited substantive change; the framing of its original focus is fair.

veracity.statement: It also extends cellar-door provisions beyond wineries, to breweries and distilleries. Currently, wineries are the only alcohol producers who can charge for samples without holding an on-licence.
veracity.explanation: Accurate description of the existing winery cellar-door exception relative to breweries/distilleries.

veracity.statement: In 2023, it is estimated that alcohol-related harm cost New Zealand $9.1 billion.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with published NZ estimates of alcohol-related harm costs around this magnitude.

veracity.statement: The Minister has been crystal clear that this bill's aim is about reducing "regulatory burden" and not about reducing harm.
veracity.explanation: Fairly characterises McKee's own framing of the bill as about removing red tape rather than harm reduction.

rigor.statement: if we set the precedent of compensating industries that have moved beyond the social licence of New Zealand, we set a dangerous precedent. There are other industries, if we are to deal, for example, with climate change, that we are likely to need to bring to an end as a Parliament, so we do not support the compensation.
rigor.explanation: A precedent/consistency argument that leans on a slippery-slope structure (compensating here will force compensation everywhere) rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: In 1833, when it became clear it was no longer acceptable for there to be slavery in the world, the British Parliament passed legislation against that slavery, but they made the terrible error of compensating the slave owners for the loss of their industry.
rigor.explanation: Reasoning by historical analogy to argue against compensation; the analogy is acknowledged as imperfect by the speaker but still carries the inference.

rigor.statement: you cannot light the fire and claim the credit for putting it out. In this case, you cannot undermine an industry and then turn around and say that you're saving it.
rigor.explanation: A rhetorical analogy making a coherent consistency point, but it asserts rather than evidences the 'undermine then save' claim.

rigor.statement: We are shutting down a domestic industry on animal welfare grounds while continuing to allow betting on overseas greyhound racing through the TAB.
rigor.explanation: Points to a genuine consistency gap between the stated welfare rationale and continued overseas betting.

rigor.statement: The simple question that needs to be asked is: what actually leads to better outcomes for animals? Is it working with an industry who care about their dogs to improve outcomes, or is it pushing the betting offshore with standards we can't set?
rigor.explanation: Frames a reasonable causal question about welfare outcomes, but presents it as a binary and assumes the industry's good faith rather than evidencing it.

rigor.statement: This change is focused on stopping those offenders from simply moving their criminal activity from store to store. This is a limited power because it will only be available to occupiers of retail, hospitality, and licensed premises to deter retail crime. The occupiers of other types of premises, including places occupied by councils, will not be able to use this power, but, of course, I'm sure the select committee will be interested in the feedback on this issue.
rigor.explanation: Links the power to a defined problem (offenders moving store to store) and bounds it, though the deterrent effect is asserted not evidenced.

rigor.statement: Alcohol is a legal product. The overwhelming majority of New Zealanders consume it without incident and without imposing costs on others. Where alcohol does cause real harm, violence, disorder, drink-driving, and harm to children, the State has both the right and the duty to act decisively, but restricting the freedom of everyone here because of a minority who behave badly is neither fair nor effective.
rigor.explanation: A structured majority/minority and proportionality argument; reasonable but rests on an unquantified 'overwhelming majority' premise.

rigor.statement: Overall, this bill will increase the availability of alcohol in our communities, including at off-licences, which cause the most alcohol-related harm. We should be reducing harm from alcohol, not promoting it to obtain economic growth, which is stated is also the point of this law.
rigor.explanation: Connects availability to harm using a public-health premise, though the 'off-licences cause the most harm' and net-availability claims are asserted rather than demonstrated here.

rigor.statement: because the largest item that they sold by turnover was Snapper—that is the Wellington public transport card—and it was slightly, slightly bigger—fractionally bigger—than the amount of food that they sold, we couldn't give them a liquor licence. They had a choice between either giving up the ability to sell public transport cards or not getting a liquor licence.
rigor.explanation: Uses a single anecdote to argue the law is arbitrary; persuasive but a generalisation from one case.

rigor.statement: there were crusades by some of the agencies. You know, whether it's the Police—the Police in particular, in some cases—or the district licensing commissioners or the public health authorities trying to shut down elements of the industry. It didn't matter how well the businesses were run, but they were still going to have a crack at them, to try and get less alcohol being sold—doesn't matter by who.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping characterisation drawn from personal experience as a commissioner, without supporting data.

rigor.statement: by allowing branded beer products which are branded almost identically to alcoholic products, you are, essentially, by subterfuge, promoting alcohol to the whole community, including young people.
rigor.explanation: A coherent marketing-by-association argument, but the claimed 'subterfuge' promotion effect is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: We are going to have our children pointing to the candy which is sitting next to a Heineken, and they'll think, "Oh, I wonder what that is. That looks flash. I'll try that next time."
rigor.explanation: An imagined-child vignette functioning as an appeal to emotion rather than evidence of an actual effect.

rigor.statement: parts of this bill are tightening up the alcohol availability, including clarifying responsibilities for rapid delivery services, which will reduce the risk of delivery to intoxicated and under-age people. It is making common-sense changes to our law; therefore I commend it to the House.
rigor.explanation: Counters critics by pointing to genuine tightening provisions; a fair point, though 'common-sense' substitutes for detailed justification.

divination.statement: if we set the precedent of compensating industries that have moved beyond the social licence of New Zealand, we set a dangerous precedent. There are other industries, if we are to deal, for example, with climate change, that we are likely to need to bring to an end as a Parliament, so we do not support the compensation.
divination.explanation: Predicts Parliament will need to shut down other industries over climate change — directionally plausible but vague on which, when or how.

divination.statement: Even if it's too late for greyhounds, to somebody listening out there, they will eventually come for your industry, and I hope that there is someone left to speak for you.
divination.explanation: A vague, fear-based prediction that unnamed 'industries' will be banned next; too unspecified and speculative to be well-supported.

divination.statement: Overall, this bill will increase the availability of alcohol in our communities, including at off-licences, which cause the most alcohol-related harm. We should be reducing harm from alcohol, not promoting it to obtain economic growth, which is stated is also the point of this law.
divination.explanation: Predicts the bill will increase alcohol availability in communities — plausible directionally but the net effect is contested given the bill's tightening provisions.

civility.statement: In 1833, when it became clear it was no longer acceptable for there to be slavery in the world, the British Parliament passed legislation against that slavery, but they made the terrible error of compensating the slave owners for the loss of their industry.
civility.explanation: Engages a policy principle and explicitly disclaims equating greyhound racing with slavery, avoiding personal attack.

civility.statement: this industry was not built in Wellington by MPs in this House or by fancy suits in the Beehive. This industry was built by hard-working New Zealanders—Kiwis with rough hands
civility.explanation: 'fancy suits in the Beehive' is a mild dismissive jab but stops short of a personal attack on an individual.

civility.statement: Lawful firearm owners were treated as criminals. This House passed legislation, unfairly taking their firearms, and, back then, ACT was the only party that stood up for them.
civility.explanation: Criticises a legislative process but uses charged framing ('treated as criminals') that edges toward sensationalism.

civility.statement: I just want to commend the good work by the Primary Production Committee to do their very best to reach better outcomes in some very challenging circumstances. There's been a lot of passion and emotion involved in this bill. I want to just leave our thoughts with all of those people who are involved and all of those animals who will find new homes, hopefully.
civility.explanation: Gracious, conciliatory and free of personal attacks despite a contentious bill.

civility.statement: This change is focused on stopping those offenders from simply moving their criminal activity from store to store. This is a limited power because it will only be available to occupiers of retail, hospitality, and licensed premises to deter retail crime. The occupiers of other types of premises, including places occupied by councils, will not be able to use this power, but, of course, I'm sure the select committee will be interested in the feedback on this issue.
civility.explanation: Policy-focused, explains scope and limits and explicitly invites select committee scrutiny.

civility.statement: To those who have concerns: back the bill to select committee. Give it proper scrutiny and suggest improvements. That is how Parliament is supposed to work. As with all my bills, my door is open to any MP who would like to better understand the changes that are being made.
civility.explanation: Respectful, process-focused and explicitly open to other MPs.

civility.statement: The Minister has been crystal clear that this bill's aim is about reducing "regulatory burden" and not about reducing harm.
civility.explanation: Critical but engages the Minister's stated rationale rather than attacking her personally.

civility.statement: I do agree with one thing that the Green Party have said, and that is that I do think it is time for us to have a good look at the Sale and Supply of Alcohol Act across the board.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of an opponent's valid point.

civility.statement: there were crusades by some of the agencies. You know, whether it's the Police—the Police in particular, in some cases—or the district licensing commissioners or the public health authorities trying to shut down elements of the industry. It didn't matter how well the businesses were run, but they were still going to have a crack at them, to try and get less alcohol being sold—doesn't matter by who.
civility.explanation: Characterises agencies as on 'crusades'; pointed but aimed at institutional conduct rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: We are going to have our children pointing to the candy which is sitting next to a Heineken, and they'll think, "Oh, I wonder what that is. That looks flash. I'll try that next time."
civility.explanation: Makes its point through illustration without attacking opponents personally.

civility.statement: parts of this bill are tightening up the alcohol availability, including clarifying responsibilities for rapid delivery services, which will reduce the risk of delivery to intoxicated and under-age people. It is making common-sense changes to our law; therefore I commend it to the House.
civility.explanation: Calm, policy-focused contribution engaging the substance raised by other speakers.

charisma.statement: this industry was not built in Wellington by MPs in this House or by fancy suits in the Beehive. This industry was built by hard-working New Zealanders—Kiwis with rough hands
charisma.explanation: Populist rural rallying that draws an us-vs-Wellington line rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: Even if it's too late for greyhounds, to somebody listening out there, they will eventually come for your industry, and I hope that there is someone left to speak for you.
charisma.explanation: Rallies sympathisers via threat rather than persuading the unconvinced.

charisma.statement: I just want to commend the good work by the Primary Production Committee to do their very best to reach better outcomes in some very challenging circumstances. There's been a lot of passion and emotion involved in this bill. I want to just leave our thoughts with all of those people who are involved and all of those animals who will find new homes, hopefully.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the difficulty for all sides and extends goodwill, though it does not actively bridge across positions.

charisma.statement: To those who have concerns: back the bill to select committee. Give it proper scrutiny and suggest improvements. That is how Parliament is supposed to work. As with all my bills, my door is open to any MP who would like to better understand the changes that are being made.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, invites opponents into the process and offers engagement rather than dismissing concerns.

charisma.statement: I do agree with one thing that the Green Party have said, and that is that I do think it is time for us to have a good look at the Sale and Supply of Alcohol Act across the board.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly finds common ground with an opposing party, modelling cross-party agreement.

authenticity.statement: ACT was the only party that stood against the zero carbon Act while every other party in the House voted for it.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with ACT's long-held contrarian positioning; cites its own voting record to establish consistency.

authenticity.statement: The Green Party have always and will always support sensible, evidence-based drug harm minimisation and this place, Parliament, needs to have the courage to do that.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with the Greens' long-standing, on-record harm-reduction stance; words align with the party's established position.

civility.statement: We are not going to be driven by Green Luddites or ill-informed people about energy security.
civility.explanation: Dismisses opponents as 'Green Luddites' and 'ill-informed' — a belittling personal characterisation rather than engagement with their energy arguments.

civility.statement: I want to finish my contribution with a tribute to my member and friend, the Hon Judith Collins, who has provided a great service to our nation and our country and to wish her well in her future career.
civility.explanation: Gracious, respectful tribute to a colleague — constructive and warm in tone.

civility.statement: In 2024, the Greens put out He Ara Anamata, our plan to reduce climate emissions five times faster than this pamphlet plan of this current Government, to transform our energy system away from fossil fuel dependency and improving peoples' quality of life at the same time.
civility.explanation: Dismissive 'pamphlet plan' jab at the Government, but the criticism is aimed at the policy, not personally.

civility.statement: The very people who are bearing the most right now, who are paying for the results of a war that they did not decide to have—a war that this Prime Minister refuses to condemn even while it still continues to have a very real impact on our people right now.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of the PM's refusal to condemn the war — about his conduct/position rather than a personal insult, but accusatory in tone.

civility.statement: He is the leader of our country and has been remarkably missing from this fuel crisis. At a time when we have care and support workers who cannot afford to go to their jobs... where is the Prime Minister?
civility.explanation: Criticism of the PM's visibility and leadership during the crisis — pointed but directed at conduct, using a repeated rhetorical 'where is' device.

civility.statement: we are now in a position where they can only help 7 percent of households, where 93 percent of household—"Too bad for you", according to this Government, "Too bad."
civility.explanation: Puts invented words ('Too bad for you') in the Government's mouth — a strawman that misrepresents the opponent's position.

civility.statement: I know it's April Fools today, but I just heard what I thought was a speech from the Labour's finance spokesperson. I was fooled, actually.
civility.explanation: Opening mockery of an opponent's speech as an April Fools joke — a cheap shot rather than engagement with substance.

civility.statement: This is somebody who wants the trust of New Zealand just to be Prime Minister and here is yet more information as the story unwinds that he does not deserve that trust.
civility.explanation: Concludes an opponent 'does not deserve trust' — an attack on character/fitness, though built on a documentary argument rather than a bare insult.

civility.statement: It's very clear to me, from the speeches that we've heard from members opposite, that what they see in leadership is seeking the limelight in the theatrette, rather than quiet work in the background to secure fuel supply.
civility.explanation: Characterises opponents as limelight-seekers rather than engaging their actual arguments — a dismissive imputation of motive.

civility.statement: That was what David Seymour spent his time on, and that shows why the ACT Party is losing in the polls at the moment.
civility.explanation: Turns a critique of Seymour's speech into a jab about his party's polling rather than the substance.

civility.statement: So Te Tai Tonga has a simple message for the Minister: leave some fish for the mokos, Shane—leave some fish for the mokos. That's the message from Te Tai Tonga: be a good kaitiaki—be a good kaitiaki.
civility.explanation: Direct, pointed appeal to the Minister by name, but framed as a values plea rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: we saw the COVID royal commission inquiry and we saw $60 billion wasted, half of that and not even associated with the direct response of COVID; shovel-ready projects that were nowhere near a shovel, lump-sum payments to dead people.
civility.explanation: Mocking characterisation ('nowhere near a shovel') of the previous government's programmes.

civility.statement: But you know why they're not signing it? Do you know why they're politicking in the midst of a campaign year? Because they're jealous. Because they didn't do it.
civility.explanation: Attributes petty 'jealousy' to opponents — a personal-motive attack rather than engagement with their reasons.

civility.statement: So in the midst of challenging times in New Zealand, I'm pleased to report that the adults are in the room and this Government will steer New Zealand through these rocky waters.
civility.explanation: 'The adults are in the room' implies opponents are childish/incompetent — a disparaging contrast.

civility.statement: I find it absolutely outrageous that the Government backbenchers, with their speaking lines over there, haven't even bothered to talk about the people that are actually doing it tough in our communities.
civility.explanation: Criticises opponents as reciting 'speaking lines' and ignoring struggling people — pointed and accusatory, but about conduct in the debate.

civility.statement: Reassurance is not a plan, talking points are not a plan, and rural New Zealand knows it.
civility.explanation: Sharp critique of the Government's response as empty words — aimed at the substance of their approach rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: So why has the upkeep of Mr Carter's grave not been included in the legislation, and can the member confirm that the grave ultimately will still be maintained?
civility.explanation: Respectful, substance-focused scrutiny of the bill, engaging directly with the select committee's report.

civility.statement: The National Party, on this side, has a variety of views. We are a broad church. You've heard from me in favour of the legislation, you'll hear from colleagues opposed to it, but, ultimately, I think that's what makes politics really, really important in this place.
civility.explanation: Respectfully recognises colleagues who hold the opposite view as part of a healthy debate.

civility.statement: I am curious to know whether the member has researched that and has satisfied himself that he's really comfortable with what happened at that period... I know that when we were speaking about this previously in the House, there may have been some sensitivities for some of those who were in the Parliament listening to a farewell speech from one of our Māori colleagues.
civility.explanation: Raises a sensitive historical question carefully and respectfully, explicitly disclaiming any accusation about the will itself.

charisma.statement: We are not going to be driven by Green Luddites or ill-informed people about energy security.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing that rallies his own side by denigrating opponents; makes no attempt to persuade or build common ground.

charisma.statement: It's very clear that we can't control oil prices, we can't control the conflict in the Middle East, but what we can control and what we can do as a Government is respond in a very considered and deliberate way.
charisma.explanation: Calm, reassuring tone aimed at a general audience, but is partisan framing of 'our Government' rather than cross-party bridge-building.

charisma.statement: For at least the past three decades, the Greens have consistently set out a pathway to better protect our people and our living systems against the inevitable topple of fossil fuel dependency—a stable planet that we can all be proud of passing on to our mokopuna.
charisma.explanation: Values-driven and inclusive in vision ('we can all be proud'), but speaks for the Greens' own position rather than reaching across the aisle.

charisma.statement: He is the leader of our country and has been remarkably missing from this fuel crisis. At a time when we have care and support workers who cannot afford to go to their jobs... where is the Prime Minister?
charisma.explanation: Effective rhetorical hook (the 'Where's Wally' frame) but purely combative, appealing to her own side.

charisma.statement: I know that the next few months will be extremely tough for this country... but this too shall pass and I remain optimistic in this country. Brighter days will return, because this Government has a good plan.
charisma.explanation: Optimistic, steadying message, but credits 'this Government' and so appeals mainly to his own side.

charisma.statement: It's very clear to me, from the speeches that we've heard from members opposite, that what they see in leadership is seeking the limelight in the theatrette, rather than quiet work in the background to secure fuel supply.
charisma.explanation: Combative contrast drawn to denigrate the other side; no attempt at common ground.

charisma.statement: I get sick and tired when I hear members of the Opposition stand up and say, "Oh, they've U-turned; oh, they've changed their mind." You know what? Isn't that amazing leadership. To listen to the people and adjust our response to make sure that we are delivering for Kiwis and what they want.
charisma.explanation: Confident rhetorical reframing, but defensive and aimed at her own side's supporters.

charisma.statement: So Te Tai Tonga has a simple message for the Minister: leave some fish for the mokos, Shane—leave some fish for the mokos. That's the message from Te Tai Tonga: be a good kaitiaki—be a good kaitiaki.
charisma.explanation: Memorable, values-based refrain ('leave some fish for the mokos'), though addressed in opposition to the Minister rather than building consensus.

charisma.statement: The four-phase plan that we've seen, that's now in the public domain, is simple yet pragmatic, and it's so good, even the Australians are starting to copy it.
charisma.explanation: Upbeat selling of the Government's plan, but boastful and appealing only to supporters.

charisma.statement: So in the midst of challenging times in New Zealand, I'm pleased to report that the adults are in the room and this Government will steer New Zealand through these rocky waters.
charisma.explanation: Reassuring steer-through-the-storm image, but self-flattering and partisan.

charisma.statement: Reassurance is not a plan, talking points are not a plan, and rural New Zealand knows it.
charisma.explanation: Crisp rhetorical line, but combative and addressed to his own side.

charisma.statement: The National Party, on this side, has a variety of views. We are a broad church. You've heard from me in favour of the legislation, you'll hear from colleagues opposed to it, but, ultimately, I think that's what makes politics really, really important in this place.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges legitimate internal disagreement and frames conscience debate as valuable — open and inclusive in tone.

specificity.statement: It's very clear that we can't control oil prices, we can't control the conflict in the Middle East, but what we can control and what we can do as a Government is respond in a very considered and deliberate way.
specificity.explanation: States a direction ('considered and deliberate') but names no mechanism, figure, or measure — generic framing of the response.

specificity.statement: That's why our Government has provided relief to 143,000 families to ease the pressure of fuel prices—as of today, 143,000 families. Yes, we have targeted those working families with children, because we know the additional costs that they face.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete figure (143,000 families) and the targeted cohort (working families with children).

specificity.statement: What we do know also from 1 April is that 1.5 million New Zealanders—whether they are superannuitants, whether they receive the veteran's pension, whether they are students, whether they are main beneficiaries... also will see a lift today on 1 April to support the cost of living challenges.
specificity.explanation: Names a figure (1.5 million) and lists the categories affected, but no amount of the lift is stated.

specificity.statement: In 2024, the Greens put out He Ara Anamata, our plan to reduce climate emissions five times faster than this pamphlet plan of this current Government, to transform our energy system away from fossil fuel dependency and improving peoples' quality of life at the same time.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete plan and a comparative magnitude ('five times faster'), but no figures or mechanisms behind the claim.

specificity.statement: The Clean Car Discount wound back, the billion dollar liquefied natural gas terminal, the $200 million for fossil fuel companies, a range of energy funds and efficiency funds that have been pulled back, and $20 billion a year on fossil fuels—$29 million a day.
specificity.explanation: Dense list of named policies and dollar figures (billion-dollar terminal, $200 million, $20 billion/year, $29 million/day).

specificity.statement: There is no civil defence payment opened up for Hokianga and the North right now. Why? Why is their stress not enough?
specificity.explanation: Names the place (Hokianga/the North) and the specific support missing, though no figures.

specificity.statement: we are now in a position where they can only help 7 percent of households, where 93 percent of household—"Too bad for you", according to this Government, "Too bad."
specificity.explanation: Uses concrete percentages, but the figures are asserted without source.

specificity.statement: The interesting thing is the possible closure of this strait wasn't just happening this year; it was actually initially happening last year, in June 2025.
specificity.explanation: Anchors the claim to a specific month and year.

specificity.statement: We've established a ministerial oversight group that is getting briefings twice daily—twice daily—from a talented group of people that are monitoring the situation.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete structure (ministerial oversight group) and cadence (twice-daily briefings).

specificity.statement: We have debt levels—nominal debt—of nearly $200 billion. The interest on that debt this year alone is nearing $10 billion.
specificity.explanation: Two precise figures (≈$200b debt, ≈$10b interest) anchoring the fiscal argument.

specificity.statement: on 5 November 2021, the COVID-19 Vaccine Technical Advisory Group provided advice to the Ministry of Health that says that younger groups are "more at risk than older age groups of myocarditis after the second dose" and it recommended consideration of one dose for those 18 and under for the education mandate.
specificity.explanation: Exact date, body, quoted wording, and the specific recommendation.

specificity.statement: they did this in March 2024—they removed the exemption for light electric vehicles and for plug-in hybrid electric vehicles. They have removed the exemption for road user charges. So they made it more expensive to own an EV.
specificity.explanation: Names the date, the specific exemptions removed, and the vehicle categories.

specificity.statement: they cancelled the Clean Car Discount, and what happened as a result of that? The number of electric vehicles (EV) being bought and put into circulation on our roads in this country fell dramatically.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy and direction of effect but gives no figures for the decline.

specificity.statement: the reforms that are before Parliament failed to address the root cause of our declining fisheries: namely overfishing, over allocation, destructive fishing practises that have persisted for far too long.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete mechanisms (overfishing, over-allocation, destructive practices) but no figures.

specificity.statement: Yet here we are, giving more fish to commercial interests, making it easier for them to catch more with less oversight, blocking camera footage on boats, legalising the dumping of fish.
specificity.explanation: Lists concrete claimed effects of the reform (camera footage, dumping, oversight).

specificity.statement: we saw the COVID royal commission inquiry and we saw $60 billion wasted, half of that and not even associated with the direct response of COVID; shovel-ready projects that were nowhere near a shovel, lump-sum payments to dead people.
specificity.explanation: Cites a headline figure and named categories of spending, but the framing is loose.

specificity.statement: We know that the Gulf supplies 20 percent but there's 80 percent of other alternatives and we're keeping all options open.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete share (20% from the Gulf, 80% alternatives), though 'keeping all options open' is vague.

specificity.statement: You can't shop around when you live an hour from town, you can't take public transport when there isn't any, and you can't just absorb rising costs where every litre of fuel underpins your livelihood, whether that's farming, forestry, tourism or simply trying to get your kids to school.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete circumstances and sectors, though without figures.

specificity.statement: Yes, I can confirm that the grave will still be maintained. It's a very good question... So the Carter Society has already given a formal undertaking to continue maintaining the grave. The select committee was satisfied with that assurance.
specificity.explanation: Cites the formal undertaking, the responsible body, and the 1961 Act origin of the obligation.

specificity.statement: it is simply about that: giving the trust the necessary time to complete those final accounts and to make the distributions and wind up the trust in an orderly manner. The rest of the bill, including the immediate repeal of the outdated ministerial powers, can commence straight away.
specificity.explanation: Explains the mechanism and which parts commence when, though without dates beyond 'six months after Royal assent'.

specificity.statement: residents will see no negative impact. Fees for contracted long-time residential care are actually already set nationally under the Residential Care and Disability Support Services Act 2018. So removing the outdated ministerial power in section 12 does not change what the residents may pay.
specificity.explanation: Cites the specific governing Act and the relevant section being repealed.

specificity.statement: The original will provide an annuity to the Anglican vicar of Carterton. The $50,000 is an agreed lump-sum equivalent that both the parish and the society have accepted in full satisfaction of that obligation. The balance then goes to the Carter Society... Public Trust, as executor, has confirmed that this is the most practical and equitable outcome.
specificity.explanation: Explains the figure, the original annuity it replaces, who agreed it, and the executor's confirmation.

specificity.statement: So why has the upkeep of Mr Carter's grave not been included in the legislation, and can the member confirm that the grave ultimately will still be maintained?
specificity.explanation: Asks a precise, well-targeted question citing section 7(a) and the specific grave-upkeep obligation.

veracity.statement: That's why our Government has provided relief to 143,000 families to ease the pressure of fuel prices—as of today, 143,000 families. Yes, we have targeted those working families with children, because we know the additional costs that they face.
veracity.explanation: Specific quantified claim that is plausible but not verifiable from the text alone.

veracity.statement: What we do know also from 1 April is that 1.5 million New Zealanders—whether they are superannuitants, whether they receive the veteran's pension, whether they are students, whether they are main beneficiaries... also will see a lift today on 1 April to support the cost of living challenges.
veracity.explanation: The 1 April adjustment is the annual indexation that happens every year; presenting it as crisis response is true but somewhat misleading context.

veracity.statement: The Clean Car Discount wound back, the billion dollar liquefied natural gas terminal, the $200 million for fossil fuel companies, a range of energy funds and efficiency funds that have been pulled back, and $20 billion a year on fossil fuels—$29 million a day.
veracity.explanation: Several specific figures, some of which are contestable or aggregate fossil-fuel spending in a way that may overstate direct government subsidy; not verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: There is no civil defence payment opened up for Hokianga and the North right now. Why? Why is their stress not enough?
veracity.explanation: Specific factual assertion about the absence of a civil defence payment; plausible but unverified.

veracity.statement: we are now in a position where they can only help 7 percent of households, where 93 percent of household—"Too bad for you", according to this Government, "Too bad."
veracity.explanation: The 7%/93% framing is a contestable interpretation and the quoted 'Too bad' is a fabricated paraphrase, making the claim misleading.

veracity.statement: The interesting thing is the possible closure of this strait wasn't just happening this year; it was actually initially happening last year, in June 2025.
veracity.explanation: Specific dated factual claim (June 2025) used to argue the Government had earlier warning; plausible but unverified.

veracity.statement: We have debt levels—nominal debt—of nearly $200 billion. The interest on that debt this year alone is nearing $10 billion.
veracity.explanation: Figures are in the right order of magnitude for NZ Crown debt and finance costs; broadly accurate though rounded.

veracity.statement: We already had a downgrade by Moody's, who have put our economy and Government on negative watch as a result, so there is no alternative to our approach.
veracity.explanation: Claims a Moody's downgrade and negative watch; NZ has historically held strong ratings, so this assertion is doubtful and unverified from the text.

veracity.statement: on 5 November 2021, the COVID-19 Vaccine Technical Advisory Group provided advice to the Ministry of Health that says that younger groups are "more at risk than older age groups of myocarditis after the second dose" and it recommended consideration of one dose for those 18 and under for the education mandate.
veracity.explanation: Dated, quoted, document-specific claim about CV-TAG advice; presented with precision though selectively framed to indict Hipkins.

veracity.statement: In response to that crisis, when we saved 20,000 lives in New Zealand, when we saved businesses, and when we saved jobs, they say we got it wrong.
veracity.explanation: The '20,000 lives saved' figure is a modelled estimate stated as fact; defensible but uncertain and uncited.

veracity.statement: they did this in March 2024—they removed the exemption for light electric vehicles and for plug-in hybrid electric vehicles. They have removed the exemption for road user charges. So they made it more expensive to own an EV.
veracity.explanation: Dated, specific policy claim (March 2024 RUC exemption removal) that matches the known record.

veracity.statement: they cancelled the Clean Car Discount, and what happened as a result of that? The number of electric vehicles (EV) being bought and put into circulation on our roads in this country fell dramatically.
veracity.explanation: EV registrations did fall sharply after the Clean Car Discount ended; broadly accurate, 'dramatically' is somewhat loose.

veracity.statement: ignoring the fact that if you get COVID, you have a greater risk of Myocarditis than there ever was from the vaccine.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the general medical finding that COVID infection carries higher myocarditis risk than vaccination; broadly accurate as a rebuttal.

veracity.statement: If we think about our deep-sea species like hoki and orange roughy, they have almost been pushed to the brink of extinction.
veracity.explanation: Orange roughy has been heavily depleted, but hoki is generally regarded as relatively well-managed; lumping them as near-extinction overstates the case.

veracity.statement: Yet here we are, giving more fish to commercial interests, making it easier for them to catch more with less oversight, blocking camera footage on boats, legalising the dumping of fish.
veracity.explanation: A pointed, contestable characterisation of the reforms ('legalising dumping') that frames provisions in their least favourable light.

veracity.statement: we saw the COVID royal commission inquiry and we saw $60 billion wasted, half of that and not even associated with the direct response of COVID; shovel-ready projects that were nowhere near a shovel, lump-sum payments to dead people.
veracity.explanation: '$60 billion wasted' and 'payments to dead people' are hyperbolic, contestable framings of COVID spending presented as established fact.

veracity.statement: The four-phase plan that we've seen, that's now in the public domain, is simple yet pragmatic, and it's so good, even the Australians are starting to copy it.
veracity.explanation: The claim that Australia is copying the plan is unsubstantiated and self-congratulatory.

veracity.statement: We know that the Gulf supplies 20 percent but there's 80 percent of other alternatives and we're keeping all options open.
veracity.explanation: The 20/80 split is a clean round figure asserted without source; plausible but unverified.

veracity.statement: they delivered a message that should concern every member of this House: when financial stress increases, so does family violence. That's not theory; that is a reality.
veracity.explanation: The link between financial stress and family violence is supported by research; stated firmly though without specific data.

veracity.statement: residents will see no negative impact. Fees for contracted long-time residential care are actually already set nationally under the Residential Care and Disability Support Services Act 2018. So removing the outdated ministerial power in section 12 does not change what the residents may pay.
veracity.explanation: Correctly notes residential care fees are nationally set under that Act; the legal point is accurate as far as can be checked.

strength.statement: That's why our Government has provided relief to 143,000 families to ease the pressure of fuel prices—as of today, 143,000 families. Yes, we have targeted those working families with children, because we know the additional costs that they face.
strength.explanation: Claims delivered support effective today, but framed as targeted tax relief whose follow-through is partly an indexation already scheduled.

strength.statement: What we do know also from 1 April is that 1.5 million New Zealanders—whether they are superannuitants, whether they receive the veteran's pension, whether they are students, whether they are main beneficiaries... also will see a lift today on 1 April to support the cost of living challenges.
strength.explanation: Real delivery, but it is routine annual indexation rather than a new crisis measure the Government drove through.

strength.statement: We've established a ministerial oversight group that is getting briefings twice daily—twice daily—from a talented group of people that are monitoring the situation.
strength.explanation: Describes a concrete monitoring mechanism actually stood up, though delivery of outcomes is still in progress.

authenticity.statement: For at least the past three decades, the Greens have consistently set out a pathway to better protect our people and our living systems against the inevitable topple of fossil fuel dependency—a stable planet that we can all be proud of passing on to our mokopuna.
authenticity.explanation: Claims long-standing consistency and immediately backs it with the historical record (Rod Donald's 2001 vision), supporting the words-match-record claim.

authenticity.statement: I get sick and tired when I hear members of the Opposition stand up and say, "Oh, they've U-turned; oh, they've changed their mind." You know what? Isn't that amazing leadership. To listen to the people and adjust our response to make sure that we are delivering for Kiwis and what they want.
authenticity.explanation: Reframes policy reversals as responsive listening — a defensible reinterpretation of shifting positions rather than denial of them.

authenticity.statement: In response to that crisis, when we saved 20,000 lives in New Zealand, when we saved businesses, and when we saved jobs, they say we got it wrong.
authenticity.explanation: Defends her own government's record consistently with Labour's prior position on the COVID response.

rigor.statement: We already had a downgrade by Moody's, who have put our economy and Government on negative watch as a result, so there is no alternative to our approach.
rigor.explanation: Concludes 'there is no alternative' — a false dichotomy that closes off other policy options without argument.

rigor.statement: If we borrow more, like the other side were wont to do, what's going to happen is the interest cost for servicing that debt goes even higher.
rigor.explanation: The premise-to-conclusion link (more borrowing → higher servicing cost) is logically sound, though it leans on a partisan characterisation of 'the other side'.

rigor.statement: Fundamentally, there are only two possibilities here. Either he really did manage to avoid reading anything through this whole period... Or when he did it, the Ministry of Health, who were issuing that advice didn't think to get on the phone and say... I don't think that that is remotely credible.
rigor.explanation: Builds a documented timeline, but the 'only two possibilities' move is a false dichotomy that excludes other explanations (e.g. imperfect recall of detail).

rigor.statement: they did this in March 2024—they removed the exemption for light electric vehicles and for plug-in hybrid electric vehicles. They have removed the exemption for road user charges. So they made it more expensive to own an EV.
rigor.explanation: Chains specific policy changes to a coherent conclusion about EV cost, though without quantifying the effect.

rigor.statement: ignoring the fact that if you get COVID, you have a greater risk of Myocarditis than there ever was from the vaccine.
rigor.explanation: Counters Seymour's framing with a relevant comparative-risk point, though stated without citation.

rigor.statement: That was what David Seymour spent his time on, and that shows why the ACT Party is losing in the polls at the moment.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur — a speech topic does not establish the cause of polling movements.

rigor.statement: the reforms that are before Parliament failed to address the root cause of our declining fisheries: namely overfishing, over allocation, destructive fishing practises that have persisted for far too long.
rigor.explanation: Identifies named causal drivers and argues the reforms miss them; reasoned, though the causal claims are asserted rather than evidenced here.

rigor.statement: But you know why they're not signing it? Do you know why they're politicking in the midst of a campaign year? Because they're jealous. Because they didn't do it.
rigor.explanation: Pure speculation about motive ('jealous') offered as explanation with no evidence.

rigor.statement: You can't shop around when you live an hour from town, you can't take public transport when there isn't any, and you can't just absorb rising costs where every litre of fuel underpins your livelihood, whether that's farming, forestry, tourism or simply trying to get your kids to school.
rigor.explanation: Builds a concrete, logically coherent case for why fuel shocks hit rural communities hardest, grounded in plausible everyday constraints.

rigor.statement: they delivered a message that should concern every member of this House: when financial stress increases, so does family violence. That's not theory; that is a reality.
rigor.explanation: Draws on a frontline organisation's evidence to connect economic pressure to social harm, a defensible if unquantified inference.

divination.statement: I know that the next few months will be extremely tough for this country... but this too shall pass and I remain optimistic in this country. Brighter days will return, because this Government has a good plan.
divination.explanation: Predicts tough months followed by recovery; directionally plausible but too vague on timeframe and magnitude to falsify precisely.

divination.statement: If we think about our deep-sea species like hoki and orange roughy, they have almost been pushed to the brink of extinction.
divination.explanation: Implies continued collapse of these stocks; directionally arguable for orange roughy but overstated and not clearly forecast.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I can confirm that the grave will still be maintained. It's a very good question... So the Carter Society has already given a formal undertaking to continue maintaining the grave. The select committee was satisfied with that assurance.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the question asked (will the grave be maintained?) with an unequivocal yes and the supporting basis.

forthrightness.statement: it is simply about that: giving the trust the necessary time to complete those final accounts and to make the distributions and wind up the trust in an orderly manner. The rest of the bill, including the immediate repeal of the outdated ministerial powers, can commence straight away.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers directly why a staggered commencement was chosen — to allow time for final accounts and orderly wind-up.

forthrightness.statement: residents will see no negative impact. Fees for contracted long-time residential care are actually already set nationally under the Residential Care and Disability Support Services Act 2018. So removing the outdated ministerial power in section 12 does not change what the residents may pay.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly addresses the question about fees and services for care-home residents with a clear 'no negative impact' and reasoning.

forthrightness.statement: Look, it's not in this specific bit of legislation, so it's not something that I've considered per se. That's speculative in terms of what changes there may be, but this bill doesn't speak to those as well.
forthrightness.explanation: Declines to answer the retirement-villages question, but legitimately on the grounds it is outside the bill's scope, and says so plainly rather than pivoting to talking points.

forthrightness.statement: Certainly nothing that I'm aware of, nor fellow Wairarapa MPs. It's never been raised. I still come back to the very generous legacy of Charles Rooking Carter.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to the question about historical land issues but only asserts unawareness, not the depth of research that was asked about, then pivots to praising the legacy.

forthrightness.statement: The original will provide an annuity to the Anglican vicar of Carterton. The $50,000 is an agreed lump-sum equivalent that both the parish and the society have accepted in full satisfaction of that obligation. The balance then goes to the Carter Society... Public Trust, as executor, has confirmed that this is the most practical and equitable outcome.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers why $50,000 goes to the parish and whether it is consistent with the will, with the underlying rationale.

forthrightness.statement: Well, international commodity prices rise and fall. That's inevitable. You don't change your approach or strategy just because of that. What I can say is that banning oil and gas put a chilling effect on this country. The Lake Onslow project, at $17 billion—to be delivered in 2037 at $8,000 a household—and $800 megawatt per hour wholesale electricity prices means that we have a failed energy policy. We have dry-year risk, and, as a result, this has actually been a good move, because it has lowered the forward electricity prices by about $25 since we made that announcement.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he stands by the LNG decision given the price spike; he implicitly defends it but pivots to attacking Lake Onslow and Labour rather than addressing the price-spike framing.

forthrightness.statement: I reject the characterisation of that question, because this is about lowering power bills by about $50 for every single household in this country. This is a backup source of energy, so that we don't end up in the situation that the member and his Government created last time.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether the Government assessed supply/price-disruption risk; gives no answer and reframes to talking points.

forthrightness.statement: This is a natural thing—that LNG prices go up and down as a global commodity price—but, irrespective of that, it is still the right answer to make sure we have a backup option to deliver dry-year risk, so we take the risk premium down—
forthrightness.explanation: Asked a pointed yes/no — 'did it assess or did it not assess' the risk — and again declines to say either way.

forthrightness.statement: Look, no disrespect, but I'm not taking lectures from that member on energy policy. I saw some wonderful comments that we should be more independent and have an independent energy policy. Well, actually, the actions of that member's Government created an importation of Indonesian coal and didn't actually create the independent energy policy that we are creating through an "and, and, and" approach of lots of initiatives.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the National Infrastructure Plan was wrong on LNG and electricity prices; never engages the Plan, as the Speaker's point of order noted.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, he was, because, actually, we have taken a policy in our Government that we table the advice, and then we make some decisions. What we don't do is create an $800 megawatt per hour cost that ends up shutting down mills, and low and middle income working New Zealanders lose their jobs. That's exactly what that member did—economic vandal, arsonist, now complaining about the fire that we're putting out that you created.
forthrightness.explanation: Does directly answer 'yes, he was wrong' about the Commissioner, but immediately diverts into attack rather than substantiating.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I think it's a bit disgraceful and embarrassing for the member to compare Ukraine with Iran. But, again, as I said yesterday, it is up for the Israelis and the Americans to give justification for the legality of their strikes. We are not party to the information or intelligence that they have received. It would be wrong of New Zealand, either way, to jump to conclusions. We need fact and evidence to be produced, and that's what we would reasonably expect.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why he accepts the US justification when NZ rejected Russia's parallel claim; he does state his reasoning (not party to the intelligence, won't pre-judge), though he sidesteps the consistency point.

forthrightness.statement: That is a matter for the Minister of Immigration; I encourage the member to direct her question to her.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he would use his power to enable visa extensions; deflects to another Minister, though arguably a legitimate transfer of portfolio responsibility.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I can assure the member that all New Zealand intelligence collected or shared is actually in accordance with New Zealand law.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically whether he has sought briefings on Rocket Lab satellites supporting US strikes; gives a general legality assurance rather than answering the question.

forthrightness.statement: Our officials are talking to the Americans. They are free to set their own requirements as they need, and, of course, those official conversations are ongoing.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to commit to transparency on biometric information sharing and safeguards; does not commit and offers only that conversations are ongoing.

forthrightness.statement: Well, as I've previously said and I've said publicly, this is a Government that wants to develop a critical minerals sector. It's very important that we do. Why is it? Because it's critical minerals that appear in EVs; it's critical minerals that appear in solar panels. We've got a lot of them, and we want to be independent, and we want to develop that sector. So we have ongoing conversations with a number of parties around the world that want access to critical minerals, as you would reasonably expect, but we have not made any final decisions, and, when we do, the member will find out about it.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why he called the matter 'frothy'/'speculative' when he had been briefed in November 2025; does not address the apparent contradiction at all.

forthrightness.statement: It is a little early to say whether the conflict is having a significant impact on the economy yet. As I said yesterday, there is likely to be an impact, but what that is and how quickly things get back to normal will depend on the nature, severity, and duration of the disruption arising from this conflict. … Key channels by which events in the Middle East could affect New Zealand are an increase in oil prices, shipping and air disruptions and freight costs, demand for New Zealand exports, and risk aversion in financial markets that affects the New Zealand dollar and global growth. To what extent those channels operate is yet to be seen. The Government is monitoring events closely.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly addresses whether Middle East events are affecting the economy, candidly conceding it is too early to know and laying out the channels.

forthrightness.statement: Brent crude oil ended the day at US$82 a barrel, up from around $72 before the weekend. Global equity markets fell, with the S&P 500 down 0.7 percent and the Nikkei down 3.1 percent. We are observing volatility in these numbers during the course of trading hours. The New Zealand dollar is 0.5c lower against the US dollar compared to yesterday.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how markets reacted overnight; answers with precise, on-point data.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, in the context in which they were given, including my statement yesterday that the member "wishes to return to the monetary policy framework that resulted in New Zealand's highest period of inflation in recent history". At a time of heightened global instability, proposing to dilute the Reserve Bank's focus on inflation is the last thing New Zealand needs.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers 'yes' she stands by her statements and reaffirms the contested one.

forthrightness.statement: In the video the member refers to, there are five things I said a National Government would do. We would stop adding costs to farmers: tick—achieved. We would make sure they had the workers they need: tick—achieved. We would bring Government spending under control: tick—that's what we're doing. We would focus the Reserve Bank on fighting inflation: tick—that's what we've done. We would let you keep more of what you earn with our plan for tax reduction: tick—we delivered tax relief.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked 'when' Kiwis will pay less at the checkout; never gives a date, pivots to a counterfactual and a five-item checklist.

forthrightness.statement: The member is being, I think, quite disingenuous. It is clear from my statement and the work that the Government is doing that our plan is about ensuring that prices in the future would be lower than would otherwise be the case. … I stand by this Government's view that increasing retail competition in the grocery sector could result in a situation in which prices are lower than would otherwise be the case.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how much the average weekly grocery bill has fallen; gives no figure and shifts to a 'lower than would otherwise be the case' counterfactual.
