forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether any protected land is off-limits to mining, he cites the DOC estate but does not directly say what is excluded.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, and particularly our income tax relief, raising thresholds for working New Zealanders.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he stands by his Government's statements and actions, he directly answers 'Yes' and offers an example.

forthrightness.statement: Well, actually, food inflation's up 3.4 percent from memory; it was up 12.5 percent under his Government. So food price inflation exists, and as I said to him yesterday, deflation is not good for an economy, but food price inflation—there's more to do, but at 3.4 percent it's better than 12.5 percent, which he delivered.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked the dollar figure of a family's weekly grocery shop, he answers with inflation rates instead of the spend figure requested.

forthrightness.statement: Well, again, that's why I would say to the member, get in behind repealing the oil and gas ban, get in behind the fast-track legislation that's generating an increase in renewables in this country.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked the dollar figure of a family's monthly power bill, he gives no figure and instead demands the questioner back his policies.

forthrightness.statement: Well, again, I'll just say to the member, if he actually cares about the impact of the cost of living on New Zealanders, why doesn't he propose some policy to actually come to the table with? Why doesn't he support the rates cap? ... And why doesn't he actually just support extending prescriptions, saving healthcare costs for regular New Zealanders?
forthrightness.explanation: Asked the monthly cost of home, contents and car insurance, he provides no figure and turns the question back on the opposition.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the good news is that we abolished the ute tax. Remember that one? ... We abolished the Auckland Regional Fuel Tax ... We've actually cancelled Labour's fuel excise hikes that were planned. We've kept that in place frozen, but we're progressing a rates cap—get on board with that.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what a tradie spends filling their ute and whether it's more or less, he lists cost-reducing measures rather than the figure, but does at least claim it is 'a lot less'.

forthrightness.statement: Well, as I've explained to the member before, the rule of economics is that if you increase Government spending by 84 percent, you drive inflation up to a 32-year high, you have 13 interest rate rises, you put the economy into slow down, if not recession, and people lose their jobs. But in the last quarter, we are pleased to see that we've created thousands of new jobs for New Zealanders.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how many more people are unemployed than when he became PM, he gives no number and instead blames prior spending.

forthrightness.statement: I'm advised that Moody's typically shifts to a negative outlook when they see at least a one-in-three chance that a downgrade could occur and that an outlook is generally resolved over 12 to 18 months. ... Budget 2026 will be released on 28 May, and members will see the latest Treasury forecasts then.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly explains what the ratings reviews mean and when more detail will come.

forthrightness.statement: To pick one, we are introducing legislation to this House to cap rates increases, unlike that member who, again, opposes yet another practical measure to help with the cost of living. You see, the problem is that that member has an opinion on everything and a policy on nothing.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about the Government increasing everyday costs, she names one offsetting measure but does not address the listed cost increases.

forthrightness.statement: There is special legislation in place for the Waitākere Ranges—the Waitākere Ranges Heritage Area Act 2008. The Act requires Auckland Council to give effect to its purpose and objectives when making plans under the Resource Management Act ... To maintain the intent of the Waitākere Ranges Heritage Area Act under the new planning system, consequential amendments will be needed, and the Environment Committee will be considering that as part of its scrutiny of the bills.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly addresses what assurances exist, explaining the legislative mechanism and the consequential-amendment process.

forthrightness.statement: I suggest the member, at the end of the night, goes back and reads the Hansard, because if she was listening, she would find out that that's not what I'm doing.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to justify advancing legislation that overrides protections, he simply denies the premise and offers no substantive answer.

forthrightness.statement: Again, I gave a pretty comprehensive answer to the primary question, which was that there are a range of consequential amendments required—there's around 100. It's not just about the Waitākere Ranges Heritage Area Act, it's about 100 other pieces of legislation that require consequential amendments, which the select committee will be considering.
forthrightness.explanation: Partly answers on the consequential-amendment process but sidesteps the weight given to community and mana whenua opposition.

forthrightness.statement: If the Government's planning reforms work as intended, I will take responsibility for the abundant development opportunities that will land in this country. I will take responsibility for the renewable energy that will be far easier to build—the windfarms that don't take six years to build. ... I will take responsibility for the prosperity that we have been denied as a country because of the straightjacket of the RMA.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he'll accept responsibility for irreversible environmental damage, he reframes entirely around taking credit for development and never addresses harm.

forthrightness.statement: The Government hasn't considered any formal advice on the matters the member is referring to.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers that no formal advice on truck weight limits has been considered.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, in a general sense. It is undoubtedly true that heavy vehicles have an impact on the road. We are considering that matter right now, and, as I say—
forthrightness.explanation: Directly agrees with the cited proposition that weight limits exist for good reasons (potholes, bridge strength).

forthrightness.statement: Well, we'll make an announcement when we've made a decision. That's generally how Government works. I know that member wasn't in Government for very long and has maybe forgotten how the Cabinet process works, but generally, on this side of the House, we go through a process, we do the work, we take a paper to Cabinet, and when we've made a decision, we announce it.
forthrightness.explanation: Largely deflects on the timing/substance by describing the Cabinet process rather than the question's content.

forthrightness.statement: Well, that's because that language is in many agreements, including the UAE agreement and the EU agreement that that member's party voted for during this term of Parliament.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Peters' challenge about the Māori clause by pointing to precedent in other agreements.

forthrightness.statement: I am advised that since around June 2024, there has been a net reduction of 25.4 fulltime-equivalent staff at Te Puni Kōkiri.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly provides the specific staffing figure asked about.

forthrightness.statement: We are not about the quantity of roles through Government but, actually, the quality of advice, and I'm very confident about the quality of the advice that the Ministry of Māori Development—Te Puni Kōkiri—is providing me.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses the philosophy behind the cuts but does not directly defend cutting roles amid new monitoring functions as asked.

forthrightness.statement: Again, the member confuses the citation of that great and diligent man Tama Potaka with the number of staff at a single agency, and I recommend that the member talk with Tama Potaka—great guy—at Copperfields after this debate.
forthrightness.explanation: Deflects the question about reconciling his own past quote with job cuts via a self-referential joke.

forthrightness.statement: Definitely the latter is my role, and also to support the Ministry of Māori Development to actually deliver on its statutory role rather than expand all roles for all New Zealanders and all Māori at the whim of a Minister.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly picks the offered option (addressing Māori disadvantage over advocating role expansion).

forthrightness.statement: I do not. This is a standard of English that has been in place since the early 2000s, across multiple Governments, and it does ensure that migrants are able to settle well in New Zealand. I would also make the point that it's only the primary applicant that has to have that level of English. Their partner and their children do not.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers 'I do not' to the cited expert view and explains her reasoning.

forthrightness.statement: Yes. The purpose of temporary work visas is to fill skills shortages where a New Zealander is not available. ... last year, Immigration New Zealand identified employers with employees coming to the end of their maximum continuous stay. They provided this information to MSD, who contacted the affected employers, and to date have filled 400 of these roles with people who are needing work.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers 'Yes' and explains the intent and the programme operationalising it.

forthrightness.statement: There are things in that question that are not linked. Any person who becomes a tax resident in this country has the ability to buy a house, and any person in this country becomes also a resident. What the member seems to be suggesting ... is that there should be the same level of English language for all resident visa holders, and, if that is the case, a refugee who is a partner of a New Zealander should also face these higher English language requirements.
forthrightness.explanation: Rejects the premise and reframes, partly answering by exposing the implication rather than addressing the 'different standards' charge head-on.

forthrightness.statement: most light vehicles under 14 years old will move to two-yearly WOF inspections, up from yearly, and new vehicles will go to four years before needing their WOF. Older vehicles, motorcycles, and light rental vehicles will move from six-monthly to yearly inspections.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers what announcements were made with concrete detail.

forthrightness.statement: From 1 November, most light vehicle users will benefit from these changes, but it is important to note that the ongoing obligation to keep your vehicle roadworthy—including your tyres—in tip-top shape, continues.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers when the changes come into effect (1 November) and adds the relevant caveat.

specificity.statement: Well, we are very interested in developing more mining in this country because we need critical minerals to make the clean, green transition. That's what we've got in this country. We're going to continue to explore them and develop all our natural resources.
specificity.explanation: States a direction (develop critical minerals) but no named site, mechanism, or figures.

specificity.statement: Again, we will find the balance, but we are prioritising economic growth in this country. We are going to get things done, we're going to get this economy moving, and we're going to offer high-paying jobs to people in regional New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Slogans ('get things done', 'get the economy moving') with no concrete mechanism.

specificity.statement: We now have stable rents in this country instead of them going up $180 a week.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete figure but without clear timeframe or baseline.

specificity.statement: How much does the average New Zealand family spend in their weekly grocery shop right now, and is that more or less than when he became the Prime Minister?
specificity.explanation: A precise, answerable question pinned to a concrete measure and timeframe.

specificity.statement: Well, does he stand by his statement in July 2024 that "food prices are falling really quickly"; if so, which food prices have fallen really quickly in the time he's been Prime Minister?
specificity.explanation: Names a dated prior statement and demands a specific test of it.

specificity.statement: Sir, it's a well-established tradition in the House that when moving from a general question to finicky pettifogging detail, you cannot expect the Prime Minister to have that detail. It's laid out in Speakers' rulings 197/2 and 197/4.
specificity.explanation: Cites specific Speakers' rulings to support the procedural point.

specificity.statement: I'm advised that Moody's typically shifts to a negative outlook when they see at least a one-in-three chance that a downgrade could occur and that an outlook is generally resolved over 12 to 18 months. ... Budget 2026 will be released on 28 May, and members will see the latest Treasury forecasts then.
specificity.explanation: Concrete probabilities, timeframes, and a dated Budget release.

specificity.statement: Over the last two Budgets, the Government has made a total of $44 billion worth of savings and reprioritisation. On the other hand, Fitch says that others would emphasise revenue measures to reduce the deficit—that means increasing taxes. People who have those plans should tell the country which taxes they'll be increasing.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete $44 billion savings figure and the contrasting strategy.

specificity.statement: We have seen the price of diesel almost double since that conflict began. Diesel is a fuel that powers not only vehicles but freight and a number of inputs into our economy ... in the past couple of weeks we've seen that diesel price come down about 55c, which demonstrates that it is in all of our interests to see the conflict in the Middle East resolved as soon as possible.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures (almost double, down ~55c) and a clear causal driver.

specificity.statement: National committed that the sum of our tax policies would deliver up to $250 a fortnight to families. We delivered on every single one of the commitments that underpin that $250. Up to $150 of that would be delivered by the FamilyBoost payment—and I have been advised that more than 10,000 families have received that payment in a fortnight—and up to $100 of that would be contributed through our changes to personal income tax thresholds and changes to Working for Families credits.
specificity.explanation: Detailed breakdown with figures ($250, $150, $100) and named mechanisms.

specificity.statement: There is special legislation in place for the Waitākere Ranges—the Waitākere Ranges Heritage Area Act 2008. The Act requires Auckland Council to give effect to its purpose and objectives when making plans under the Resource Management Act ... To maintain the intent of the Waitākere Ranges Heritage Area Act under the new planning system, consequential amendments will be needed, and the Environment Committee will be considering that as part of its scrutiny of the bills.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific Act, the bills, the committee, and the consequential-amendment requirement.

specificity.statement: Again, I gave a pretty comprehensive answer to the primary question, which was that there are a range of consequential amendments required—there's around 100. It's not just about the Waitākere Ranges Heritage Area Act, it's about 100 other pieces of legislation that require consequential amendments, which the select committee will be considering.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete figure (~100 pieces of legislation) and the process handling them.

specificity.statement: If the Government's planning reforms work as intended, I will take responsibility for the abundant development opportunities that will land in this country. I will take responsibility for the renewable energy that will be far easier to build—the windfarms that don't take six years to build. ... I will take responsibility for the prosperity that we have been denied as a country because of the straightjacket of the RMA.
specificity.explanation: Gestures at windfarms, transmission, roads and rail but with no figures, sites, or timeframes.

specificity.statement: What weight has the Minister given to the strong opposition from local communities and mana whenua who are concerned that his RMA reform will undermine the Waitākere Ranges Heritage Area Act 2008, and why are these concerns not currently reflected in the Planning Bill and Natural Environment Bill?
specificity.explanation: A precise question naming the Act, the bills, and the specific stakeholders.

specificity.statement: Is there any chance that these changes might allow families with a horse paddock in Henderson, where they've been trying to build homes for decades, to actually provide those homes that would do a lot more for mana whenua and many others complaining than any of the carping we've heard in this question so far?
specificity.explanation: Concrete illustrative example (horse paddock in Henderson) but no policy detail.

specificity.statement: Right now, New Zealand seafood exporters face tariffs of 33 percent in India but under the FTA, 90 percent of our exports in seafood will move to a zero tariff rate, phased in over seven years. We've also, for the first time, had a commitment from India ... that perishable goods will cross their border and be cleared within 24 hours.
specificity.explanation: Precise tariff figures, coverage percentage, phase-in period, and the 24-hour clearance commitment.

specificity.statement: Our seafood is better than theirs; Indians deserve to eat it.
specificity.explanation: A boosterish assertion with no measure or substantiation.

specificity.statement: The agreement delivers immediate tariff elimination on 95 percent of New Zealand's forestry and wood exports on day one. Australian forestry exports, under their free-trade agreement, increased by 120 percent under their FTA in the first 12 months, while our exports during that period fell.
specificity.explanation: Concrete coverage and comparative figures (95% day-one elimination, 120% Australian growth).

specificity.statement: Right now, apples face a 50 percent tariff into India; under this free-trade agreement, that tariff rate will reduce to 25 percent, with an initial quota of 32,500 tonnes that matches our current apple exports to India. This quota will grow to 45,000 tonnes, or 300 million apples every year, over the next six years.
specificity.explanation: Exact tariff change, quota tonnages, apple count, and timeframe.

specificity.statement: It's growing the economy, giving Kiwis choices, actually allowing opportunity for New Zealand businesses, and leveling the playing field so that in a market like India with 1.4 billion people, Kiwi companies can not only compete fairly against Australians but they will beat them in that market.
specificity.explanation: Cites the 1.4 billion market size but otherwise general claims about growth and competition.

specificity.statement: Why sign an FTA which included the phrase, "nothing in this Agreement shall preclude the adoption by New Zealand of measures it deems necessary to accord more favourable treatment to Māori", given that this language runs counter to the coalition Government's approach that all New Zealanders should be equal under the law?
specificity.explanation: Quotes the exact clause and ties it to a stated principle.

specificity.statement: I am advised that since around June 2024, there has been a net reduction of 25.4 fulltime-equivalent staff at Te Puni Kōkiri.
specificity.explanation: Precise figure (25.4 FTE) with a timeframe.

specificity.statement: I am aware that there was an increase of about a third in the Public Service between 2017 and 2023, and at this time a number of health and wealth indicators in this country absolutely deteriorated—most appalling for me, indicators such as the 2-year-old immunisation rate of Māori, which dropped from about 90 percent to below 65 percent. ... Minister Goldsmith and Minister Mitchell, who have seen a reduction in the number of serious persistent young offenders who are Māori, from 784 to 594 in the last two years.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures: ~one-third growth, immunisation rates, and offender numbers (784 to 594).

specificity.statement: Cherry growers, for example, will have tariffs eliminated from the current 33 percent down to zero over 10 years. In other parts of the country, kiwifruit growers will also see tariffs eliminated for kiwifruit within quota.
specificity.explanation: Concrete tariff figures and phase-in period for named products.

specificity.statement: Tariffs on wine will be reduced from 150 percent to either 25 or 50 percent, depending on the value of the wine, over 10 years—plus a most favoured nation commitment.
specificity.explanation: Exact tariff bands, conditions, timeframe, and the MFN clause.

specificity.statement: The good news for Whanganui and other honey-producing regions is that tariffs on mānuka honey will be cut from 66 percent to 16.5 percent over five years.
specificity.explanation: Precise before/after tariff figures and timeframe for mānuka honey.

specificity.statement: I do not. This is a standard of English that has been in place since the early 2000s, across multiple Governments, and it does ensure that migrants are able to settle well in New Zealand. I would also make the point that it's only the primary applicant that has to have that level of English. Their partner and their children do not.
specificity.explanation: Notes the standard's history and that it applies only to the primary applicant, though without the specific band requirement.

specificity.statement: Yes. The purpose of temporary work visas is to fill skills shortages where a New Zealander is not available. ... last year, Immigration New Zealand identified employers with employees coming to the end of their maximum continuous stay. They provided this information to MSD, who contacted the affected employers, and to date have filled 400 of these roles with people who are needing work.
specificity.explanation: Describes the agencies involved and a concrete figure (400 roles filled).

specificity.statement: most light vehicles under 14 years old will move to two-yearly WOF inspections, up from yearly, and new vehicles will go to four years before needing their WOF. Older vehicles, motorcycles, and light rental vehicles will move from six-monthly to yearly inspections.
specificity.explanation: Precise inspection intervals by vehicle category.

specificity.statement: The cost-benefit analysis done by officials shows that these changes are expected to deliver between $2.6 billion and $4.1 billion in net benefits to Kiwis over 30 years through reduced inspection fees, less time spent on compliance, and fewer unnecessary repairs.
specificity.explanation: Cites a quantified net-benefit range and 30-year horizon with the source.

specificity.statement: From 1 November, most light vehicle users will benefit from these changes, but it is important to note that the ongoing obligation to keep your vehicle roadworthy—including your tyres—in tip-top shape, continues.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete start date and the continuing roadworthiness obligation.

specificity.statement: Why is he prioritising regulatory relief for the trucking industry when ordinary New Zealanders are paying record prices at the pump just to get to work, drop their kids off at school, and put food on the table?
specificity.explanation: Concrete everyday examples but no figures or policy specifics.

specificity.statement: Does she stand by her statement that "This Government has got your back." when 70 percent of workers didn't get a pay rise above inflation in the last year?
specificity.explanation: Pins a slogan against a concrete statistic (70% of workers).

specificity.statement: Is it having New Zealanders' back in a cost of living crisis when her Government is increasing the everyday costs through her gas tax, increases to car registration, the reinstatement of prescription fees, increases in line charges, and increases in council rates?
specificity.explanation: Enumerates five concrete cost increases tied to government decisions.

specificity.statement: Has his Government departed from the commitment of previous Governments first made under Sir John Key in 2012 that there would be no mining in World Heritage areas like the spectacular Te Wāhipounamu?
specificity.explanation: References a dated, named prior commitment and a specific World Heritage area.

specificity.statement: One hundred and nineteen families and individuals on the rich list hold as much wealth as nearly half of all New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: A concrete figure (119 individuals/families) framed against half the population.

specificity.statement: Research released just yesterday showed that six of the biggest fossil fuel companies are making $3,000 per second in profits during a crisis where ordinary people are struggling—$37 million a day above what they made last year.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures ($3,000/second, $37 million/day) attributed to recent research.

specificity.statement: They know that when New Zealanders see that there are 32,000 thousand fewer jobs in this country ... when there are 2,000 people leaving the country every week ... 15 percent—that's ... business liquidations, that's what it's increased by. ... the 18 percent increase in power prices. There are people in this country that are paying 100 bucks to visit the doctor.
specificity.explanation: A battery of concrete figures (jobs, emigration, liquidations, power prices, GP cost).

specificity.statement: We've come up with a solution to that. We're going to use a capital gains tax to pay for three free GP visits for everyone in the country.
specificity.explanation: A concrete policy (CGT funding three free GP visits) though without rates or thresholds.

specificity.statement: Being very interested in clean, green outcomes, I think it's very important that we join with the different stakeholders in our community and explore the role that hydrogen can play boosting our fuel resilience, our energy resilience ... It is important, however, that when people apply for innocuous prospecting permits, they are not pilloried, they are not cancelled, and they are not harassed by opponents to mining when they are legally entitled to go and get an innocuous permit.
specificity.explanation: Names hydrogen and fuel/energy resilience but otherwise general about the permit process.

charisma.statement: Well, what I know New Zealanders are not OK about is not having high-paying jobs in regional New Zealand and actually banning oil and gas and mining projects that ends up having Kiwis leave New Zealand to go to Australia to access those jobs in those sectors.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically confident but appeals only to his own side's framing; no attempt to bring opponents along.

charisma.statement: Over the last two Budgets, the Government has made a total of $44 billion worth of savings and reprioritisation. On the other hand, Fitch says that others would emphasise revenue measures to reduce the deficit—that means increasing taxes. People who have those plans should tell the country which taxes they'll be increasing.
charisma.explanation: Largely a partisan contrast that challenges opponents rather than building consensus.

charisma.statement: We have seen the price of diesel almost double since that conflict began. Diesel is a fuel that powers not only vehicles but freight and a number of inputs into our economy ... in the past couple of weeks we've seen that diesel price come down about 55c, which demonstrates that it is in all of our interests to see the conflict in the Middle East resolved as soon as possible.
charisma.explanation: Frames the issue around shared interest ('all of our interests') rather than blame.

charisma.statement: That comment was that a free-trade agreement with India—so that our exporters can sell their goods and services there—would unleash a "butter chicken tsunami". Well, shame on you, Shane Jones. ... that kind of race-based rhetoric has no place in New Zealand politics. To those New Zealanders of Indian descent ... I want you to know that we hear you and we back you.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, explicitly reaches out to Indian New Zealanders, though it does so by publicly condemning a colleague.

charisma.statement: That is the state of Labour today: bark at every passing car, have an opinion on everything, a policy on nothing.
charisma.explanation: Purely combative; alienates rather than persuades.

charisma.statement: If the Government's planning reforms work as intended, I will take responsibility for the abundant development opportunities that will land in this country. I will take responsibility for the renewable energy that will be far easier to build—the windfarms that don't take six years to build. ... I will take responsibility for the prosperity that we have been denied as a country because of the straightjacket of the RMA.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically energetic but rallies his own side around a one-sided framing of the RMA as a 'straightjacket'.

charisma.statement: Does he also anticipate taking responsibility for far more development opportunity created for Māori than the Māori Party could ever dream of creating?
charisma.explanation: Us-versus-them framing that scores points against opponents rather than persuading.

charisma.statement: As Minister of Transport, is it his understanding that food on the table more often than not comes on trucks, and, if that is true, will the Government have any communication plans to get that across to some of the simpler members of the Labour Party?
charisma.explanation: Belittling humour aimed at the other side, alienating rather than unifying.

charisma.statement: Our seafood is better than theirs; Indians deserve to eat it.
charisma.explanation: An applause line that flatters domestic producers rather than persuading the unconvinced.

charisma.statement: He does know what it's like to lose his seat. He had one in the Wairarapa and he lost it at the last election. ... Kieran McAnulty, who's actually given up on his ambition to lead the Labour Party at the moment because of a lack of policy.
charisma.explanation: Combative point-scoring against an individual opponent.

charisma.statement: It's growing the economy, giving Kiwis choices, actually allowing opportunity for New Zealand businesses, and leveling the playing field so that in a market like India with 1.4 billion people, Kiwi companies can not only compete fairly against Australians but they will beat them in that market.
charisma.explanation: Confident and aspirational, but rallies his own side around a pro-trade vision rather than reaching across.

charisma.statement: We are not about the quantity of roles through Government but, actually, the quality of advice, and I'm very confident about the quality of the advice that the Ministry of Māori Development—Te Puni Kōkiri—is providing me.
charisma.explanation: Frames the contrast as 'cash bazooka' versus 'fiscal prudence', appealing to his own side.

charisma.statement: five years ago some relations of people in this House sought to resolve the issues arising over 150 years with the Nelson Tenths and ... the previous Government absolutely failed to deliver on their aspirations, and it took this Government to actually step up and deal with those concerns, after 150 years.
charisma.explanation: Personalises a redress story but uses it largely to contrast with the previous Government.

charisma.statement: does he think New Zealanders are OK with his Government trading off a place with outstanding universal value for short-term, private profits?
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically appeals to one side's values rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: Mr Winston Peters wants us to blame migrants. ... Mr David Seymour wants us to blame Māori. ... The Prime Minister, Mr Luxon, wants us to blame beneficiaries for unemployment.
charisma.explanation: Us-versus-them framing that rallies her side by casting opponents as scapegoaters.

charisma.statement: Nurses and police and cleaners and bus drivers and early childhood education teachers know that they are, effectively, paying more effective tax than the wealthy owning tens and dozens and loads of houses.
charisma.explanation: Names everyday workers to build solidarity, but within an us-versus-the-wealthy frame.

charisma.statement: Being very interested in clean, green outcomes, I think it's very important that we join with the different stakeholders in our community and explore the role that hydrogen can play boosting our fuel resilience, our energy resilience ... It is important, however, that when people apply for innocuous prospecting permits, they are not pilloried, they are not cancelled, and they are not harassed by opponents to mining when they are legally entitled to go and get an innocuous permit.
charisma.explanation: Opens with 'join with the different stakeholders' but pivots to defending miners against 'opponents', appealing to his own side.

veracity.statement: Just remember, 30 percent of this country is in the Department of Conservation estate. We have very important national parks of very high environmental quality, and we'll continue to protect those, obviously.
veracity.explanation: The roughly one-third DOC-estate figure is broadly accurate for New Zealand.

veracity.statement: Well, actually, food inflation's up 3.4 percent from memory; it was up 12.5 percent under his Government. So food price inflation exists, and as I said to him yesterday, deflation is not good for an economy, but food price inflation—there's more to do, but at 3.4 percent it's better than 12.5 percent, which he delivered.
veracity.explanation: The 12.5% peak under the previous government is roughly accurate but selectively compares a past peak to a current rate, which is somewhat misleading.

veracity.statement: Well, the good news is that we abolished the ute tax. Remember that one? ... We abolished the Auckland Regional Fuel Tax ... We've actually cancelled Labour's fuel excise hikes that were planned. We've kept that in place frozen, but we're progressing a rates cap—get on board with that.
veracity.explanation: The Government did repeal the Clean Car Discount ('ute tax') and the Auckland Regional Fuel Tax; broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: Well, as I've explained to the member before, the rule of economics is that if you increase Government spending by 84 percent, you drive inflation up to a 32-year high, you have 13 interest rate rises, you put the economy into slow down, if not recession, and people lose their jobs. But in the last quarter, we are pleased to see that we've created thousands of new jobs for New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: The 84% spending and 32-year-high inflation figures are contestable framings; the causal attribution is overstated.

veracity.statement: We now have stable rents in this country instead of them going up $180 a week.
veracity.explanation: The '$180 a week' framing is a misleading comparison; rents had not been rising by that amount weekly.

veracity.statement: The interest cost on Government debt is already around $9 billion a year. A credit rating downgrade would increase this interest bill further if debt increased, and even more so if New Zealand faced higher interest rates from being considered a riskier country.
veracity.explanation: The ~$9 billion annual debt-servicing figure is in the accurate range for the period.

veracity.statement: The agreement delivers immediate tariff elimination on 95 percent of New Zealand's forestry and wood exports on day one. Australian forestry exports, under their free-trade agreement, increased by 120 percent under their FTA in the first 12 months, while our exports during that period fell.
veracity.explanation: The figures are plausible but presented selectively to maximise the contrast; not independently verifiable here.

veracity.statement: Well, that's because that language is in many agreements, including the UAE agreement and the EU agreement that that member's party voted for during this term of Parliament.
veracity.explanation: Peters immediately disputes the claim that his party voted for that agreement, so the factual accuracy is contested within the text.

veracity.statement: The questioner, in his question, insinuated that a foreigner without any status in this country nevertheless could make financial contributions to political parties. That statement is false. It's outside the law, and he's been here long enough to have learnt that.
veracity.explanation: New Zealand law restricts overseas/anonymous donations, so the assertion that foreign nationals without status cannot lawfully donate is broadly correct.

veracity.statement: I am aware that there was an increase of about a third in the Public Service between 2017 and 2023, and at this time a number of health and wealth indicators in this country absolutely deteriorated—most appalling for me, indicators such as the 2-year-old immunisation rate of Māori, which dropped from about 90 percent to below 65 percent. ... Minister Goldsmith and Minister Mitchell, who have seen a reduction in the number of serious persistent young offenders who are Māori, from 784 to 594 in the last two years.
veracity.explanation: The figures are specific and plausible but the implied connection between staffing growth and worse outcomes is not substantiated.

veracity.statement: One hundred and nineteen families and individuals on the rich list hold as much wealth as nearly half of all New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: A striking wealth-concentration claim broadly consistent with NZ inequality data, though the precise comparison is contestable.

veracity.statement: Research released just yesterday showed that six of the biggest fossil fuel companies are making $3,000 per second in profits during a crisis where ordinary people are struggling—$37 million a day above what they made last year.
veracity.explanation: Cites unnamed 'research released yesterday'; the dramatic per-second framing is the kind of figure that often selectively maximises impact and cannot be verified from the text.

veracity.statement: it was actually only a week ago that Christopher Luxon, under huge pressure, put up a confidence vote in caucus and almost lost to an empty chair. ... double digits of his caucus voted no.
veracity.explanation: Asserts internal caucus vote details ('double digits voted no', 'almost lost to an empty chair') hedged with 'from what I've been hearing'—unverifiable and likely exaggerated.

veracity.statement: They know that when New Zealanders see that there are 32,000 thousand fewer jobs in this country ... when there are 2,000 people leaving the country every week ... 15 percent—that's ... business liquidations, that's what it's increased by. ... the 18 percent increase in power prices. There are people in this country that are paying 100 bucks to visit the doctor.
veracity.explanation: The figures are presented assertively without sources; several are plausible but rounded and selectively framed for impact.

veracity.statement: They're crowing about making it easier to access prescriptions, but let's not forget they used to be free. They put the charges back on them, make it slightly easier, and say, "Aren't we great?"
veracity.explanation: Prescription co-payments were removed and then reinstated, so the underlying sequence is broadly accurate.

civility.statement: Well, again, I'll just say to the member, if he actually cares about the impact of the cost of living on New Zealanders, why doesn't he propose some policy to actually come to the table with? Why doesn't he support the rates cap? ... And why doesn't he actually just support extending prescriptions, saving healthcare costs for regular New Zealanders?
civility.explanation: Implies the questioner doesn't care about cost of living, but largely lists policy points rather than personal attacks.

civility.statement: How much does the average New Zealand family spend in their weekly grocery shop right now, and is that more or less than when he became the Prime Minister?
civility.explanation: A pointed but legitimate policy-focused question with no personal attack.

civility.statement: Is the reason he can't answer a single one of those questions about the day-to-day reality New Zealand families face under his Government and instead resorts to blame and excuses, that he doesn't know the answers or that he just doesn't care?
civility.explanation: Frames the PM as either ignorant or uncaring; a loaded characterisation rather than substance.

civility.statement: Sir, it's a well-established tradition in the House that when moving from a general question to finicky pettifogging detail, you cannot expect the Prime Minister to have that detail. It's laid out in Speakers' rulings 197/2 and 197/4.
civility.explanation: Dismisses opponents' questions as 'finicky pettifogging' but frames it as a procedural argument.

civility.statement: To pick one, we are introducing legislation to this House to cap rates increases, unlike that member who, again, opposes yet another practical measure to help with the cost of living. You see, the problem is that that member has an opinion on everything and a policy on nothing.
civility.explanation: Closes with a personal jab ('an opinion on everything and a policy on nothing') rather than engaging the listed costs.

civility.statement: That comment was that a free-trade agreement with India—so that our exporters can sell their goods and services there—would unleash a "butter chicken tsunami". Well, shame on you, Shane Jones. ... that kind of race-based rhetoric has no place in New Zealand politics. To those New Zealanders of Indian descent ... I want you to know that we hear you and we back you.
civility.explanation: 'Shame on you, Shane Jones' is a direct personal rebuke, but it is in defence of a community against demeaning rhetoric.

civility.statement: That is the state of Labour today: bark at every passing car, have an opinion on everything, a policy on nothing.
civility.explanation: A belittling caricature of the opposition rather than engagement with their positions.

civility.statement: I suggest the member, at the end of the night, goes back and reads the Hansard, because if she was listening, she would find out that that's not what I'm doing.
civility.explanation: Dismissive and condescending ('if she was listening') rather than engaging the concern.

civility.statement: Well, we'll make an announcement when we've made a decision. That's generally how Government works. I know that member wasn't in Government for very long and has maybe forgotten how the Cabinet process works, but generally, on this side of the House, we go through a process, we do the work, we take a paper to Cabinet, and when we've made a decision, we announce it.
civility.explanation: Condescending dig that the member 'wasn't in Government for very long' and has 'forgotten how the Cabinet process works'.

civility.statement: It's a simple matter of economics and maths—and I know maths aren't the Labour Party's strong suit, as we get a daily demonstration of, but I invite the member to actually look at the facts.
civility.explanation: Personal jab that 'maths aren't the Labour Party's strong suit' rather than addressing the substance.

civility.statement: What weight has the Minister given to the strong opposition from local communities and mana whenua who are concerned that his RMA reform will undermine the Waitākere Ranges Heritage Area Act 2008, and why are these concerns not currently reflected in the Planning Bill and Natural Environment Bill?
civility.explanation: A substantive, policy-focused question with no personal attack.

civility.statement: Is there any chance that these changes might allow families with a horse paddock in Henderson, where they've been trying to build homes for decades, to actually provide those homes that would do a lot more for mana whenua and many others complaining than any of the carping we've heard in this question so far?
civility.explanation: Dismisses opponents' questions as 'carping' while making a substantive housing point.

civility.statement: Does he also anticipate taking responsibility for far more development opportunity created for Māori than the Māori Party could ever dream of creating?
civility.explanation: A partisan jab at the Māori Party rather than a genuine question.

civility.statement: As Minister of Transport, is it his understanding that food on the table more often than not comes on trucks, and, if that is true, will the Government have any communication plans to get that across to some of the simpler members of the Labour Party?
civility.explanation: Direct insult calling opponents 'the simpler members of the Labour Party'.

civility.statement: He does know what it's like to lose his seat. He had one in the Wairarapa and he lost it at the last election. ... Kieran McAnulty, who's actually given up on his ambition to lead the Labour Party at the moment because of a lack of policy.
civility.explanation: Personal jabs about losing a seat and leadership ambitions rather than engaging policy.

civility.statement: The questioner, in his question, insinuated that a foreigner without any status in this country nevertheless could make financial contributions to political parties. That statement is false. It's outside the law, and he's been here long enough to have learnt that.
civility.explanation: Corrects the record but with a barbed implication that the member knowingly made a 'foul insinuation'.

civility.statement: Again, the member confuses the citation of that great and diligent man Tama Potaka with the number of staff at a single agency, and I recommend that the member talk with Tama Potaka—great guy—at Copperfields after this debate.
civility.explanation: Light-hearted rather than hostile, but evades through humour.

civility.statement: Does he admit that the latest job cuts prove the Government's negative Māori agenda is ramping up, and for all his rhetoric about thriving whānau, the only things thriving under National are more cuts and misery for Māori?
civility.explanation: An accusatory framing ('negative Māori agenda', 'cuts and misery') challenged as out of order under Speakers' rulings.

civility.statement: Why is he prioritising regulatory relief for the trucking industry when ordinary New Zealanders are paying record prices at the pump just to get to work, drop their kids off at school, and put food on the table?
civility.explanation: A pointed but legitimate challenge framing the priorities, with mild loaded framing ('prioritising... industry').

civility.statement: Is it having New Zealanders' back in a cost of living crisis when her Government is increasing the everyday costs through her gas tax, increases to car registration, the reinstatement of prescription fees, increases in line charges, and increases in council rates?
civility.explanation: Pointed but engages with policy substance rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: does he think New Zealanders are OK with his Government trading off a place with outstanding universal value for short-term, private profits?
civility.explanation: Loaded framing ('desecrating'/'trading off... for short-term, private profits') though aimed at policy not person.

civility.statement: Mr Winston Peters wants us to blame migrants. ... Mr David Seymour wants us to blame Māori. ... The Prime Minister, Mr Luxon, wants us to blame beneficiaries for unemployment.
civility.explanation: Characterises opponents' motives in the worst light rather than engaging their stated positions.

civility.statement: it was actually only a week ago that Christopher Luxon, under huge pressure, put up a confidence vote in caucus and almost lost to an empty chair. ... double digits of his caucus voted no.
civility.explanation: Personal attack on the PM's standing, though framed around political leadership rather than character slurs.

civility.statement: They're crowing about making it easier to access prescriptions, but let's not forget they used to be free. They put the charges back on them, make it slightly easier, and say, "Aren't we great?"
civility.explanation: Mocking tone ('Aren't we great?') but tied to a substantive policy critique.

civility.statement: Andy Foster got given an additional supplementary question from the Speaker and he didn't know what to say, because no one had written it down for him. He just sat there like a deer in the headlights.
civility.explanation: A personal put-down of a named member ('deer in the headlights') rather than a policy point.

strength.statement: Well, the good news is that we abolished the ute tax. Remember that one? ... We abolished the Auckland Regional Fuel Tax ... We've actually cancelled Labour's fuel excise hikes that were planned. We've kept that in place frozen, but we're progressing a rates cap—get on board with that.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for delivered actions (abolishing the ute tax and Auckland fuel tax, cancelling excise hikes) that were in fact enacted.

strength.statement: Over the last two Budgets, the Government has made a total of $44 billion worth of savings and reprioritisation. On the other hand, Fitch says that others would emphasise revenue measures to reduce the deficit—that means increasing taxes. People who have those plans should tell the country which taxes they'll be increasing.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for delivered savings/reprioritisation across two Budgets, partially verifiable.

strength.statement: National committed that the sum of our tax policies would deliver up to $250 a fortnight to families. We delivered on every single one of the commitments that underpin that $250. Up to $150 of that would be delivered by the FamilyBoost payment—and I have been advised that more than 10,000 families have received that payment in a fortnight—and up to $100 of that would be contributed through our changes to personal income tax thresholds and changes to Working for Families credits.
strength.explanation: Claims delivery of the tax package; the '$250' was an 'up to' figure that few households received in full, so follow-through is partial.

strength.statement: Right now, New Zealand seafood exporters face tariffs of 33 percent in India but under the FTA, 90 percent of our exports in seafood will move to a zero tariff rate, phased in over seven years. We've also, for the first time, had a commitment from India ... that perishable goods will cross their border and be cleared within 24 hours.
strength.explanation: Describes a concrete, signed agreement delivering specified market-access gains, though benefits are prospective and phased.

strength.statement: five years ago some relations of people in this House sought to resolve the issues arising over 150 years with the Nelson Tenths and ... the previous Government absolutely failed to deliver on their aspirations, and it took this Government to actually step up and deal with those concerns, after 150 years.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for progressing the long-standing Nelson Tenths/Whakatū settlement, though he refers to legislation yet to be passed ('on the day we pass that legislation').

strength.statement: Yes. The purpose of temporary work visas is to fill skills shortages where a New Zealander is not available. ... last year, Immigration New Zealand identified employers with employees coming to the end of their maximum continuous stay. They provided this information to MSD, who contacted the affected employers, and to date have filled 400 of these roles with people who are needing work.
strength.explanation: Points to a delivered outcome (400 New Zealanders placed) from a stated policy, though modest in scale.

strength.statement: We've come up with a solution to that. We're going to use a capital gains tax to pay for three free GP visits for everyone in the country.
strength.explanation: An opposition promise with no delivery; pure commitment from a party not in government.

rigor.statement: Well, as I've explained to the member before, the rule of economics is that if you increase Government spending by 84 percent, you drive inflation up to a 32-year high, you have 13 interest rate rises, you put the economy into slow down, if not recession, and people lose their jobs. But in the last quarter, we are pleased to see that we've created thousands of new jobs for New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a causal chain from spending to inflation to job losses, leaning on figures but presenting it as an inevitable 'rule of economics' without establishing the links.

rigor.statement: Well, does he stand by his statement in July 2024 that "food prices are falling really quickly"; if so, which food prices have fallen really quickly in the time he's been Prime Minister?
rigor.explanation: Tests a prior claim against subsequent evidence, a sound evidentiary challenge.

rigor.statement: Is the reason he can't answer a single one of those questions about the day-to-day reality New Zealand families face under his Government and instead resorts to blame and excuses, that he doesn't know the answers or that he just doesn't care?
rigor.explanation: Presents a false dichotomy (doesn't know / doesn't care) excluding other explanations.

rigor.statement: The interest cost on Government debt is already around $9 billion a year. A credit rating downgrade would increase this interest bill further if debt increased, and even more so if New Zealand faced higher interest rates from being considered a riskier country.
rigor.explanation: A coherent conditional argument linking downgrades, debt and interest costs.

rigor.statement: We have seen the price of diesel almost double since that conflict began. Diesel is a fuel that powers not only vehicles but freight and a number of inputs into our economy ... in the past couple of weeks we've seen that diesel price come down about 55c, which demonstrates that it is in all of our interests to see the conflict in the Middle East resolved as soon as possible.
rigor.explanation: Links a specific external shock to fuel prices and cost of living with internal consistency.

rigor.statement: It's a simple matter of economics and maths—and I know maths aren't the Labour Party's strong suit, as we get a daily demonstration of, but I invite the member to actually look at the facts.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a fuel-economy logic (fewer trips, more per trip) but presents it as self-evident without supporting figures.

rigor.statement: Forty minutes ago, we had a long conversation at the front end of question time about food costs and people paying prices at the supermarkets. Guess what will happen if the fuel crisis gets worse and those fuel costs are passed on to consumers? That will show up in food prices. Regulatory relief like we're talking about, at least on the margins, takes the heat off the food price increases.
rigor.explanation: Connects fuel costs to freight to food prices in a coherent chain, though the marginal effect is asserted rather than quantified.

rigor.statement: The agreement delivers immediate tariff elimination on 95 percent of New Zealand's forestry and wood exports on day one. Australian forestry exports, under their free-trade agreement, increased by 120 percent under their FTA in the first 12 months, while our exports during that period fell.
rigor.explanation: Uses the Australian FTA comparison to argue for the benefit, though it implies causation from a single comparison.

rigor.statement: Why sign an FTA which included the phrase, "nothing in this Agreement shall preclude the adoption by New Zealand of measures it deems necessary to accord more favourable treatment to Māori", given that this language runs counter to the coalition Government's approach that all New Zealanders should be equal under the law?
rigor.explanation: Identifies an apparent tension between the clause and the 'equal under the law' position, though it assumes the two are incompatible.

rigor.statement: I am aware that there was an increase of about a third in the Public Service between 2017 and 2023, and at this time a number of health and wealth indicators in this country absolutely deteriorated—most appalling for me, indicators such as the 2-year-old immunisation rate of Māori, which dropped from about 90 percent to below 65 percent. ... Minister Goldsmith and Minister Mitchell, who have seen a reduction in the number of serious persistent young offenders who are Māori, from 784 to 594 in the last two years.
rigor.explanation: Juxtaposes public-service growth with deteriorating indicators, implying a link without establishing causation.

rigor.statement: Does he admit that the latest job cuts prove the Government's negative Māori agenda is ramping up, and for all his rhetoric about thriving whānau, the only things thriving under National are more cuts and misery for Māori?
rigor.explanation: Treats staffing cuts as 'proof' of a negative agenda—an unsubstantiated leap.

rigor.statement: There are things in that question that are not linked. Any person who becomes a tax resident in this country has the ability to buy a house, and any person in this country becomes also a resident. What the member seems to be suggesting ... is that there should be the same level of English language for all resident visa holders, and, if that is the case, a refugee who is a partner of a New Zealander should also face these higher English language requirements.
rigor.explanation: Draws out the logical consequence of the questioner's position (it would apply to refugee partners too) as a reductio.

rigor.statement: Has his Government departed from the commitment of previous Governments first made under Sir John Key in 2012 that there would be no mining in World Heritage areas like the spectacular Te Wāhipounamu?
rigor.explanation: Tests current policy against a documented past commitment, a sound consistency challenge.

rigor.statement: Research released just yesterday showed that six of the biggest fossil fuel companies are making $3,000 per second in profits during a crisis where ordinary people are struggling—$37 million a day above what they made last year.
rigor.explanation: Uses cited figures but leans on emotive 'cash in', 'exploit' framing to carry the argument.

rigor.statement: Nurses and police and cleaners and bus drivers and early childhood education teachers know that they are, effectively, paying more effective tax than the wealthy owning tens and dozens and loads of houses.
rigor.explanation: Makes an effective-tax-rate argument but asserts what workers 'know' rather than presenting the underlying figures.

rigor.statement: They're crowing about making it easier to access prescriptions, but let's not forget they used to be free. They put the charges back on them, make it slightly easier, and say, "Aren't we great?"
rigor.explanation: A coherent point that the Government reinstated a charge it had removed and now claims credit for easing it.

authenticity.statement: National committed that the sum of our tax policies would deliver up to $250 a fortnight to families. We delivered on every single one of the commitments that underpin that $250. Up to $150 of that would be delivered by the FamilyBoost payment—and I have been advised that more than 10,000 families have received that payment in a fortnight—and up to $100 of that would be contributed through our changes to personal income tax thresholds and changes to Working for Families credits.
authenticity.explanation: Frames the policy as matching a campaign commitment, though the 'up to $250' framing leaves room for gap between promise and typical outcome.

authenticity.statement: That comment was that a free-trade agreement with India—so that our exporters can sell their goods and services there—would unleash a "butter chicken tsunami". Well, shame on you, Shane Jones. ... that kind of race-based rhetoric has no place in New Zealand politics. To those New Zealanders of Indian descent ... I want you to know that we hear you and we back you.
authenticity.explanation: Calls out racism even from her own coalition partner, showing willingness to apply the standard against her own side.

authenticity.statement: Does she stand by her statement that "This Government has got your back." when 70 percent of workers didn't get a pay rise above inflation in the last year?
authenticity.explanation: Targets a perceived gap between the Government's 'got your back' slogan and worker outcomes—an authenticity challenge to the opponent, not a self-signal.

divination.statement: Forty minutes ago, we had a long conversation at the front end of question time about food costs and people paying prices at the supermarkets. Guess what will happen if the fuel crisis gets worse and those fuel costs are passed on to consumers? That will show up in food prices. Regulatory relief like we're talking about, at least on the margins, takes the heat off the food price increases.
divination.explanation: Predicts that worsening fuel costs will flow through to food prices—directionally plausible, magnitude uncertain.

divination.statement: The cost-benefit analysis done by officials shows that these changes are expected to deliver between $2.6 billion and $4.1 billion in net benefits to Kiwis over 30 years through reduced inspection fees, less time spent on compliance, and fewer unnecessary repairs.
divination.explanation: Projects $2.6–4.1bn benefits over 30 years; long-horizon official estimates of this kind are highly uncertain.

charisma.statement: without that advocacy over the years of all those people,”—all those people that we’ve mentioned here and the thousands of others that we haven’t directly named—“without their work, we wouldn’t be here. So yes, it does work. It really, really does.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, generous credit-sharing with advocates and other parties; unifying rather than combative, though it preaches to the converted on this bill.

charisma.statement: I love it when we have “Kumbaya” moments in this House—that’s why I love Treaty settlement days most of all—but we are a debating chamber for good reason. When we debate things and we debate them well and we debate them faithfully, we actually get better law and we get better policy.
charisma.explanation: Bridge-building: welcomes opposition and frames adversarial debate as a shared route to better outcomes.

charisma.statement: I think it’s good that we’ve got a thoughtful party that is not yet convinced by this.
charisma.explanation: Generous toward opponents, inviting them in rather than shutting them out.

charisma.statement: Good on Greg Fleming and good on Camilla Belich for going around Brooke van Velden, who has been very busy in the area of workplace relations, doing all the wrong things, eroding workplace relations here, there, and everywhere.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing that rallies his own side against a minister rather than building consensus.

charisma.statement: I’m sure the House will look forward to the contributions from the ACT Party as they try to explain themselves out of this little corner.
charisma.explanation: Combative point-scoring that alienates rather than persuades the party it targets.

charisma.statement: Let me be absolutely clear: modern slavery is a moral abomination. The exploitation of human beings has no place here in New Zealand or around the world. There is not a single person in this House who is soft on slavery.
charisma.explanation: Seeks common ground by affirming shared values before dissenting — disarms the 'ACT is soft on slavery' framing.

charisma.statement: I’m old enough to know when we first introduced health and safety legislation and we fundamentally started with a reporting mechanism and a policy development. Over time, that legislation grew teeth, it grew strength, and it grew, most importantly, accountability for those who do wrong.
charisma.explanation: Reframes ACT's 'weak bill' critique constructively, building a case that a modest start is legitimate without attacking opponents.

charisma.statement: I do acknowledge the ACT member for talking about being judged by the outcomes of our legislation, and not just that we have legislation, but I think it has been traversed clearly in this House that this is the starting point that we need.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges an opponent's valid argument and folds it into a case for the bill — consensus-seeking.

charisma.statement: We hear that they will vote against this, preaching personal liberty. But Te Pāti Māori, in this House, we ask, “Whose liberty—the liberty of a business to ignore blood in its supply chain, or the liberty of human beings to live without chains?”
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically powerful but draws a sharp moral line against an opposing party rather than seeking to bring them along.

charisma.statement: the fact that we can come together across the parties—well, most of the parties—is a really, really historic day. This is what’s good about politics. Sometimes people don’t see that; sometimes we don’t see that ourselves, but this is what’s good about politics.
charisma.explanation: Emphasises cross-party unity and a positive vision of politics; the 'well, most of the parties' aside lightly notes ACT's absence without attacking them.

charisma.statement: One thing that we have all agreed on is our position against and on migrant exploitation. We’ve followed that really closely when we review Immigration New Zealand and where that’s going and the work that we’re doing around that.
charisma.explanation: Emphasises cross-committee agreement and constructive collaboration.

charisma.statement: When Kiwis buy products, they should, and they deserve to, know the origin of them.
charisma.explanation: Frames the issue around a broadly shared consumer-rights value to build wide support.

charisma.statement: I was staggered to hear the ACT Party member saying they’re not even going to support a bill that’s only about transparency and disclosure of modern slavery—slavery—in supply chains.
charisma.explanation: Expresses incredulity at the opposing party rather than engaging their reasoning to win them over.

charisma.statement: if you want to have the free flow of capital around the world, for goodness’ sake, do something about maintaining social licence for that, like actually protecting some basic ethical standards, which is what this bill does. If you don’t, you risk losing public confidence and public support in the very system that you want.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to free-market supporters in their own terms to bring them toward the bill rather than dismissing them.

charisma.statement: I cannot sit here and not note that it is my colleague Greg Fleming, a member of the National-led Government, the National Party, that has actually got this to the House during our Government. Labour had the opportunity in 2021; they didn’t get it there, so well done Greg and well done to Camilla.
charisma.explanation: Converts a 'Kumbaya' moment into partisan credit-claiming, which cuts against the cross-party tone others built.

charisma.statement: We on this side of the House are all about free markets. We’re all about competition. We’re all about price transparency. The Government’s doing its bit. We do not need a piece of legislation like this.
charisma.explanation: Defines his position by 'this side of the House' against the rest — affirms his own side rather than reaching across it.

specificity.statement: without that advocacy over the years of all those people,”—all those people that we’ve mentioned here and the thousands of others that we haven’t directly named—“without their work, we wouldn’t be here. So yes, it does work. It really, really does.
specificity.explanation: Affirms that advocacy 'works' but offers no figures, mechanisms, or concrete causal detail — a warm but vague claim.

specificity.statement: Country Road did their check, and they were horrified to find that their main sock supply did actually have a clear instance of modern slavery. They were able to address it because of the requirement on them of this kind of reporting.
specificity.explanation: Names the company and the specific supply-chain finding rather than speaking in generalities.

specificity.statement: This bill will require reporting entities to report on how they identify, address, mitigate, and remediate incidents of modern slavery. It will require the Minister to report annually on progress towards combating modern slavery and to issue guidance on reporting suspected incidents of modern slavery processes that Government agencies should follow in response.
specificity.explanation: Precise, accurate summary of the bill's operative mechanisms — reporting duties, annual ministerial reporting, and guidance obligations.

specificity.statement: why are we just looking at bigger companies when, actually, exploitation in the form of modern slavery can often happen within small businesses and it could often happen in other circumstances which are not part of the supply chain?
specificity.explanation: Names the gap (small businesses, non-supply-chain settings) but does not propose a concrete alternative threshold or mechanism.

specificity.statement: Under this bill, a company may not exploit a single human being, it could even be a model employer, but if it misses a paperwork deadline or files a deficient statement, it faces up to $200,000 in fines. This is not a policy brought on a cornerstone of freeing victims; it is built on filling in forms and ticking boxes.
specificity.explanation: Cites the concrete penalty figure and the precise compliance mechanism she objects to.

specificity.statement: do we really trust that a future Minister, with the stroke of a pen, won’t actually change that to $100,000 or $10,000? That in itself is really concerning.
specificity.explanation: Pinpoints a concrete drafting feature (ministerial discretion over the $100m threshold) as the locus of concern.

specificity.statement: New Zealand is not the first country to run this experiment, and despite the ability to look at other jurisdictions, like Australia and like the United Kingdom, it seems we’d rather be a fast follower than a smart follower.
specificity.explanation: Names comparator jurisdictions but the 'fast vs smart follower' point is a slogan without a concrete alternative design.

specificity.statement: The latest Global Slavery Index estimates that 50 million people globally are trapped in modern slavery, and 8,000 of them are right here in Aotearoa.
specificity.explanation: Cites named source plus precise global and national figures.

specificity.statement: We know that global entities like CRRC, which supplies the very buses and trains that make our cities go around, have been linked to alleged forced labour in international supply chains.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific company and ties it concretely to NZ public transport.

specificity.statement: Unlike the UK or Australian models, this bill introduces real teeth: director liability. This bill goes further by including penalties and liabilities for directors. If you profit from slave labour, the buck stops at the boardroom table.
specificity.explanation: Pinpoints the distinguishing feature (director liability) and contrasts it with overseas models.

specificity.statement: We must confront the inequality that allows $8 billion worth of goods made with forced or child labour to enter our ports every year.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the import problem with a concrete annual figure.

specificity.statement: the 2023 Global Survey Index recognised that there would be approximately 8,000 people living in modern slavery in New Zealand. That’s 8,000 people living on our shores who are living in the most horrific and horrendous conditions that we could imagine.
specificity.explanation: Cites a source and a concrete figure, though the source name is slightly garbled.

specificity.statement: One thing that we have all agreed on is our position against and on migrant exploitation. We’ve followed that really closely when we review Immigration New Zealand and where that’s going and the work that we’re doing around that.
specificity.explanation: Points to concrete committee activity (reviewing Immigration NZ) but without specific findings or measures.

specificity.statement: when I was managing a school bus company, I observed students in some remote communities, and some not so remote communities, who were kept out of school for various reasons, not travelling on the school bus when they should’ve been, who were then being, in some cases, used by their parents to work in spaces, whether they were illegal or not, for no employment.
specificity.explanation: Concrete lived example with a specific setting, though the scale and prevalence are left vague.

specificity.statement: When Kiwis buy products, they should, and they deserve to, know the origin of them.
specificity.explanation: A values statement about consumer transparency with no mechanism, threshold, or measure.

specificity.statement: Xinjiang province, which produces about 20 percent of the world’s cotton consumption. Campaigners allege—the Chinese Government denies it, but campaigners allege and have produced evidence—that there are hundreds of thousands, if not more than a million, people engaged in State-imposed forced labour in Xinjiang province.
specificity.explanation: Concrete location, production share, and population estimates.

specificity.statement: Ken Roth, the former director of Human Rights Watch, is one of the international experts on this, and he was in New Zealand only days ago. He argues that due diligence should be the target, not just disclosure.
specificity.explanation: Names the expert and the precise policy distinction (due diligence vs disclosure) at stake at select committee.

specificity.statement: having sat on the board of a company in Australia that was required by the Australian legislation to report under their version of what will soon be law here in New Zealand. It is a conversation that occurs around that table, of “Have we gone far enough visiting the factory in Vietnam? Do we actually know X, Y, or Z from that part of our supply chain in Europe?”
specificity.explanation: Concrete illustration of the real compliance questions directors face, with named supply-chain locations.

specificity.statement: Every cost that is incurred increases the cost of the supply chain, and ultimately of the products that New Zealanders are buying. There is a way to do this and make it practical and ensure that cost is minimised but the outcome is achieved.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the cost-pass-through concern but offers no concrete figure or mechanism for keeping it 'realistic'.

specificity.statement: The first is the Conduct of Financial Institutions regime, which we brought into place in March 2025. That requires, of course, all financial institutions to operate fairly and transparently towards consumers in the products they offer. Next, we do have the Financial Markets Conduct Amendment Bill, which is before the Finance and Expenditure Committee at the moment.
specificity.explanation: Names specific regimes and bills with a date and the committee handling them, to substantiate that existing instruments cover the issue.

specificity.statement: thankfully we’ve got a greater use of fintechs out there, companies that are bypassing through technology and enabling customers to transfer at next to nothing for international money transfers. We should be encouraging this.
specificity.explanation: Points to fintech competition as the mechanism but names no providers, figures, or cost comparisons.

specificity.statement: We on this side of the House are all about free markets. We’re all about competition. We’re all about price transparency. The Government’s doing its bit. We do not need a piece of legislation like this.
specificity.explanation: The closing rests on slogan-like restatements of free-market values rather than added concrete detail.

civility.statement: I love it when we have “Kumbaya” moments in this House—that’s why I love Treaty settlement days most of all—but we are a debating chamber for good reason. When we debate things and we debate them well and we debate them faithfully, we actually get better law and we get better policy.
civility.explanation: Respects the dissenting ACT party's right to debate and frames disagreement as productive rather than as bad faith.

civility.statement: I think it’s good that we’ve got a thoughtful party that is not yet convinced by this.
civility.explanation: Characterises the lone dissenting party (ACT) as 'thoughtful' rather than attacking them — respectful of an opponent.

civility.statement: I particularly want to thank Laura McClure for her very thoughtful comments.
civility.explanation: Direct, respectful acknowledgement of the opposing speaker's critique despite disagreement.

civility.statement: Good on Greg Fleming and good on Camilla Belich for going around Brooke van Velden, who has been very busy in the area of workplace relations, doing all the wrong things, eroding workplace relations here, there, and everywhere.
civility.explanation: Sweeping personal swipe at van Velden ('doing all the wrong things') with no specific policy substance — character/competence attack rather than engaged critique.

civility.statement: I’m sure the House will look forward to the contributions from the ACT Party as they try to explain themselves out of this little corner.
civility.explanation: Taunting, pre-emptive mockery of ACT rather than engaging the substance of their objections.

civility.statement: Let me be absolutely clear: modern slavery is a moral abomination. The exploitation of human beings has no place here in New Zealand or around the world. There is not a single person in this House who is soft on slavery.
civility.explanation: Explicitly credits all members, including opponents, as opposed to slavery before raising her disagreement.

civility.statement: This bill is a near perfect encapsulation of what Milton Friedman warned us about when he said, “One of the greatest mistakes is to judge policies and programs by their intentions rather than their results.”
civility.explanation: Frames her objection around outcomes and policy quality, not the proponents' character.

civility.statement: Under this bill, a company may not exploit a single human being, it could even be a model employer, but if it misses a paperwork deadline or files a deficient statement, it faces up to $200,000 in fines. This is not a policy brought on a cornerstone of freeing victims; it is built on filling in forms and ticking boxes.
civility.explanation: Pointed but aimed at the bill's design, not the proponents personally.
