specificity.statement: 5,580 more people left the benefit for work... We also saw the number of people receiving jobseeker support decrease by 8,289, alongside the number of working-age people on a main benefit dropping by 17,661 people; more Kiwis off a benefit, in work.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures with the comparison period.

specificity.statement: Our economic plan is to grow the economy by fundamentally tacking the barriers that have held back our productivity and growth for many, many years. In doing that, we will create not only sustainable growth but also more jobs and higher incomes that keep up with the cost of living.
specificity.explanation: Generic 'tackle the barriers' with no mechanism or figures.

specificity.statement: This Government has introduced the most significant reform of conservation legislation in nearly 40 years—40 years—modernising a system that has become too slow; too complex; and frustrating for businesses, iwi, conservation groups, and communities alike... We cannot protect a modern conservation estate with a loosey-goosey, 1980s system wrapped up in red and green tape.
specificity.explanation: States scale ('nearly 40 years') but the diagnosis stays general.

specificity.statement: More than 1,600 businesses already operate on conservation land, contributing an estimated $5.3 billion to our economy each year.
specificity.explanation: Concrete counts and dollar figure.

specificity.statement: Kāore. No. The proposed changes strike an appropriate balance between improved consumer protections for residents and ensuring continued growth, innovation, and consumer choice within the retirement sector.
specificity.explanation: 'Appropriate balance' is somewhat abstract though the trade-off is named.

specificity.statement: In 2024, I set some concession targets, processing targets, and since then, applications have doubled in pace, they're processed twice as fast, and the backlog has been halved.
specificity.explanation: Quantified improvements (doubled, twice as fast, halved).

specificity.statement: Did you know that about 80 percent of the plans, conservation management strategies, everything else, are out of date—10 years out of date.
specificity.explanation: Gives a percentage and a timeframe.

specificity.statement: Yes, we are going to charge foreigners to go on some tracks around the country. That's OK, because, actually, when we go to Hawaii and when we go to the United States and when we go to Australia and other places, we pay to go into the national parks.
specificity.explanation: Concrete on the policy but vague on which sites and amounts ('details, shmetails').

specificity.statement: For those that are accepted, the Government then intends to pass bespoke legislation in 2027 giving effect to those proposals. For the remaining councils, they will fall into a slower backstop pathway. This will take effect following the 2028 local government elections and will replace regional councils.
specificity.explanation: Names years (2027, 2028 elections) and the two-pathway mechanism.

specificity.statement: I am aware of the enormous surge in confidence in our farming community... The broader primary sector, with $60 billion-odd of exports, is going really well, and that is, I think, probably attributed to a suite of Government policies. Particularly, I think I'd look to the Resource Management Act reform.
specificity.explanation: Cites an export figure and names RMA reform.

specificity.statement: Look, our conservation land makes up a third of New Zealand, and it's time for us to manage our conservation estate more efficiently and better... The current Conservation Act is almost 40 years old. It's out of date, and it is time for change.
specificity.explanation: Concrete on scale and age but general on the change itself.

specificity.statement: Te Pāti Māori is appalled to hear of the prospect that iwi will have to relitigate the Crown's commitment to uphold their Treaty settlements. In Ngāi Tahu, 30 years on from commitments which have already been made—they are now being further undermined by this bill.
specificity.explanation: Names the issue and a specific iwi with a timeframe.

specificity.statement: Te Pāti Māori's support for changes to section 4 is conditional on broad support by te iwi Māori on proposed changes made with iwi Māori, while acknowledging the independent voices of whānau, hapū, and iwi, who may take different positions.
specificity.explanation: Defines the condition (broad iwi support, made with iwi) precisely.

divination.statement: The projects are expected to create tens of thousands of jobs and inject billions into the economy. So far, over 8,000 new homes have been approved, about the size of Greymouth.
divination.explanation: Forecasts tens of thousands of jobs and billions injected; optimistic and uncertain over an unspecified timeframe.

divination.statement: Another example, which I know my friend and colleague Matua Jones will be interested in—the Waihī goldmining expansion—could generate $5.2 billion in additional silver and gold exports over 18 years.
divination.explanation: Specific 18-year export forecast; plausible but inherently uncertain over a long horizon.

divination.statement: The member will hopefully have seen the Stats NZ result last week which showed unemployment falling, which is very positive news... But we continue to forecast that, into the future, unemployment will fall, notwithstanding that events in the Middle East are making that a more challenging path.
divination.explanation: Forecasts unemployment will fall over time; plausible but uncertain and hedged on external events.

divination.statement: For those that are accepted, the Government then intends to pass bespoke legislation in 2027 giving effect to those proposals. For the remaining councils, they will fall into a slower backstop pathway. This will take effect following the 2028 local government elections and will replace regional councils.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a legislative timetable and outcome; plausible plan but contingent on future decisions.

veracity.statement: The projects are expected to create tens of thousands of jobs and inject billions into the economy. So far, over 8,000 new homes have been approved, about the size of Greymouth.
veracity.explanation: The 8,000 homes-approved figure is a plausible, checkable fast-track statistic.

veracity.statement: We saw $800 megawatt per hour prices in 2024 thanks to a bunch of bumper stickers and Post-it notes.
veracity.explanation: Spot prices did spike sharply in 2024, but attributing it to slogans is a misleading oversimplification.

veracity.statement: despite it being challenging, in the last year, we saw 84,000 New Zealanders leave welfare into work. That's why I'm confident that what we are doing is working.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable benefit-exit figure; plausible though presented without the inflow context.

veracity.statement: we are unwilling to tolerate the fact that a young person going on to welfare under the age of 25 will stay there for 20 years. That's not good enough.
veracity.explanation: The '20 years' figure is presented as fact but is an extreme projection, not a typical outcome.

veracity.statement: This decision does not change New Zealand's climate targets, nor the approach the Government has set for meeting them. Businesses will continue to be required to meet their obligations under the emissions trading scheme.
veracity.explanation: Plausible characterisation that the statutory bar leaves ETS obligations and targets intact.

veracity.statement: With over 60 percent of the world's emissions coming from China, India, Russia, and the United States, how is the Government's target going?
veracity.explanation: The combined share of those four is roughly in that range; broadly accurate though presented to minimise NZ's role.

veracity.statement: There are more people in work.
veracity.explanation: Employment rising with population growth is plausible; a checkable claim.

veracity.statement: The member will hopefully have seen the Stats NZ result last week which showed unemployment falling, which is very positive news... But we continue to forecast that, into the future, unemployment will fall, notwithstanding that events in the Middle East are making that a more challenging path.
veracity.explanation: Refers to a real recent Stats NZ unemployment result; checkable.

veracity.statement: 5,580 more people left the benefit for work... We also saw the number of people receiving jobseeker support decrease by 8,289, alongside the number of working-age people on a main benefit dropping by 17,661 people; more Kiwis off a benefit, in work.
veracity.explanation: Specific official-style statistics presented as the comparison year; broadly checkable.

veracity.statement: In fact, what our Government did was rescue the Apprenticeship Boost scheme which the last Government left unfunded with a massive fiscal cliff. We rescued that programme, and I am certain that many Māori and Pasifika will have benefitted.
veracity.explanation: The 'left unfunded with a fiscal cliff' characterisation is a partisan claim not substantiated here.

veracity.statement: More than 1,600 businesses already operate on conservation land, contributing an estimated $5.3 billion to our economy each year.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable economic statistic on conservation-land activity.

veracity.statement: In 2024, I set some concession targets, processing targets, and since then, applications have doubled in pace, they're processed twice as fast, and the backlog has been halved.
veracity.explanation: Self-reported performance figures; plausible but not independently sourced here.

veracity.statement: Did you know that about 80 percent of the plans, conservation management strategies, everything else, are out of date—10 years out of date.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable claim about out-of-date DOC plans; plausible but unverified here.

veracity.statement: Very well. I'm pleased to report that the Head Start proposals have been received positively by not only ratepayers and the business community but also the local government sector. Local Government New Zealand welcomed the announcement as a step forward.
veracity.explanation: Cites named endorsements (LGNZ, EMA); selectively positive but the specific quotes are checkable.

veracity.statement: In terms of the Mayors' Taskforce for Jobs, my understanding is that the funding hasn't been cut, but there has been a reallocation of resources to areas in greater need... the member is looking at this through far too narrow a prism; you've got to look at the wider work programme that the Government's doing.
veracity.explanation: 'Funding hasn't been cut, just reallocated' is contested by the example of jobs falling from 30 to 12.

veracity.statement: I am aware of the enormous surge in confidence in our farming community... The broader primary sector, with $60 billion-odd of exports, is going really well, and that is, I think, probably attributed to a suite of Government policies. Particularly, I think I'd look to the Resource Management Act reform.
veracity.explanation: The ~$60 billion primary export figure is roughly accurate; the causal attribution to policy is his inference.

veracity.statement: Look, our conservation land makes up a third of New Zealand, and it's time for us to manage our conservation estate more efficiently and better... The current Conservation Act is almost 40 years old. It's out of date, and it is time for change.
veracity.explanation: DOC manages roughly a third of NZ's land and the Act dates to 1987—both broadly accurate.

strength.statement: The Ashbourne project was approved on 21 April: hundreds of news homes and two solar farms in the Waikato. On 1 May, the Pound Road Industrial Development was approved in Canterbury... Over $450 million is expected to be contributed to the economy. Then, on 7 May, also in Canterbury, the Ryans Road Industrial Development was also approved, enabling the development and subdivision of 126 industrial lots.
strength.explanation: Describes concrete approvals delivered under the fast-track regime he is responsible for, not mere aspiration.

strength.statement: In 2024, I set some concession targets, processing targets, and since then, applications have doubled in pace, they're processed twice as fast, and the backlog has been halved.
strength.explanation: Claims concrete operational delivery against targets he set, not just intention.

rigor.statement: Some applicants have said to me that fast track is driving competition in the consenting system... in some cases, this is leading to more reasonable behaviour by councils, acting in a more proportionate way. Isn't competition a wonderful thing?
rigor.explanation: Relies on anecdotal applicant feedback ('have said to me') rather than evidence; rhetorical flourish at the end.

rigor.statement: We saw $800 megawatt per hour prices in 2024 thanks to a bunch of bumper stickers and Post-it notes.
rigor.explanation: Caricatures opponents' policy instead of arguing causation with evidence.

rigor.statement: I'm ignoring the OECD! OK. It's a lovely report, but we actually have our own view on how we put energy policy together in this country, and we're not going to do the mistake that the Labour-Greens Government did, where you created $800 megawatt power prices and lower-middle income working people lost their jobs.
rigor.explanation: Dismisses the OECD evidence ('a lovely report') without rebuttal and asserts blame as fact.

rigor.statement: Is the Prime Minister comfortable with near-record power company profits and dividends being paid out to shareholders, helping to improve the look of the Government's books, while 65,000 more New Zealanders could not afford to heat their home adequately last winter?
rigor.explanation: Builds a pointed contrast using a specific figure, though framed to indict; a checkable claim underlies it.

rigor.statement: For too long, Government sent the wrong message to farmers that if you do the right thing and invest in preserving or creating wetlands and native bush, you'll be punished with more controls on what you can do on your own land. This initiative flips the script from more regulation to incentives.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a 'wrong message' narrative without evidence, though the policy logic is stated.

rigor.statement: despite it being challenging, in the last year, we saw 84,000 New Zealanders leave welfare into work. That's why I'm confident that what we are doing is working.
rigor.explanation: Cites a gross outflow figure as proof of success without addressing rising jobseeker numbers.

rigor.statement: we are unwilling to tolerate the fact that a young person going on to welfare under the age of 25 will stay there for 20 years. That's not good enough.
rigor.explanation: Uses a '20 years' worst-case to justify policy; rhetorically effective but an unevidenced framing.

rigor.statement: Ongoing litigation in the High Court where civil claims have been made is creating uncertainty in business confidence in investment... Therefore, the Government will amend the Climate Change Response Act 2002 to prevent findings of tort liability for activities that involve the emissions of greenhouse gas and climate change harm.
rigor.explanation: Lays out a premise (litigation uncertainty) to a conclusion (statutory bar), though the link to reduced investment is asserted.

rigor.statement: With over 60 percent of the world's emissions coming from China, India, Russia, and the United States, how is the Government's target going?
rigor.explanation: Implies NZ targets are futile because big emitters dominate—a relevance/whataboutism move rather than reasoned argument.

rigor.statement: Any suggestions that the mandatory repayment time frame be moved to a three-month period go completely against financial responsibility, and it fails to take into account the incentives and the types of business practices that we need to ensure that aged care remains viable.
rigor.explanation: Argues from financial viability of the sector; reasoned but the 'completely against' assertion is strong without evidence.

rigor.statement: Yes, we are going to charge foreigners to go on some tracks around the country. That's OK, because, actually, when we go to Hawaii and when we go to the United States and when we go to Australia and other places, we pay to go into the national parks.
rigor.explanation: Justifies the charge by analogy to overseas parks; reasonable but an appeal to analogy rather than analysis.

rigor.statement: In terms of the Mayors' Taskforce for Jobs, my understanding is that the funding hasn't been cut, but there has been a reallocation of resources to areas in greater need... the member is looking at this through far too narrow a prism; you've got to look at the wider work programme that the Government's doing.
rigor.explanation: Argues 'reallocation not cut' but mostly reframes rather than addressing the Kaikōura-specific reduction cited.

rigor.statement: I am aware of the enormous surge in confidence in our farming community... The broader primary sector, with $60 billion-odd of exports, is going really well, and that is, I think, probably attributed to a suite of Government policies. Particularly, I think I'd look to the Resource Management Act reform.
rigor.explanation: Attributes the confidence surge to Government policy ('probably') without isolating causes.

rigor.statement: Everywhere else in the world, you pay to see the sights, you pay to see the attractions, and you should do the same here in New Zealand so that we can use that money and put it back into improving and protecting our environment and biodiversity.
rigor.explanation: 'Everywhere else in the world' is an overgeneralised appeal to analogy supporting the charging policy.

rigor.statement: In my past life, I was an environmental lawyer, and I did act for a number of clients on trying to get concessions from the Department of Conservation, and it was very difficult... There have been Ministers since back in the day of Eugenie Sage... who have been making that point—that there does need to be a change to this legislation; it needs some work.
rigor.explanation: Argues from first-hand evidence and prior cross-party recognition of the problem.

rigor.statement: But what this bill does is an entire paradigm shift. It's not what we're expecting when we hear speeches from the other side saying, 'Oh, this is just about efficiency and modernisation.' No—this is a paradigm shift.
rigor.explanation: Makes a substantive claim that the bill goes beyond modernisation, though the 'paradigm shift' label is asserted before the detail follows.

rigor.statement: I stand today to raise the alarm on this coalition Government's ram raid of conservation in Aotearoa, on the inheritance of our mokopuna.
rigor.explanation: Opens with charged framing rather than argument, though substantive points follow later.

rigor.statement: Te Pāti Māori is appalled to hear of the prospect that iwi will have to relitigate the Crown's commitment to uphold their Treaty settlements. In Ngāi Tahu, 30 years on from commitments which have already been made—they are now being further undermined by this bill.
rigor.explanation: Concrete concern (relitigating settlements) tied to the Ngāi Tahu example, though 'undermined' is asserted.

rigor.statement: Is the Minister aware of any circumstances in the private housing market where sellers can expect a 10 percent payment within five days and the remainder within three months as a guarantee?
rigor.explanation: A pointed analogy to the housing market to test the three-month repayment demand; persuasive but a friendly framing device.

authenticity.statement: The Minister explained his comments well, and, actually, I'm quite confident that he did not at any time direct RNZ or TVNZ.
authenticity.explanation: Defends a colleague; consistency with prior standards not verifiable from the text.

authenticity.statement: Yes, and the way trust is built is by delivering improved outcomes for Māori.
authenticity.explanation: Reaffirms a commitment to building trust with Māori while his Government weakens Treaty clauses—words in tension with actions raised in the follow-ups.

authenticity.statement: We think there's a problem with generic Treaty principle clauses. We want to create certainty and make sure that everyone is very clear about their specific roles and obligations to each other.
authenticity.explanation: Justifies the legislative change but the words-vs-actions tension with his trust pledge remains unaddressed.

authenticity.statement: In fact, what our Government did was rescue the Apprenticeship Boost scheme which the last Government left unfunded with a massive fiscal cliff. We rescued that programme, and I am certain that many Māori and Pasifika will have benefitted.
authenticity.explanation: Claims credit for rescuing a scheme while the asked-about cut goes unaddressed; the 'fiscal cliff' framing is contestable.

authenticity.statement: I can assure the member that I'm a staunch advocate for the Mayors' Taskforce for Jobs. I have a peripheral involvement with the Clutha District in the Jobbortunities initiative there; I do know that it works.
authenticity.explanation: Professes to be a 'staunch advocate' while accepting funding has been reoriented and saying it isn't his portfolio—words sit in some tension with the described changes.

forthrightness.statement: Questions about the Prime Minister’s views are better addressed to the Prime Minister. My role is to articulate the Government’s position, and that is what I have done.
forthrightness.explanation: Walters asked whether the PM directed or requested the position; Peters reframes to 'my role is to articulate the Government's position', avoiding the direct question.

forthrightness.statement: Because the job I am entrusted with is the Minister of Foreign Affairs of New Zealand, not the professor of international law at Woketown University, we take judicious, prudent decisions based on the national interest rather than offering empty virtue signalling.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to a point of order about whether the PM directed him with rhetoric, not an answer.

forthrightness.statement: The reality is that this is an international matter, and all sorts of advice is being sought and being worked out. A decision will be made in good time.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically whether legal advice was sought on the US/Israel action; gives a vague 'all sorts of advice' without confirming legal advice.

forthrightness.statement: We have a habit of when we make a mistake, we admit it. We don’t think that we’re perfect... In this case, I made an assumption, and I should have had it checked out, and that’s the reason why we’re updating our systems at the moment.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly acknowledges his own mistake and the corrective action, answering the question asked.

forthrightness.statement: That question is totally illogical. It comes to a conclusion without any evidence whatsoever, and so I’m not wasting my time answering it.
forthrightness.explanation: Explicitly refuses to answer Tuiono's question about the legality of the strikes.

forthrightness.statement: The reality was that I was offshore, late at night, and got an enquiry, and we just sent back, in an abbreviated text, how it would possibly look and part of our discussion, and then went straight back to the original decision we made. That’s how we landed on that.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he stands by his office's 'imprudent' description; explains the context but never directly affirms or retracts the description.

forthrightness.statement: The Minister of Foreign Affairs is charged with that responsibility but in consultation with the Prime Minister, obviously; the ministerial contacts, as well; and other MPs, including sometimes crossing the House to make sure that there is a unified view in this country.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers who the final decision-maker is (the Foreign Minister, in consultation).

forthrightness.statement: For the umpteenth time, and I’ll say it slowly... the person in charge of foreign policy is the Foreign Minister. That’s me, not the Prime Minister. Could the member get some updating—I know she had a lot of academic training but obviously no practical understanding of this game whatsoever.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers who is in charge but ignores the specific 'Morning Report too challenging' premise of the question.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I stand by my full statement from November last year, which was, “Our Government is determined that New Zealanders who are seeking work can find it. That’s why we’re so focused on strengthening the foundations from which local businesses can grow and create new jobs...”
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers 'does she stand by' with a clear yes and the full statement.

forthrightness.statement: Because, as I said in my statement, since being elected we have worked hard to fix the damage done to our economy during a period of reckless Government spending, sky-high inflation, and rising interest rates, with inflation having come down significantly and interest rates having reduced as well.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about ~28,000 fewer young people in work; pivots to inflation and interest rates without addressing the youth jobs figure.

forthrightness.statement: Because we still have in place a very workable pay equity regime, which is fully funded.
forthrightness.explanation: Brief direct response on pay equity but sidesteps the claimed 14,600 fewer women in work and the repeal of 23 claims.

forthrightness.statement: In answer to the second part of the question: the number of people leaving New Zealand is actually lower now than it was under the period of the previous Prime Minister, Chris Hipkins.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses only the emigration part of the question, leaving the jobs claim unanswered.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, those alternatives were considered. The member can find advice on the alternatives on the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment’s website.
forthrightness.explanation: Direct yes plus a pointer to where the advice can be found.

forthrightness.statement: The Government is going through a procurement process... but we will not leave this country high and dry without a solution to the dry-winter challenge, which is what the last Government did, leading to all of the challenges we saw in winter 2024.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he sought fresh advice after the Iran strikes/LNG spike; gives process assurance rather than a yes/no on new advice.

forthrightness.statement: This Government is going through a procurement process... and the solution we provide won’t require waiting till 2037, costing $16 billion.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how New Zealanders can have faith he hasn't pre-decided; repeats process talking points without addressing the concern.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, the Government acknowledges the impact of high electricity prices... the lines charge component of household electricity prices increased by 14 percent, while the energy and other component increased by 9 percent... We’ve reversed the previous Government’s ban on oil and gas exploration, which was the single biggest reason that wholesale prices skyrocketed in the first place.
forthrightness.explanation: Acknowledges the issue and gives figures, then sets out actions, though only partly addressing 'energy hardship'.

forthrightness.statement: The decision this Government has made to provide certainty to the electricity sector... whether that is... reverse the previous Government’s ban on oil and gas exploration, having a strategic coal stockpile at Huntly, removing the previous Government’s target of 100 percent renewable by 2030, or getting rid of Lake Onslow... has seen the megawatt wholesale price for electricity reduce under this Government, with the forward price reducing.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked for concrete actions to reduce bills this winter for 200,000 cold households; lists structural decisions rather than this-winter measures.

forthrightness.statement: The best thing the Government can do is to make sure we lower power prices... That means having a market with lower wholesale market prices, and that is what this Government has done.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically about cutting $178 million from energy-efficiency and outreach programmes; never addresses the cut and pivots to wholesale prices.

forthrightness.statement: We’re now seeing inflation down to 3.1 percent, and we’ve seen interest rates reduce so that someone with an average mortgage of $500,000 is $10,000 a year better off.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to justify inaction on energy hardship given wages up 2 percent vs energy bills up 12 percent; answers about inflation and mortgages instead.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I am confident that my health and safety reforms focus on practical, common-sense changes that set businesses up for success in keeping people safe. The advice I received from my officials is that my reforms shift the focus towards managing critical risks and support the continued reduction in the incidence of serious workplace injuries and fatalities, thereby reducing the costs of these incidents for ACC.
forthrightness.explanation: Direct 'yes' and engages the cost-to-ACC premise of the question with her officials' advice.

forthrightness.statement: I listened to small businesses and workers on my roadshows who told me that some health and safety professionals advised them to go to a lot of effort on ineffective paper-based compliance that does not reduce harm.
forthrightness.explanation: Reframes rather than directly engaging whether the experts calling it a 'regression' are correct.

forthrightness.statement: I am not excluding psychosocial risk. If a psychosocial risk is likely to result in a death, notifiable injury, illness, or incident, then it must be managed as a critical risk. An example would be where stress could lead to serious accidents in the workplace.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly rebuts the premise of removal and explains the threshold, though doesn't address the 97 percent / 40 suicides figures specifically.

forthrightness.statement: I’m not responsible for ACC itself, however the scale of ACC costs are not the sole indicator of whether or not the health and safety system is working well... I hear this constantly from the Opposition. It is clearly misleading.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to promise ACC levies will not rise; declines to engage with the levy question, citing it's not her responsibility.

forthrightness.statement: We are focused on putting in place the settings which enable New Zealanders to be able to uptake those vehicles... We’re not into subsidising coal-powered Teslas. We’re into ensuring we have plenty of renewable energy to fund those electric vehicles.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether cutting EV import incentives was working fast enough on climate; deflects to charging infrastructure and a slogan.

forthrightness.statement: We are very proud of the work that we’re doing... around the introduction of a national adaptation framework and, importantly, New Zealand’s first national flood map. This is tangible delivery and action to help New Zealanders who are dealing with the impacts of climate change... that is action over and above words—and that is pretty much all we heard from the last Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about a $6 billion cut to the national resilience plan; answers with what was delivered instead, not the cut.

forthrightness.statement: On this side of the House, surprisingly, we don’t believe that the only way in which we can help New Zealanders is by writing blank cheques and spraying money everywhere and, hopefully, it hits a target. On this side of the House, we apply a little bit of substance, which is called fiscal discipline.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about cuts to nationwide public transport; never addresses the cut, pivoting to fiscal discipline.

forthrightness.statement: I make no apology for this Government backing New Zealand farmers, who are some of the most carbon-efficient farmers on the planet, full stop. This Government is working with farmers, not against them, in order to get certainty and clarity around emissions reduction policy.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about cutting methane targets and the advised $270/year household cost; defends backing farmers without engaging the cost claim.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I can, and as someone who sees a lot of public transport in the city of Auckland, it is much appreciated by citizens of Auckland, in particular, because of the benefits that provides, particularly with the high fuel prices.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly confirms the question (public transport funding increased) with a 'yes, I can'.

forthrightness.statement: I have heard concerns from RTOs about sustainable funding. That’s why I released the Tourism Growth Roadmap, and that’s also why our Government has invested significantly into the regions, including $13 million into Regional Tourism Boost campaigns to attract more visitors, encourage regional dispersal, and drive economic growth.
forthrightness.explanation: Acknowledges RTO funding concerns but doesn't directly accept or reject Tourism NZ's warning of serious impact on domestic tourism.

forthrightness.statement: That member is asserting that regional tourism organisations won’t be as effective as they are today, and I dispute that. I think they do an incredible job of growing domestic tourism.
forthrightness.explanation: Disputes the premise about billions at risk but doesn't engage the 60 percent / $44 billion figures put to her.

forthrightness.statement: This is a very common practice about commencement dates, and it avoids situations where, you know, from time to time you may set a specific date and the bill may not be passed by that specific date. I can think of one particularly relevant example of that that the member might be able to think of as well. So that’s the reason.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers why 'day after Royal assent' was chosen over a fixed calendar date.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I’m very comfortable. The name of the bill is the Regulatory Systems (Transport) Amendment Bill, because it amends parts of the transport and regulatory system.
forthrightness.explanation: Direct, complete answer to whether the title is appropriate.

specificity.statement: New Zealand is not taking part in the conflict and does not intend to. New Zealand supports de-escalation, an end to this conflict, and the restoration of freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.
specificity.explanation: States a concrete NZ position (non-participation, de-escalation, freedom of navigation in a named strait) though without mechanisms or actions.

specificity.statement: From now on, votes, if they are necessary, will be attributed to individual members of the monetary policy committee. The committee has also decided that... any material differences of view or judgments will also be attributed to members in the committee’s record of meetings.
specificity.explanation: Concrete, named procedural changes to MPC transparency.

specificity.statement: The committee’s charter has been amended to ease restrictions on members speaking publicly... committee members who wish to publicly communicate their individual views... are now encouraged to do so.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete amendment to the charter and its effect.

specificity.statement: In February, I commissioned an independent review of the Reserve Bank’s monetary policy response to the COVID-19 pandemic. The review will focus on decisions by the monetary policy committee... I will consider the findings of the review when it is completed later this year.
specificity.explanation: Names the action (commissioned review), timing (February, completing later this year), and scope.

specificity.statement: We do have a plan, and that plan is to ensure that manufacturers face better conditions in which to invest and grow jobs. That includes... making sure the Resource Management Act ties them up in less red tape... the Investment Boost policy... making sure that our energy system actually has firming generation available in a dry year.
specificity.explanation: Names several concrete policy levers (RMA reform, Investment Boost, firming generation) though without figures or timelines.

specificity.statement: How can she claim that, when she slashed funding to the mayor’s task force for jobs and now there are almost 28,000 fewer 15- to 24-year-olds in work compared to two years ago?
specificity.explanation: Cites a named programme cut and a concrete employment figure.

specificity.statement: How can she claim that, when there are 14,600 fewer women in work compared to two years ago, and her Government has repealed pay equity legislation, which undid the work of 23 active claims?
specificity.explanation: Precise numbers plus a named legislative change.

specificity.statement: Whilst solar plays an important role and an increasingly important role, it is particularly important to support inter-day peaks and, with battery, a potentially slightly longer period, but it doesn’t necessarily solve the dry-winter problem... I would point to the member’s solution, being a lake in the middle of the mountains by 2037, not being fast enough.
specificity.explanation: Names mechanisms (inter-day peaks, batteries) and the 2037 timeframe of the alternative.

specificity.statement: This Government is going through a procurement process... and the solution we provide won’t require waiting till 2037, costing $16 billion.
specificity.explanation: Cites the 2037 date and $16 billion cost of the contrasted alternative.

specificity.statement: Earlier this month, our Government announced a nationwide expansion of community infusion services... This includes delivering 14 new infusion centres and expanding a further 14 sites across the country. Around 13,000 additional cancer infusions are expected in 2025‑26—a 12 percent increase compared with prior volumes.
specificity.explanation: Precise counts (14 new + 14 expanded centres, ~13,000 infusions, 12 percent) and timeframe.

specificity.statement: The Government’s $604 million investment into new medicines delivered 33 new cancer treatments... Once fully implemented, the expansion will deliver 218 more chair days of treatment space each week... with each chair typically used by three to five patients per day.
specificity.explanation: Dollar figures, treatment counts, and operational detail (chair days, patients per chair).

specificity.statement: New centres have already been opened in the Bay of Islands, Buller, and Waitakere; services have been expanded in Whangārei, South Auckland, Taupō, Wairoa, Napier, Wanganui, Wellington, Christchurch, and Timaru.
specificity.explanation: Named locations of already-opened centres and expanded services.

specificity.statement: Just this term alone, we have reinstated the faster cancer treatment health target; given a $604 million boost to Pharmac... delivering 33 new cancer treatments; expanded breast screening to women aged 70 to 74... and we acknowledge there is still much more work to be done.
specificity.explanation: An itemised list of named, concrete initiatives with figures and age bands.

specificity.statement: Yes, the Government acknowledges the impact of high electricity prices... the lines charge component of household electricity prices increased by 14 percent, while the energy and other component increased by 9 percent... We’ve reversed the previous Government’s ban on oil and gas exploration, which was the single biggest reason that wholesale prices skyrocketed in the first place.
specificity.explanation: Cites 14 percent and 9 percent component increases and named policy actions.

specificity.statement: Has he sought advice on alternative proposals... such as those proposed by the Sustainable Energy Association, the Smart Energy Alliance... Rewiring Aotearoa, Master Electricians, Consumer New Zealand, and the Bioenergy Association, to meet dry-year risk by rapidly rolling out rooftop solar, moving households off gas, and better managing our hydro lakes instead of committing to expensive LNG?
specificity.explanation: Names numerous specific organisations and concrete alternative measures.

specificity.statement: Yes, I am confident that my health and safety reforms focus on practical, common-sense changes that set businesses up for success in keeping people safe. The advice I received from my officials is that my reforms shift the focus towards managing critical risks and support the continued reduction in the incidence of serious workplace injuries and fatalities, thereby reducing the costs of these incidents for ACC.
specificity.explanation: Describes the direction (critical-risk focus) but without figures or specific provisions.

specificity.statement: I am not excluding psychosocial risk. If a psychosocial risk is likely to result in a death, notifiable injury, illness, or incident, then it must be managed as a critical risk. An example would be where stress could lead to serious accidents in the workplace.
specificity.explanation: Defines the 'critical risk' trigger and gives a concrete example.

specificity.statement: In response to the sustained impact of high fuel prices, we have increased by 50 percent the vehicle mileage reimbursement rates for eligible treatment-related travel... This targeted and temporary increase will remain in place while fuel prices stay elevated and is being kept under continual review with a clear threshold linked to petrol prices returning to more stable levels.
specificity.explanation: Names a precise change (50 percent mileage increase), its purpose, and the threshold/review mechanism.

specificity.statement: A number of veterans spoke to me throughout the day to express their appreciation for the recent changes passed by Parliament unanimously—thank you—in recognising the service of all of those who have served New Zealand... In the words of one gentleman at the Waimoku service... they no longer feel like second-class citizens on Anzac Day.
specificity.explanation: Anchored to a real event and a concrete sentiment, though the legislative change itself is described only generally.

specificity.statement: Our forces are working hard towards becoming an increasingly integrated combat capable Anzac force, integrated by 2035.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete target year (2035) for integration.

specificity.statement: We are very proud of the work that we’re doing... around the introduction of a national adaptation framework and, importantly, New Zealand’s first national flood map. This is tangible delivery and action to help New Zealanders who are dealing with the impacts of climate change... that is action over and above words—and that is pretty much all we heard from the last Government.
specificity.explanation: Names the adaptation framework and 'first national flood map' as concrete outputs.

specificity.statement: Was he working as fast as he could on the climate challenge when his Government cut New Zealand’s methane targets, when his own Cabinet paper advised that this would increase costs for New Zealand households?
specificity.explanation: Points to a specific decision (cutting methane targets) and a named source (his own Cabinet paper).

specificity.statement: This month, we are conducting a major foot-and-mouth disease preparedness exercise in Taranaki: operation “Farm Gate”... New Zealand has never had a case of foot-and-mouth disease, but if we did, it would cost this country around $15 billion in lost exports... and in destroyed herds and flocks.
specificity.explanation: Names the exercise, location, and a concrete $15 billion impact estimate.

specificity.statement: We have the toughest biosecurity border protection in the world. But risk can never be zero... well-established readiness and response plans have helped us to eradicate four separate incursions of fruit fly during this term of Government.
specificity.explanation: Cites the specific count of fruit-fly incursions eradicated.

specificity.statement: The response team has now captured and identified over 4,500 exotic hornets, but none has been found since 2 April, and no nests have been found since late March... The Government has been determined in its intention to eradicate yellow-legged hornets and supported it with an investment of $12 million.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures and dates (4,500 hornets, none since 2 April, $12 million).

specificity.statement: Earlier this week, the Hon Todd McClay... announced the signing of the Indian free-trade agreement (FTA)... giving Kiwi exporters access to 1.4 billion customers... Manufacturing is an industry made up of 23,000 businesses that employ about 250,000 Kiwis. It contributes roughly 8 percent of GDP and accounts for around 60 percent of our exports.
specificity.explanation: Multiple concrete figures (23,000 businesses, 250,000 employees, 8 percent GDP, 60 percent of exports).

specificity.statement: With tariffs eliminated or reduced on 95 percent of New Zealand’s exports, and duty-free access on almost 57 percent of New Zealand exports from day one, more of our value-added goods can reach Indian customers.
specificity.explanation: Precise tariff figures (95 percent reduced, 57 percent duty-free from day one).

specificity.statement: In 2025, New Zealand businesses exported over $80 million worth of iron and steel into India, where tariffs are currently as high as 22 percent. Under this agreement, these tariffs will be phased out over the next 10 years.
specificity.explanation: Dollar value, product, tariff rate, and phase-out timeline all stated.

specificity.statement: I have heard concerns from RTOs about sustainable funding. That’s why I released the Tourism Growth Roadmap, and that’s also why our Government has invested significantly into the regions, including $13 million into Regional Tourism Boost campaigns to attract more visitors, encourage regional dispersal, and drive economic growth.
specificity.explanation: Names the Roadmap and a specific $13 million Regional Tourism Boost investment.

specificity.statement: One of the main concerns that I have with the bill as drafted is that there’s a risk that it’s bypassing local communities in Auckland and over representing Government interests, because the appointees to the Auckland Regional Transport Committee are half from the Government of the day and the Minister, and half, really, from the mayor.
specificity.explanation: Names the body and the concrete half/half appointment structure.

specificity.statement: The Green Party supports the principle of subsidiarity—decisions are made at the lowest level at which they affect people. That means local government, who’s responsible for so much infrastructure.
specificity.explanation: Articulates a clear principle but stops short of specific funding or design proposals here.

civility.statement: On the other side of this House, though, we sometimes wonder who is the Opposition spokesperson of foreign affairs: Helen Clark or Phil Goff? Because in the podcasts and the speeches I’ve heard today, I’m beginning to wonder who’s running the show over there.
civility.explanation: A mocking jab at the opposition's internal coherence rather than engagement with the substance.

civility.statement: Because the job I am entrusted with is the Minister of Foreign Affairs of New Zealand, not the professor of international law at Woketown University, we take judicious, prudent decisions based on the national interest rather than offering empty virtue signalling.
civility.explanation: Sneering 'Woketown University' caricature and 'empty virtue signalling' — dismissive of opponents rather than engaging the question.

civility.statement: We have a habit of when we make a mistake, we admit it. We don’t think that we’re perfect... In this case, I made an assumption, and I should have had it checked out, and that’s the reason why we’re updating our systems at the moment.
civility.explanation: Self-deprecating and constructive, no attack.

civility.statement: That question is totally illogical. It comes to a conclusion without any evidence whatsoever, and so I’m not wasting my time answering it.
civility.explanation: Dismissive of the question, though aimed at the logic rather than the person.

civility.statement: For the umpteenth time, and I’ll say it slowly... the person in charge of foreign policy is the Foreign Minister. That’s me, not the Prime Minister. Could the member get some updating—I know she had a lot of academic training but obviously no practical understanding of this game whatsoever.
civility.explanation: Personal attack disparaging the member's competence ('no practical understanding').

civility.statement: The member may think that job creation comes from a glossy strategy printed by bureaucrats in an office in Wellington; here on this side of the House, with practical experience, we understand that what businesses need is the economic conditions to support job creation.
civility.explanation: Caricatures the opponent's position ('glossy strategy printed by bureaucrats') — a mild strawman.

civility.statement: How can she claim that, when she slashed funding to the mayor’s task force for jobs and now there are almost 28,000 fewer 15- to 24-year-olds in work compared to two years ago?
civility.explanation: Pointed and accusatory ('slashed') but focused on policy and outcomes, not the person.

civility.statement: How can she claim that this Government is “determined that New Zealanders who are seeking work can find it.”, when, actually, the only thing she has grown is the number of people who can’t find work and the number of New Zealanders leaving our country for good?
civility.explanation: Sharp rhetorical framing ('the only thing she has grown') but aimed at record/outcomes.

civility.statement: Whilst solar plays an important role and an increasingly important role, it is particularly important to support inter-day peaks and, with battery, a potentially slightly longer period, but it doesn’t necessarily solve the dry-winter problem... I would point to the member’s solution, being a lake in the middle of the mountains by 2037, not being fast enough.
civility.explanation: Pointed jab at Woods' Onslow proposal but engages its substance (speed).

civility.statement: I would have thought that member would have supported fast track, which is seeing... the biggest wind farm in New Zealand’s history... consented in the South Island... but no, he voted no to that. He’s voting no— to the very solutions that solve the problem he’s making.
civility.explanation: Criticises the member's voting record — legitimate but accusatory ('the problem he's making').

civility.statement: I’m not responsible for ACC itself, however the scale of ACC costs are not the sole indicator of whether or not the health and safety system is working well... I hear this constantly from the Opposition. It is clearly misleading.
civility.explanation: Accuses the Opposition of being 'clearly misleading' — combative but about the argument, not the person.

civility.statement: Was he working as fast as he could on the climate challenge when his Government cut New Zealand’s methane targets, when his own Cabinet paper advised that this would increase costs for New Zealand households?
civility.explanation: Pressing and repetitive but framed around policy decisions and official advice.

civility.statement: We have an insane wish list of hyper-expensive, unfundable highways that the Government wants to pay for, and then, of course, local government has the real heavy lifting and responsibility to deliver public transport, walking, and cycling.
civility.explanation: 'Insane wish list' is hyperbolic, though aimed at the policy/spending, not a person.

civility.statement: You could have Simeon Brown as your transport Minister, and that’s an absolute nightmare, because he’s got some really weird ideas that, frankly, you know—
civility.explanation: Personal characterisation of a named minister as a 'nightmare' with 'weird ideas' rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: It may have been perhaps that, you know, the inability of the Government to progress its legislative agenda has meant that we’ve passed that particular date. If the Government saw this as a priority, it could’ve scheduled this a little bit earlier.
civility.explanation: A pointed dig at the Government's legislative management, but about process rather than personal.

charisma.statement: On the other side of this House, though, we sometimes wonder who is the Opposition spokesperson of foreign affairs: Helen Clark or Phil Goff? Because in the podcasts and the speeches I’ve heard today, I’m beginning to wonder who’s running the show over there.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them ridicule of opponents; rallies his own side rather than building consensus.

charisma.statement: The Minister of Foreign Affairs is charged with that responsibility but in consultation with the Prime Minister, obviously; the ministerial contacts, as well; and other MPs, including sometimes crossing the House to make sure that there is a unified view in this country.
charisma.explanation: Notes crossing the House for a 'unified view' — a consensus-seeking note.

charisma.statement: For the umpteenth time, and I’ll say it slowly... the person in charge of foreign policy is the Foreign Minister. That’s me, not the Prime Minister. Could the member get some updating—I know she had a lot of academic training but obviously no practical understanding of this game whatsoever.
charisma.explanation: Belittling and condescending; alienating rather than persuasive.

charisma.statement: The member may think that job creation comes from a glossy strategy printed by bureaucrats in an office in Wellington; here on this side of the House, with practical experience, we understand that what businesses need is the economic conditions to support job creation.
charisma.explanation: Partisan 'this side of the House' framing that appeals only to her own side.

charisma.statement: I would have thought that member would have supported fast track, which is seeing... the biggest wind farm in New Zealand’s history... consented in the South Island... but no, he voted no to that. He’s voting no— to the very solutions that solve the problem he’s making.
charisma.explanation: Combative challenge rather than an attempt to bring the member along.

charisma.statement: A number of veterans spoke to me throughout the day to express their appreciation for the recent changes passed by Parliament unanimously—thank you—in recognising the service of all of those who have served New Zealand... In the words of one gentleman at the Waimoku service... they no longer feel like second-class citizens on Anzac Day.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the unanimous cross-party support and thanks the House — inclusive and unifying.

charisma.statement: On this side of the House, surprisingly, we don’t believe that the only way in which we can help New Zealanders is by writing blank cheques and spraying money everywhere and, hopefully, it hits a target. On this side of the House, we apply a little bit of substance, which is called fiscal discipline.
charisma.explanation: Mocking, partisan framing rather than persuasion.

charisma.statement: You could have Simeon Brown as your transport Minister, and that’s an absolute nightmare, because he’s got some really weird ideas that, frankly, you know—
charisma.explanation: Crowd-pleasing dig rather than persuasion of the unconvinced.

rigor.statement: If you’re going to have the rule of law, for the rule of law to actually happen, it has to, sooner or later, like on the streets of New Zealand, be enforced.
rigor.explanation: A coherent general principle about enforcement, but leans on analogy and doesn't connect to the specific matter asked about.

rigor.statement: That question is totally illogical. It comes to a conclusion without any evidence whatsoever, and so I’m not wasting my time answering it.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a fair concern (the question assumes its conclusion) but uses it only to dodge.

rigor.statement: We do have a plan, and that plan is to ensure that manufacturers face better conditions in which to invest and grow jobs. That includes... making sure the Resource Management Act ties them up in less red tape... the Investment Boost policy... making sure that our energy system actually has firming generation available in a dry year.
rigor.explanation: Coherent argument that conditions drive investment, but asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: How can she claim that this Government is “determined that New Zealanders who are seeking work can find it.”, when, actually, the only thing she has grown is the number of people who can’t find work and the number of New Zealanders leaving our country for good?
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical 'only thing' overstatement weakens an otherwise outcome-based critique.

rigor.statement: Whilst solar plays an important role and an increasingly important role, it is particularly important to support inter-day peaks and, with battery, a potentially slightly longer period, but it doesn’t necessarily solve the dry-winter problem... I would point to the member’s solution, being a lake in the middle of the mountains by 2037, not being fast enough.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned distinction between solar's role in peaks vs the dry-year problem; evidence asserted not cited.

rigor.statement: I would have thought that member would have supported fast track, which is seeing... the biggest wind farm in New Zealand’s history... consented in the South Island... but no, he voted no to that. He’s voting no— to the very solutions that solve the problem he’s making.
rigor.explanation: Implies the vote is inconsistent with the goal, but treats fast track as the sole 'solution' to the problem.

rigor.statement: Has he sought advice on alternative proposals... such as those proposed by the Sustainable Energy Association, the Smart Energy Alliance... Rewiring Aotearoa, Master Electricians, Consumer New Zealand, and the Bioenergy Association, to meet dry-year risk by rapidly rolling out rooftop solar, moving households off gas, and better managing our hydro lakes instead of committing to expensive LNG?
rigor.explanation: Marshals a list of expert bodies and named mechanisms to support the alternative, though framed as a leading question.

rigor.statement: I listened to small businesses and workers on my roadshows who told me that some health and safety professionals advised them to go to a lot of effort on ineffective paper-based compliance that does not reduce harm.
rigor.explanation: Rests on anecdotes from roadshows rather than the official advice cited against her reforms.

rigor.statement: We are focused on putting in place the settings which enable New Zealanders to be able to uptake those vehicles... We’re not into subsidising coal-powered Teslas. We’re into ensuring we have plenty of renewable energy to fund those electric vehicles.
rigor.explanation: The 'coal-powered Teslas' line is a rhetorical caricature rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: On this side of the House, surprisingly, we don’t believe that the only way in which we can help New Zealanders is by writing blank cheques and spraying money everywhere and, hopefully, it hits a target. On this side of the House, we apply a little bit of substance, which is called fiscal discipline.
rigor.explanation: Sets up a false dichotomy (blank cheques vs discipline) and caricatures the opposing approach.

rigor.statement: This is a very common practice about commencement dates, and it avoids situations where, you know, from time to time you may set a specific date and the bill may not be passed by that specific date. I can think of one particularly relevant example of that that the member might be able to think of as well. So that’s the reason.
rigor.explanation: A sound practical justification — fixed dates risk being missed if passage slips.

rigor.statement: One of the main concerns that I have with the bill as drafted is that there’s a risk that it’s bypassing local communities in Auckland and over representing Government interests, because the appointees to the Auckland Regional Transport Committee are half from the Government of the day and the Minister, and half, really, from the mayor.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a specific structural mechanism (appointment split) and reasons from it to the representation concern.

rigor.statement: The Green Party supports the principle of subsidiarity—decisions are made at the lowest level at which they affect people. That means local government, who’s responsible for so much infrastructure.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in a stated principle (subsidiarity) and applies it consistently to local government.

rigor.statement: We have an insane wish list of hyper-expensive, unfundable highways that the Government wants to pay for, and then, of course, local government has the real heavy lifting and responsibility to deliver public transport, walking, and cycling.
rigor.explanation: Makes a fair structural point about funding imbalance but leans on charged adjectives ('insane', 'unfundable') rather than figures.

rigor.statement: It may have been perhaps that, you know, the inability of the Government to progress its legislative agenda has meant that we’ve passed that particular date. If the Government saw this as a priority, it could’ve scheduled this a little bit earlier.
rigor.explanation: Speculative ('may have been perhaps') inference about why the commencement date slipped.

authenticity.statement: We have a habit of when we make a mistake, we admit it. We don’t think that we’re perfect... In this case, I made an assumption, and I should have had it checked out, and that’s the reason why we’re updating our systems at the moment.
authenticity.explanation: Owns the error rather than deflecting; words match the admission of fault.

authenticity.statement: Just this term alone, we have reinstated the faster cancer treatment health target; given a $604 million boost to Pharmac... delivering 33 new cancer treatments; expanded breast screening to women aged 70 to 74... and we acknowledge there is still much more work to be done.
authenticity.explanation: Tempers the achievements with 'there is still much more work to be done', avoiding overclaim.

strength.statement: From now on, votes, if they are necessary, will be attributed to individual members of the monetary policy committee. The committee has also decided that... any material differences of view or judgments will also be attributed to members in the committee’s record of meetings.
strength.explanation: Describes a decided change being implemented, not merely aspired to.

strength.statement: The committee’s charter has been amended to ease restrictions on members speaking publicly... committee members who wish to publicly communicate their individual views... are now encouraged to do so.
strength.explanation: An enacted change ('has been amended') rather than a promise.

strength.statement: In February, I commissioned an independent review of the Reserve Bank’s monetary policy response to the COVID-19 pandemic. The review will focus on decisions by the monetary policy committee... I will consider the findings of the review when it is completed later this year.
strength.explanation: A concrete action already taken, with follow-through pending the report.

strength.statement: Earlier this month, our Government announced a nationwide expansion of community infusion services... This includes delivering 14 new infusion centres and expanding a further 14 sites across the country. Around 13,000 additional cancer infusions are expected in 2025‑26—a 12 percent increase compared with prior volumes.
strength.explanation: Describes delivery of infrastructure, though 'announced' and 'expected' mean follow-through is partly in progress.

strength.explanation: Points to delivered products (framework, flood map) over rhetoric.

New Zealand has never had a case of foot-and-mouth disease, but if we did, it would cost this country around $15 billion in lost exports... and in destroyed herds and flocks.
strength.explanation: Describes an active readiness exercise underway, building on a signed industry agreement.

The Government has been determined in its intention to eradicate yellow-legged hornets and supported it with an investment of $12 million.
strength.explanation: Reports concrete progress on a funded eradication effort.

That’s why I released the Tourism Growth Roadmap, and that’s also why our Government has invested significantly into the regions, including $13 million into Regional Tourism Boost campaigns to attract more visitors, encourage regional dispersal, and drive economic growth.
strength.explanation: Points to a delivered investment and a released strategy.

veracity.statement: Because we still have in place a very workable pay equity regime, which is fully funded.
veracity.explanation: Characterises the post-repeal regime as 'very workable' and 'fully funded' against a question asserting legislation was repealed undoing 23 claims — contestable and arguably minimising.

veracity.statement: In answer to the second part of the question: the number of people leaving New Zealand is actually lower now than it was under the period of the previous Prime Minister, Chris Hipkins.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable comparative claim about net migration/departures; plausible but depends on the period and metric chosen.

veracity.statement: How can she claim that, when she slashed funding to the mayor’s task force for jobs and now there are almost 28,000 fewer 15- to 24-year-olds in work compared to two years ago?
veracity.explanation: Specific statistical claim (~28,000 fewer young workers vs two years ago); plausible directionally but unverified here.

veracity.statement: How can she claim that, when there are 14,600 fewer women in work compared to two years ago, and her Government has repealed pay equity legislation, which undid the work of 23 active claims?
veracity.explanation: Specific figures (14,600 fewer women in work; 23 active claims) — checkable, plausible but unverified here.

veracity.statement: The Government is going through a procurement process... but we will not leave this country high and dry without a solution to the dry-winter challenge, which is what the last Government did, leading to all of the challenges we saw in winter 2024.
veracity.explanation: Attributes 'winter 2024' challenges to the previous Government — a contestable causal claim.

veracity.statement: Earlier this month, our Government announced a nationwide expansion of community infusion services... This includes delivering 14 new infusion centres and expanding a further 14 sites across the country. Around 13,000 additional cancer infusions are expected in 2025‑26—a 12 percent increase compared with prior volumes.
veracity.explanation: Concrete, checkable figures presented as fact; plausible from a ministerial announcement.

We’ve reversed the previous Government’s ban on oil and gas exploration, which was the single biggest reason that wholesale prices skyrocketed in the first place.
veracity.explanation: 'Single biggest reason that wholesale prices skyrocketed' for the gas ban is a strong, contested causal attribution.

veracity.statement: The decision this Government has made to provide certainty to the electricity sector... whether that is... reverse the previous Government’s ban on oil and gas exploration, having a strategic coal stockpile at Huntly, removing the previous Government’s target of 100 percent renewable by 2030, or getting rid of Lake Onslow... has seen the megawatt wholesale price for electricity reduce under this Government, with the forward price reducing.
veracity.explanation: Claims wholesale and forward prices are reducing — directionally checkable, attribution to these decisions is contestable.
